Sharp dimensional analysis of midpoint methods for Langevin sampling

Fan Chen ††thanks: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Email: fanchen@mit.edu.    Sinho Chewi ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, Yale University. Email: sinho.chewi@yale.edu.    Jianfeng Lu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Duke University. Email: jianfeng@math.duke.edu.    Matthew S. Zhang ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Email: shuns436@mit.edu.
September 2026
Abstract

We study deterministic and randomized midpoint discretizations of Langevin dynamics for a target π∝e−V\pi\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V}, where 0≺α​I⪯∇2V⪯β​I0\prec\alpha I\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\beta I and κ≔β/α\kappa\coloneqq\beta/\alpha. To achieve α​W2⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}\leqslant\varepsilon, we show that deterministic Heun uses at most O~(κ4/3d1/3ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}) gradient queries, and underdamped exponential midpoint uses O~(κ5/4d1/4ε−1/2)\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{5/4}d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-1/2}). The proofs exploit cancellation at stationarity and smoothing using techniques from Malliavin calculus, outperforming previous upper bounds based on standard couplings. At bounded condition number, a lower bound matches the dd and ε\varepsilon powers of both deterministic methods. To contrast, for the randomized midpoint methods and Poisson midpoint with at least two grid points (both overdamped and underdamped variants), a simple Gaussian calculation yields a lower bound d1/3ε−1/3d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3} to get an ε\varepsilon-close sample despite starting at a benign initialization. This shows surprisingly that in high dimensions, deterministic discretizations can outperform their random counterparts.

1 Introduction

We study sampling from π⁡(d​x)∝e−V⁡(x)​d​x\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, where V∈C2​(ℝd)V\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies

0≺α​Id⪯∇2V​(x)⪯β​Id,x∈ℝd.0\prec\alpha I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V(x)\preceq\beta I_{d}\,,\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,. (1.1)

Write κ≔β/α\kappa\coloneqq\beta/\alpha. No bounds on third or higher derivatives of VV are assumed. We count gradient evaluations needed to produce a distribution μ\mu with

α​W2​(μ,π)⩽ε,\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\mu,\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon\,, (1.2)

where W2W_{2} is the 22-Wasserstein distance.

A basic approach is to discretize overdamped or underdamped Langevin dynamics. Euler methods evaluate the gradient at the initial point of each step; midpoint methods correct this Euler prediction with additional gradient evaluations to improve accuracy. In this work we compare deterministic quadrature11 1 Deterministic refers only to quadrature times; the Brownian increments remain random.—Heun and underdamped exponential midpoint—with both randomized midpoint (RLMC and RULMC) [48, 28, 55, 1] and Poisson midpoint (PLMC and PULMC) [33, 50].

At bounded condition number, prior analyses suggested the following hierarchy of performance. The best known complexity of overdamped Euler, known as Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC), in our setting was for a long time O~​(d​ε−2)\widetilde{O}(d\varepsilon^{-2}) [21], and deterministic midpoint quadrature seemed to offer no improvement under (1.1). Randomization improved the guarantee to O~​(d1/2​ε−1)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1}) [28], while introducing momentum (i.e., discretizing underdamped Langevin dynamics) improved both: to O~​(d1/2​ε−1)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1}) for deterministic exponential Euler [14], and O~(d1/3ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}) for randomized midpoint [48]. This gave rise to the intuition that randomization and momentum each bring an advantage, reducing the exponent of d​ε−2d\varepsilon^{-2} from 11 to 1/21/2, and then to 1/31/3 when combined.

Two recent results challenged this picture. Pedrotti and Whalley [44] show that LMC already matches the classical randomized overdamped guarantee. The recently proposed Poisson midpoint method [50] obtained accuracy rates ε−1/3\varepsilon^{-1/3} exceeding the conjectured exponent above. These results reveal cancellations missed by conventional bounds and reopen the question of comparison between deterministic and randomized quadrature. In response to this, we investigate the convergence properties of several classes of midpoint methods in the present work.

1.1 Our results and their implications

Key takeaways. At bounded condition number, our results give three conclusions.

  1. (i)

    Improved complexity estimates for midpoint schemes. Heun achieves O~(d1/3ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}), and underdamped exponential midpoint achieves O~(d1/4ε−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-1/2}), using two gradient evaluations per step. This is incredibly surprising — until the recent work of [11], the d1/4d^{1/4} rate would have been state-of-the-art. The underdamped rate also completely bypasses the complexity required for path approximation in [8], and shows that the former does not constrain distributional approximation.

  2. (ii)

    Deterministic can beat randomized. This is perhaps the most shocking result in the context of current literature. The d1/3d^{1/3} and d1/4d^{1/4} deterministic rates both improve on the classical randomized midpoint guarantees; at fixed accuracy, the underdamped deterministic rate even beats the d1/3d^{1/3} lower bound for every randomized method studied here.

  3. (iii)

    Lower bounds make the separations sharp. We give lower bounds for every method in Table 1. They match the deterministic dimension and accuracy powers, establish a common d1/3d^{1/3} obstruction for all randomized discretizations, and match PULMC’s leading rate in its regime of sufficiently small ε\varepsilon. These are concrete limits of the methods, rather than just differences between available analyses; they are stated more precisely below.

The following summarizes our upper bounds; see Theorems 3.1 and 4.1.

Theorem 1.1 (Deterministic midpoint guarantees, informal).

Assume (1.1) and 0<ε⩽d/20<\varepsilon\leqslant\sqrt{d}/2. Then, Heun initialized at the minimizer x⋆x_{\star} attains (1.2) with

O~(κ4/3d1/3ε−2/3){\widetilde{O}\bigl(\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}\bigr)}

gradient queries. Underdamped exponential midpoint with friction 2​β2\sqrt{\beta}, initialized with X0=x⋆X_{0}=x_{\star} and independent P0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}), attains the same position accuracy with

O~(κ5/4d1/4ε−1/2){\widetilde{O}\bigl(\kappa^{5/4}d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\bigr)}

gradient queries. Here O~\widetilde{O} suppresses logarithmic factors.

Theorem 1.2 (Stationary bias and iteration lower bounds, informal).

For each method in Table 1, and every sufficiently small normalized step hh, there exist a strongly convex, smooth target with bounded condition number and an initial distribution satisfying

𝔼⁡[V⁡(X0)−V⁡(x⋆)]⩽C​d,x⋆≔arg​min⁡V,\mathbb{E}[V(X_{0})-V(x_{\star})]\leqslant Cd\,,\qquad x_{\star}\coloneqq\argmin V\,,

such that for every sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, achieving α​W2​(νN,π)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\nu_{N},\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon requires at least the query complexity in Table 1’s lower bound column, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here νN\nu_{N} is the position distribution after NN steps. In the underdamped case, this initial distribution is on X0X_{0} (with P0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) independent of X0X_{0}).

The stationary bounds are stated in Propositions 5.1, 5.3, 6.1 and 6.2. The finite iteration bounds and their initialization conditions are in Corollary 6.3; Theorem 5.2 additionally quantifies the condition number dependence for Heun.

Deterministic upper bounds.

The proofs uncover higher-order, distributional cancellations at stationarity which had been missed in previous coupling analyses. A discrete Poisson corrector [44] combined with Malliavin–Stein and Gaussian smoothing estimates [43] are the main techniques for analyzing overdamped Heun. For exponential midpoint, weighted divergence estimates in H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1} reveal cancellation in the conditional mean, and a transport interpolation controls the full local error, extending [10] to a non-Gaussian base measure. See Appendices A and B.

Randomized algorithm bounds.

Substituting ϵ=ε/d\epsilon=\varepsilon/\sqrt{d} in the tolerance ϵ​d/α\epsilon\sqrt{d/\alpha} of [50, Corollaries 1–2] gives PLMC’s O~(d2/3ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(d^{2/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}) upper bound and, for each fixed integer p⩾3p\geqslant 3, the PULMC upper bound

O~p(d1/3ε−1/3+d3​p+28​p+6ε−p+24​p+3).\widetilde{O}_{p}\bigl(d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3}+d^{\frac{3p+2}{8p+6}}\varepsilon^{-\frac{p+2}{4p+3}}\bigr)\,.

For any fixed p>3p>3, sufficiently small accuracy ε⩽d−p/(2(p−3))\varepsilon\leqslant d^{-p/(2\,(p-3))} makes the first term dominate, up to logarithms. This d1/3ε−1/3d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3} scale matches our lower bound. The PLMC bound has no such parameter, and does not match the lower bound. With respect to upper bounds, PULMC retains an accuracy advantage over deterministic exponential midpoint, while the latter wins in dimension: neither upper bound dominates for all (d,ε)(d,\varepsilon), whereas both RLMC and RULMC have uncompetitive upper bounds. We leave proofs of improved upper bounds, where they are currently loose, as a question for future work.

Lower bounds and sharpness.

The deterministic lower bounds match the dimension and accuracy powers of Theorem 1.1 at bounded condition number. Heun requires an oscillatory target, whereas a Gaussian target already gives the matching exponential midpoint bound. An anisotropic Gaussian extends the deterministic exponential midpoint lower bound to the case where κ≫1\kappa\gg 1; see Proposition 5.3. For Heun, coupling the oscillatory coordinates to a weakly confined coordinate also gives

N≳κd1/3ε−2/3log(1/ε),d−1⩽ε⩽ε0,N\gtrsim\kappa d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}\log(1/\varepsilon)\,,\qquad d^{-1}\leqslant\varepsilon\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}\,,

under the initialization condition in Theorem 5.2. The condition number dependence is not fully matched by the corresponding upper bound.

For the randomized methods, isotropic Gaussian targets reveal a different obstruction. Conditional on past quadrature choices, all coordinates have the same random variance. Its fluctuations make their squared magnitudes vary together, creating an error in the distribution of ∥X∥\lVert X\rVert that cannot be detected by inspecting one coordinate alone. This shared fluctuation explains the common dimension obstruction for overdamped and underdamped randomized methods; see Section 6.

Finally, other approaches can provide better complexity guarantees in this setting, including Metropolization [16, 2], the proximal sampler [34, 12], first-order rejection sampling (FORS) [9, 11], and discretizations of Hamiltonian dynamics [10]. We limit the present study to the midpoint discretizations described above.

1.2 Related work

Euler discretizations.

Early non-asymptotic analyses of overdamped Euler (LMC) appeared in [20]. W2W_{2} guarantees were developed in [21, 23] and sharpened in [18]. At bounded condition number, the classical guarantee under (1.1) was O~​(d​ε−2)\widetilde{O}(d\varepsilon^{-2}). The analysis extended to KL divergence in [13, 22], and to targets satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality in [53]. Rényi guarantees followed in [26, 24], with extensions under a Poincaré inequality and intermediate functional inequalities in [15]. Underdamped exponential Euler followed a similar trajectory: W2W_{2} analysis in [14], refined in [19]; KL analysis in [37]; and Rényi guarantees in [26, 2], with weaker smoothness and functional inequality assumptions treated in [57]. Its classical Wasserstein guarantee at bounded condition number is O~​(d1/2​ε−1)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1}), improving on the older overdamped rate. See [17, Chapters 4–5] for a survey. The recent work of Pedrotti and Whalley [44] revises the overdamped baseline significantly: they show that LMC attains O~​(κ​d​ε−1)\widetilde{O}(\kappa\sqrt{d}\,\varepsilon^{-1}) under (1.1), without changing the algorithm. In their work, a discrete Poisson corrector removes the leading conditional discretization error, revealing cancellations missed by standard pathwise estimates.

Deterministic midpoint methods.

Just as with ODE integrators, more accurate quadrature provides a natural improvement to Euler. Classical weak and invariant distribution error expansions explain its advantage under additional smoothness [52, 38]. Runge–Kutta and midpoint splitting schemes were analyzed in [35, 46, 42]. Anticipating Girsanov theory [7, 41] provides another route to KL and Rényi analysis of midpoint interpolations, as developed in [59]. Under additional Hessian regularity, that work obtains a d1/4ε−1/2d^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-1/2} guarantee for a deterministic underdamped double midpoint variant. Under only (1.1), however, the standard estimates did not establish an advantage for deterministic midpoint rules over Euler.

Randomized midpoint.

Shen and Lee [48] evaluate the predicted path at a uniformly random time. Conditional on that path, this gives an unbiased estimate of its force integral. Separating bias from centered fluctuations yields the classical guarantees O~​(d1/2​ε−1)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1}) for RLMC and O~(d1/3ε−2/3)\widetilde{O}(d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}) for RULMC [48, 28, 55]. These improvements suggested that randomization was essential without higher derivative bounds. Cao, Lu, and Wang [8] reinforced this intuition by proving optimality for strong approximation: no algorithm in their oracle model improves the worst case error dN−3/2\sqrt{d}\,N^{-3/2} in approximating a prescribed diffusion path. This leaves open whether the same rate limits sampling from the target distribution. Further work on these algorithms studied invariant bias and asymptotic behavior [28], sharpened Wasserstein bounds [55], and extended the analysis to KL divergence through shifted composition [3, 1].

Poisson midpoint.

Kandasamy and Nagaraj [33] use a different randomization: on a fine grid, each gradient correction is independently retained with probability equal to the reciprocal of the grid size. Only a constant number of gradients is queried in expectation, and their analysis controls distributional error through Gaussian perturbations. Srinivasan and Nagaraj [50] then exploit higher order centering and Gaussian smoothing to obtain accuracy dependence ε−2/3\varepsilon^{-2/3} for PLMC and ε−1/3\varepsilon^{-1/3} for PULMC. The latter goes beyond the apparent strong approximation barrier, though the dimension dependence is more intricate; the full bounds and their moment parameter pp are discussed in Section 1.1. Together with the revised Euler analysis, these results motivate a comparison based directly on sampling error rather than pathwise error.

Related settings and discretizations.

In diffusion models, [58] analyzes randomized midpoint for the reverse-time SDE and obtains sublinear dimension dependence for DDPM sampling. Related midpoint and leapfrog splittings also appear in HMC [6], including the construction of algorithmic warm starts in [56]. Random ODE approximations provide a further family of methods, including the shifted ODE method and its numerical implementations [25, 47].

AI usage.

This research project was initially motivated by the desire to understand the optimal complexity bounds for (Poisson) randomized midpoint discretizations. GPT-5.6 Sol produced both upper and lower bounds for these methods, which did not fully match; the lower bounds are included in this work. In an effort to produce algorithms matching the lower bounds, we gradually realized that deterministic midpoint methods were better candidates, and that their complexity bounds surprisingly surpassed the randomized midpoint lower bounds. At this point, we switched the focus of the project to pinning down the optimal rates for deterministic midpoint methods. GPT-5.6 Sol proved the main theorems in this paper and organized the initial draft. We then edited and simplified the proofs and prepared the manuscript. We take full responsibility for its contents.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notation and normalization

We assume (1.1) throughout and write x⋆x_{\star} for the unique minimizer of VV. For probability measures with finite second moments,

W22​(μ,ν)≔infΓ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)∫∥x−y∥2​Γ​(𝑑x,𝑑y),W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\nu)\coloneqq\inf_{\Gamma\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\lVert x-y\rVert^{2}\,\Gamma(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}y)\,,

where Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) is the set of their couplings. We denote this space of measures by 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. We write KL⁡(μ∥ν)≔∫log⁡(𝑑μ/𝑑ν)​𝑑μ\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mathrel{\|}\nu)\coloneqq\int\log(\mathrm{d}\mu/\mathrm{d}\nu)\,\mathrm{d}\mu when μ≪ν\mu\ll\nu, and +∞+\infty otherwise. For a Markov kernel KK, μ​K\mu K is the distribution after applying one update to a point drawn from μ\mu. For an integrable function ff, write μ⁡(f)≔∫f​𝑑μ\mu(f)\coloneqq\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu. Vector norms are Euclidean; ∥⋅∥p\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p} denotes a probabilistic LpL^{p} norm when the underlying distribution is specified. Matrix norms carry an operator, Hilbert–Schmidt, or Schatten subscript. We use A≲BA\lesssim B for A⩽C​BA\leqslant CB with a universal constant, and ≳\gtrsim and ≍\asymp analogously. The constants c,C>0c,C>0 may change between displays. The notation O~\widetilde{O} hides fixed powers of logarithms in d,κ,ε−1d,\kappa,\varepsilon^{-1}.

The algorithms and main theorems are stated in the original units. For the upper bound proofs we normalize β=1\beta=1, so that α=κ−1\alpha=\kappa^{-1}. Indeed, replacing xx by β​x\sqrt{\beta}\,x and time by β​t\beta t for overdamped dynamics, or by β​t\sqrt{\beta}\,t for underdamped dynamics, preserves the form of the algorithms. Momentum is unchanged in the latter rescaling. The normalized steps are therefore β​h\beta h and β​h\sqrt{\beta}\,h, respectively. The proofs use hh for the normalized step; the scaled distance α​W2\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2} is unchanged. This convention applies to the proof outlines and upper bound appendices unless original units are explicitly stated. We fix a sufficiently small universal h0∈(0,1/3]h_{0}\in(0,1/3] for short-time estimates; stronger restrictions are stated where needed.

2.2 Overdamped dynamics and algorithms

The overdamped Langevin diffusion is

d​Xt=−∇V​(Xt)​d​t+2​d​Bt.\mathrm{d}X_{t}=-\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}\,. (2.1)

Here, BB is standard Brownian motion in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Its generator is L≔Δ−∇V⋅∇L\coloneqq\Delta-\nabla V\cdot\nabla, and Ph≔eh​LP_{h}\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{hL} denotes its transition kernel over time hh. The target π\pi is reversible for PhP_{h}.

Given the current position xx, first predict the path by keeping the gradient equal to ∇V​(x)\nabla V(x):

Xtpred≔x−t∇V(x)+2Bt,0⩽t⩽h.X_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}\coloneqq x-t\,\nabla V(x)+\sqrt{2}\,B_{t}\,,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant h\,.

All methods below reuse this predictor and the same Brownian path within a step. Across steps, Brownian paths and all additional random variables are independent.

Deterministic Heun.

The Heun method [30] predicts the endpoint,

Xhpred≔x−h∇V(x)+2Bh,X_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}}\coloneqq x-h\,\nabla V(x)+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,, (2.2)

and averages the initial and predicted gradients:

X+≔x−h2​{∇V​(x)+∇V​(Xhpred)}+2​Bh.X^{+}\coloneqq x-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(x)+\nabla V(X_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}})\}+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,. (2.3)

We denote its kernel by KhHeunK_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}. It uses two gradient queries per step. Here, deterministic refers to the quadrature times; the Brownian increment remains random.

Randomized midpoint (RLMC).

Draw Θ∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿⁡[0,1]\Theta\sim\mathsf{Unif}[0,1], independently of BB, and set

X+≔x−h∇V(XΘ​hpred)+2Bh.X^{+}\coloneqq x-h\,\nabla V(X_{\Theta h}^{\mathrm{pred}})+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,. (2.4)

This is the randomized midpoint update of [48, 28] (see also [17, Section 5.1]); its kernel is KhRLMCK_{h}^{\mathrm{RLMC}}. It uses one gradient at xx to form the predictor and one at the predicted point. The scalar Θ\Theta is common to all coordinates.

Poisson midpoint (PLMC).

Fix k⩾1k\geqslant 1, put si≔i/ks_{i}\coloneqq i/k, and draw independent indicators 𝖡i∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(1/k)\mathsf{B}_{i}\sim\mathsf{Bernoulli}(1/k) for i∈{1,…,k−1}i\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\}, independently of BB. One step of length hh, also called a batch, is

X+≔x−h∇V(x)+h∑i=1k−1𝖡i{∇V(x)−∇V(Xsi​hpred)}+2Bh.X^{+}\coloneqq x-h\,\nabla V(x)+h\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathsf{B}_{i}\,\{\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(X_{s_{i}h}^{\mathrm{pred}})\}+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,. (2.5)

The correction at time zero would vanish and is omitted. Reusing the initial gradient, the expected query count is 1+(k−1)/k=2−1/k1+(k-1)/k=2-1/k. For k=1k=1, the sum is empty and the update is the Euler-Maruyama scheme, known as unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA). We write KhPLMC,kK_{h}^{\mathrm{PLMC},k} for this kernel [33, 50].

2.3 Underdamped dynamics and algorithms

The underdamped Langevin diffusion evolves a position and a momentum:

d​Xt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{t} =Pt​d​t,\displaystyle=P_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t\,,
d​Pt\displaystyle\mathrm{d}P_{t} =−∇V​(Xt)​d​t−γ​Pt​d​t+2​γ​d​Bt.\displaystyle=-\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-\gamma P_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}B_{t}\,.

Its invariant distribution is

𝝅⁡(d​x,d​p)≔π⁡(d​x)​𝖭​(0,Id)​(d​p).\bm{\pi}(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}p)\coloneqq\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})(\mathrm{d}p)\,.

For a distribution μ\mu on phase space, μx\mu_{x} denotes the position marginal; the required accuracy is α​W2​(μx,π)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\mu_{x},\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon.

Remark 2.1 (Friction).

We choose γ=2​β\gamma=2\sqrt{\beta}, following the synchronous coupling analysis of underdamped Langevin in [17, Theorem 5.3.6]. This choice permits contraction in a fixed norm combining position and momentum. It becomes γ=2\gamma=2 under the normalization in Section 2.1. Our results do not address discretizations with smaller friction.

Integrating the friction term exactly gives

Xt\displaystyle X_{t} =x+atp−∫0tat−s∇V(Xs)ds+2​γ∫0tat−sdBs,\displaystyle=x+a_{t}p-\int_{0}^{t}a_{t-s}\nabla V(X_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{t}a_{t-s}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,,
Pt\displaystyle P_{t} =e−γ​tp−∫0te−γ⁡(t−s)∇V(Xs)ds+2​γ∫0te−γ⁡(t−s)dBs,\displaystyle=\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma t}p-\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(t-s)}\nabla V(X_{s})\,\mathrm{d}s+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(t-s)}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,,

where

at≔1−e−γ​tγ,ct≔∫0tas​𝑑s=t−atγ.a_{t}\coloneqq\frac{1-\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma}\,,\qquad c_{t}\coloneqq\int_{0}^{t}a_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s=\frac{t-a_{t}}{\gamma}\,.

Evaluating the gradient at the initial point xx in the position formula gives the predictor

Xtpred≔x+atp−ct∇V(x)+2​γ∫0tat−sdBs,0⩽t⩽h.X_{t}^{\mathrm{pred}}\coloneqq x+a_{t}p-c_{t}\nabla V(x)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{t}a_{t-s}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant h\,. (2.6)

This is the position component of the usual ULMC update, evaluated at an intermediate time; see [17, Section 5.3.2]. All stochastic integrals within a step use the same Brownian path. Conditional on the evaluation times they are jointly Gaussian, so the algorithms require only finitely many Gaussian draws with the appropriate covariance, rather than an entire Brownian path.

Exponential midpoint (ExpMid).

Predict the position at time h/2h/2 using (2.6), and approximate each gradient integral using the gradient evaluated at this predicted midpoint:

X^hExpMid\displaystyle\widehat{X}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} ≔x+ahp−hah/2∇V(Xh/2pred)+2​γ∫0hah−sdBs,\displaystyle\coloneqq x+a_{h}p-ha_{h/2}\nabla V(X_{h/2}^{\mathrm{pred}})+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}a_{h-s}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,, (2.7)
P^hExpMid\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} ≔e−γ​hp−he−γh/2∇V(Xh/2pred)+2​γ∫0he−γ⁡(h−s)dBs.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma h}p-h\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma h/2}\nabla V(X_{h/2}^{\mathrm{pred}})+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(h-s)}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,. (2.8)

These formulas define the exponential midpoint method studied here, with kernel KhExpMidK_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}}. Each step uses two gradient queries. We write (X^n,P^n)(\widehat{X}_{n},\widehat{P}_{n}) for its iterates.

Randomized midpoint (RULMC).

The usual underdamped randomized midpoint method draws a common Θ∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿⁡[0,1]\Theta\sim\mathsf{Unif}[0,1], independently of BB, and sets

X^hRULMC\displaystyle\widehat{X}_{h}^{\mathrm{RULMC}} ≔x+ahp−ha(1−Θ)​h∇V(XΘ​hpred)+2​γ∫0hah−sdBs,\displaystyle\coloneqq x+a_{h}p-ha_{(1-\Theta)h}\nabla V(X_{\Theta h}^{\mathrm{pred}})+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}a_{h-s}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,,
P^hRULMC\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{h}^{\mathrm{RULMC}} ≔e−γ​hp−he−γ⁡(1−Θ)​h∇V(XΘ​hpred)+2​γ∫0he−γ⁡(h−s)dBs.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma h}p-h\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(1-\Theta)h}\nabla V(X_{\Theta h}^{\mathrm{pred}})+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(h-s)}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,.

This is Algorithm 1 of Shen and Lee [48], expressed in the underdamped convention above. Its kernel is KhRULMCK_{h}^{\mathrm{RULMC}}.

Poisson midpoint (PULMC).

Fix k⩾1k\geqslant 1, let Δ≔h/k\Delta\coloneqq h/k and ti≔i​Δt_{i}\coloneqq i\Delta, and draw independent 𝖡i∼𝖡𝖾𝗋𝗇𝗈𝗎𝗅𝗅𝗂⁡(1/k)\mathsf{B}_{i}\sim\mathsf{Bernoulli}(1/k) for i∈{1,…,k−1}i\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\}, independently of BB. For i∈{0,…,k−1}i\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}, define

ωix\displaystyle\omega_{i}^{x} ≔∫titi+1ah−s​𝑑s=ch−ti−ch−ti+1,ωip≔∫titi+1e−γ⁡(h−s)​𝑑s=ah−ti−ah−ti+1.\displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i+1}}a_{h-s}\,\mathrm{d}s=c_{h-t_{i}}-c_{h-t_{i+1}}\,,\qquad\omega_{i}^{p}\coloneqq\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i+1}}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(h-s)}\,\mathrm{d}s=a_{h-t_{i}}-a_{h-t_{i+1}}\,.

The update is

X^hPULMC,k\displaystyle\widehat{X}_{h}^{\mathrm{PULMC},k} ≔x+ahp−ch∇V(x)\displaystyle\coloneqq x+a_{h}p-c_{h}\nabla V(x)
−k∑i=1k−1𝖡iωix{∇V(Xtipred)−∇V(x)}+2​γ∫0hah−sdBs,\displaystyle\quad-k\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathsf{B}_{i}\omega_{i}^{x}\,\{\nabla V(X_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{pred}})-\nabla V(x)\}+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}a_{h-s}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,, (2.9)
P^hPULMC,k\displaystyle\widehat{P}_{h}^{\mathrm{PULMC},k} ≔e−γ​hp−ah∇V(x)\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma h}p-a_{h}\nabla V(x)
−k∑i=1k−1𝖡iωip{∇V(Xtipred)−∇V(x)}+2​γ∫0he−γ⁡(h−s)dBs.\displaystyle\quad-k\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathsf{B}_{i}\omega_{i}^{p}\,\{\nabla V(X_{t_{i}}^{\mathrm{pred}})-\nabla V(x)\}+\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma(h-s)}\,\mathrm{d}B_{s}\,. (2.10)

We write KhPULMC,kK_{h}^{\mathrm{PULMC},k} for the kernel, using the finite grid formulation of [50]. As in PLMC, the time zero correction vanishes, and a batch has expected query count 2−1/k2-1/k. For k=1k=1 this is the ordinary ULMC update, with the gradient evaluated at the initial point.

3 Overdamped upper bound

The deterministic Heun method achieves a squared stationary error of order h3h^{3} under strong convexity and a Lipschitz gradient, without a bound on third derivatives. The step threshold h0h_{0} and the normalization used in the proof are fixed in Section 2.1.

Theorem 3.1 (Heun upper bound).

There are universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that, if 0<β​h⩽h00<\beta h\leqslant h_{0}, then KhHeunK_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}} has a unique invariant distribution π^hHeun\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}} and

α​W22​(π^hHeun,π)⩽C​κ​d​(β​h)3.\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\pi)\leqslant C\kappa d\,(\beta h)^{3}\,. (3.1)

For every μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and integer N⩾0N\geqslant 0,

αW22(μ(KhHeun)N,π)⩽Ce−cNβh/καW22(μ,π)+Cκd(βh)3.\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\mu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{N},\pi)\leqslant C\mathrm{e}^{-cN\beta h/\kappa}\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\pi)+C\kappa d\,(\beta h)^{3}\,. (3.2)

In particular, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, the number of gradient queries sufficient for (1.2) is at most

C⁡(κ+κ4/3​d1/3ε2/3)​log⁡(e+α​W22​(μ,π)ε2).C\,\Bigl(\kappa+\frac{\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}}{\varepsilon^{2/3}}\Bigr)\log\Bigl(\mathrm{e}+\frac{\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\pi)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigr)\,.

Initialization at the minimizer x⋆x_{\star} satisfies α​W22​(δx⋆,π)⩽d\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\delta_{x_{\star}},\pi)\leqslant d, and hence, for 0<ε⩽d/20<\varepsilon\leqslant\sqrt{d}/2, gives

N∇V⩽C​κ4/3​d1/3ε2/3​log⁡dε2.N_{\nabla V}\leqslant C\,{\frac{\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}}{\varepsilon^{2/3}}}\log\frac{d}{\varepsilon^{2}}\,. (3.3)

We explain the proof in the normalized units β=1\beta=1, α=κ−1\alpha=\kappa^{-1} of Section 2.1. The technical estimates are proved in Appendix A. The first ingredient is contraction of the numerical kernel itself, which is relatively standard.

Proposition 3.2 (Contractivity of the Heun kernel).

For 0<h⩽10<h\leqslant 1 and all μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

W2​(μ​KhHeun,ν​KhHeun)⩽ρ​W2​(μ,ν),ρ⩽1−h2​κ.W_{2}(\mu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})\leqslant\rho W_{2}(\mu,\nu)\,,\qquad\rho\leqslant 1-\frac{h}{2\kappa}\,. (3.4)

In particular, KhHeunK_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}} has a unique invariant distribution in 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Rescaling Proposition 3.2 to the original units gives contraction factor ρ⩽1−α​h/2\rho\leqslant 1-\alpha h/2 whenever 0<h⩽1/β0<h\leqslant 1/\beta, with the same existence and uniqueness conclusion.

The usual Langevin displacement estimate also gives an elementary comparison, which when combined with contraction would give only κ−1​W22​(π^hHeun,π)≲κ​d​h\kappa^{-1}W_{2}^{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\pi)\lesssim\kappa dh. To recover two further powers of hh, we instead seek a different route of analysis. First, separate the conditional mean of the error from the centered fluctuation. This is the organizing principle of local error analysis; see [17, Section 5.1.1 and Lemma 5.1.2] and [10, Lemma 4.4].

To measure the error of one Heun step, we compare it with the Langevin diffusion run for the same time hh from the same starting point and driven by the same Brownian motion. Let (Xt)0⩽t⩽h(X_{t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} solve (2.1) with X0∼πX_{0}\sim\pi. Since π\pi is invariant, Xt∼πX_{t}\sim\pi for every tt; we call this the stationary path, and we call XhX_{h} its endpoint, i.e., the exact position after one step. In integral form,

Xh=X0−∫0h∇V​(Xt)​𝑑t+2​Bh.X_{h}=X_{0}-\int_{0}^{h}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,.

The Heun step (2.3) from X0X_{0} evaluates its second gradient at the predictor XhpredX_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}}, which is only an approximation of XhX_{h}. To separate this approximation from the quadrature error, we first analyze an idealized step that evaluates the second gradient at the endpoint XhX_{h} itself:

X~h≔X0−h2​{∇V​(X0)+∇V​(Xh)}+2​Bh.\widetilde{X}_{h}\coloneqq X_{0}-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(X_{h})\}+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,.

This step cannot be implemented, because XhX_{h} is unknown, and we use it only as an intermediate object in the proof; we call it the auxiliary step, and its transition kernel K~h\widetilde{K}_{h} is defined in (A.4). It differs from KhHeunK_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}} by only O⁡(d​h5)O(\sqrt{dh^{5}}) in the comparisons needed below. Subtracting the two displays, the error of the auxiliary step is

X~h−Xh=∫0h∇V​(Xt)​𝑑t−h2​{∇V​(X0)+∇V​(Xh)},\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h}=\int_{0}^{h}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(X_{h})\}\,,

the error of the trapezoidal rule for the integral of ∇V\nabla V along the path. Its conditional mean given the endpoint is eh​(Xh)e_{h}(X_{h}), where, by reversibility of π\pi,

eh≔∫0hPt​(∇V)​𝑑t−h2​{∇V+Ph​(∇V)}.e_{h}\coloneqq\int_{0}^{h}P_{t}(\nabla V)\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V+P_{h}(\nabla V)\}\,.

Thus, the systematic error is the trapezoidal quadrature defect for the semigroup.

This systematic error is the main obstacle. Unlike the centered fluctuation X~h−Xh−eh​(Xh)\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h}-e_{h}(X_{h}), which is discussed below, it is a deterministic function of the current position. The fresh noise of the next step therefore does not damp it, and contraction alone would let it accumulate over the relaxation time. We instead cancel it in advance by shifting the point at which the comparison is made. Fix a vector field χ:ℝd→ℝd\chi\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, to be chosen below, and consider two points:

  • •

    the output of the auxiliary step started from the shifted point X0+χ⁡(X0)X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}) instead of X0X_{0}, using the same Brownian motion; and

  • •

    the shifted endpoint Xh+χ⁡(Xh)X_{h}+\chi(X_{h}), which has the same distribution as the shifted starting point X0+χ⁡(X0)X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}), because X0X_{0} and XhX_{h} both have distribution π\pi.

If the first point is close to the second on average, then the auxiliary step nearly preserves the distribution of X0+χ⁡(X0)X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}). Up to terms of order h​∥χ∥L2​(π)h\,\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}, which come from evaluating ∇V\nabla V at the shifted points rather than at X0X_{0} and XhX_{h}, the difference between the two points is

χ⁡(X0)+(X~h−Xh)−χ⁡(Xh).\chi(X_{0})+(\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h})-\chi(X_{h})\,.

Given the endpoint, reversibility of π\pi gives 𝔼⁡[χ⁡(X0)∣Xh]=Ph​χ​(Xh)\mathbb{E}[\chi(X_{0})\mid X_{h}]=P_{h}\chi(X_{h}), so the conditional mean of this difference is (Ph​χ+eh−χ)​(Xh)(P_{h}\chi+e_{h}-\chi)(X_{h}). It vanishes exactly when χ\chi solves the discrete Poisson equation

(I−Ph)​χ=eh.(I-P_{h})\chi=e_{h}\,.

Equivalently, χ=∑n=0∞Phn​eh\chi=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{h}^{n}e_{h} is the total systematic error accumulated over all future steps, each step’s contribution ehe_{h} being transported by the exact dynamics. Shifting the starting point by χ\chi accounts for this accumulated bias at once, so that the remaining conditional mean comes only from the terms of order h​∥χ∥L2​(π)h\,\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)} neglected above. We call χ\chi the corrector. Such Poisson equations have long been used to isolate systematic discretization error [38, 32, 36]; a related discrete corrector appears in the analysis of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm in [44]. It motivates the reference distribution

ν≔(I+χ)#​π.\nu\coloneqq(I+\chi)_{\#}\pi\,. (3.5)

The spectral calculation in Section A.2 gives ∥χ∥L2​(π)⩽C​d​h3\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{3}}, and hence W2​(ν,π)⩽C​d​h3W_{2}(\nu,\pi)\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{3}}. At this shifted reference distribution, the conditional mean of the error is only O⁡(d​h5)O(\sqrt{dh^{5}}).

The centered fluctuation still has size O⁡(d​h3)O(\sqrt{dh^{3}}). However, as the next step supplies fresh Gaussian noise, this fluctuation cost is only O⁡(d​h5)O(\sqrt{dh^{5}}) in W2W_{2}. The reason is that a centered perturbation affects a Gaussian convolution to second order; see Lemma A.10. We use the convolution estimate of [43, Theorem E.4 and Remark E.6(ii)], with the sharp constant proved directly in Lemma A.10; [10, Lemma 4.11] develops the same smoothing principle for perturbations that can depend on the smoothing Gaussian. The appendix verifies the bounds using Malliavin calculus, which is the main analytic ingredient.

The following elementary consequence of contractivity then accumulates the two costs.

Lemma 3.3 (Bias accumulation at a reference law).

Let 0<h⩽10<h\leqslant 1, let ρ\rho be as in (3.4), and let ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Then

W2​(π^hHeun,ν)⩽W2​(ν​KhHeun,ν)+W2​(ν​(KhHeun)2,ν​KhHeun)1−ρ.W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\nu)\leqslant W_{2}(\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\nu)+\frac{W_{2}\bigl(\nu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{2},\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\bigr)}{1-\rho}\,. (3.6)

The proofs of Proposition 3.2 and Lemma 3.3 are in Section A.1. For the reference distribution (3.5), Section A.6 proves

W2​(ν​KhHeun,ν)⩽C​d​h3,W2​(ν​(KhHeun)2,ν​KhHeun)⩽C​d​h5.W_{2}(\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\nu)\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{3}}\,,\qquad W_{2}\bigl(\nu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{2},\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\bigr)\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{5}}\,.

The first bound pays for the full local error once. The second pays for its smaller effect after the next step and is multiplied by the relaxation time (1−ρ)−1≲κ/h(1-\rho)^{-1}\lesssim\kappa/h. Together with W2​(ν,π)⩽C​d​h3W_{2}(\nu,\pi)\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{3}}, Lemma 3.3 proves the stationary bound. Section A.7 then gives the convergence and query bounds in Theorem 3.1.

Remark 3.4 (The remaining dependence on the condition number).

The bound (3.3) contains κ4/3d1/3ε−2/3\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}. The lower bound in Theorem 5.2 contains κd1/3ε−2/3\kappa d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3} for d−1⩽ε⩽ε0d^{-1}\leqslant\varepsilon\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}, so the exponents of dd and ε\varepsilon agree while a factor κ1/3\kappa^{1/3} remains. In the upper bound, this loss comes from accumulating the distance between consecutive iterates by the triangle inequality. Improving that accumulation would require further cancellation across steps; the present proof does not establish it.

4 Underdamped upper bound

Before proceeding, we note that contraction is measured in the same twisted metric as the continuous underdamped Langevin dynamics in [17, Theorem 5.3.6]. Friction acts directly on momentum; the cross term in this metric transfers its dissipation to position. For z≔(x,p)z\coloneqq(x,p), define

Tγ≔[Id0Id2γ​Id],Mγ≔Tγ⊤​Tγ=[2​Id2γ​Id2γ​Id4γ2​Id],T_{\gamma}\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}&0\\ I_{d}&\frac{2}{\gamma}\,I_{d}\end{bmatrix}\,,\qquad M_{\gamma}\coloneqq T_{\gamma}^{\top}T_{\gamma}=\begin{bmatrix}2I_{d}&\frac{2}{\gamma}\,I_{d}\\[5.0pt] \frac{2}{\gamma}\,I_{d}&\frac{4}{\gamma^{2}}\,I_{d}\end{bmatrix}\,,

and the hypocoercive norm ∥z∥Mγ2≔z⊤​Mγ​z=∥Tγ​z∥2\lVert z\rVert_{M_{\gamma}}^{2}\coloneqq z^{\top}M_{\gamma}z=\lVert T_{\gamma}z\rVert^{2}. The associated Wasserstein distance is denoted by W2,MγW_{2,M_{\gamma}}. In the normalized setting β=1\beta=1 and γ=2\gamma=2, we omit the subscript and write TT, MM, and W2,MW_{2,M}.

Now, we show that the exponential midpoint method (2.7)–(2.8) with γ=2​β\gamma=2\sqrt{\beta} achieves d1/4d^{1/4} query complexity in Wasserstein distance under the Hessian bounds (1.1).

Theorem 4.1 (Exponential midpoint upper bound).

There are universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that, for 0<βh⩽cκ−1/40<\sqrt{\beta}\,h\leqslant{c\kappa^{-1/4}}, the kernel KhExpMidK_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} has a unique invariant distribution 𝛑hExpMid\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} in 𝒫2​(ℝ2​d)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}), and

α​W2​((𝝅hExpMid)x,π)⩽C​κ​d​(β​h)2.\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}})_{x},\pi\bigr)\leqslant C\sqrt{\kappa d}\,(\sqrt{\beta}\,h)^{2}\,. (4.1)

For the initialization X^0=x⋆\widehat{X}_{0}=x_{\star} and P^0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)\widehat{P}_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}), independent of the driving Brownian motion, for every integer n⩾0n\geqslant 0,

αW2(Law(X^n),π)⩽Cde−cnβh/κ+Cκ​d(βh)2.\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(\widehat{X}_{n}),\pi\bigr)\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,\mathrm{e}^{-cn\sqrt{\beta}\,h/\kappa}+C\sqrt{\kappa d}\,(\sqrt{\beta}\,h)^{2}\,. (4.2)

Consequently, for 0<ε⩽d/20<\varepsilon\leqslant\sqrt{d}/2, the number N∇VN_{\nabla V} of gradient queries required to attain the accuracy criterion (1.2) satisfies

N∇V⩽C​κ5/4​d1/4ε1/2​log⁡dε2.N_{\nabla V}\leqslant{C\,\frac{\kappa^{5/4}d^{1/4}}{\varepsilon^{1/2}}\,\log\frac{d}{\varepsilon^{2}}}\,. (4.3)

Just as in the overdamped case, there is a discrepancy in the condition number exponent, which cannot easily be rectified in the current proof.

The remainder of this section outlines the proof; the technical components are carried out in Appendix B. The propositions below use the coordinate normalization in Section 2.1. First, the following contractivity lemma is proved by some elementary coupling analysis.

Proposition 4.2 (Numerical hypocoercive contraction).

There is a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, for 0<h⩽cκ−1/40<h\leqslant{c\kappa^{-1/4}} and all μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝ2​d)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}),

W2,M​(μ​KhExpMid,ν​KhExpMid)⩽(1−h4​κ)​W2,M​(μ,ν).W_{2,M}(\mu K_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}},\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}})\leqslant\Bigl(1-\frac{h}{4\kappa}\Bigr)\,W_{2,M}(\mu,\nu)\,.

The second ingredient is the one-step error at stationarity, which carries the full order h3h^{3}.

Proposition 4.3 (One-step error at stationarity).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0},

W2,M​(𝝅​KhExpMid,𝝅)⩽C​d​h3.W_{2,M}(\bm{\pi}K_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}},\bm{\pi})\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}\,.

A fixed-point argument gives a unique invariant distribution and W2,M​(𝝅hExpMid,𝝅)⩽C​κ​d​h2W_{2,M}(\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}},\bm{\pi})\leqslant C\kappa\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}: divide the one-step error by the contraction gap. Iterating from δx⋆⊗𝖭⁡(0,Id)\delta_{x_{\star}}\otimes\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) gives (4.2).

The main work is therefore Proposition 4.3.

The local error.

Let (Xt,Pt)0⩽t⩽h(X_{t},P_{t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} be the underdamped Langevin diffusion started at (X0,P0)∼𝝅(X_{0},P_{0})\sim\bm{\pi}. Since 𝝅\bm{\pi} is invariant, the endpoint Zh≔(Xh,Ph)Z_{h}\coloneqq(X_{h},P_{h}), i.e., the exact phase space position after one step, also has distribution 𝝅\bm{\pi}. The exact solution formulas in Section 2.3 express ZhZ_{h} through the two gradient integrals

∫0hah−t∇V(Xt)dtand∫0he−2​(h−t)∇V(Xt)dt.\int_{0}^{h}a_{h-t}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\qquad\text{and}\qquad\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-2(h-t)}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\,.

The exponential midpoint method approximates each integral by hh times its integrand at t=h/2t=h/2, with the predictor Xh/2predX_{h/2}^{\mathrm{pred}} in place of the exact midpoint Xh/2X_{h/2}. The predictor differs from Xh/2X_{h/2} by O⁡(d​h3)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}) in L2L^{2}, and the gradient enters with a coefficient of order hh, so replacing the predictor by the exact midpoint changes the output by only O⁡(d​h4)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{4}). With the exact midpoint, the method started at (X0,P0)(X_{0},P_{0}) and driven by the same Brownian motion outputs Zh+ℰhZ_{h}+\mathcal{E}_{h}, where the local error ℰh\mathcal{E}_{h} collects the errors of the midpoint rule for the two integrals; see (B.4). Since Zh∼𝝅Z_{h}\sim\bm{\pi}, Proposition 4.3 reduces to the question of how far the random displacement Zh↦Zh+ℰhZ_{h}\mapsto Z_{h}+\mathcal{E}_{h} moves the distribution 𝝅\bm{\pi} in W2W_{2}.

The naïve bound only gives ∥ℰh∥L2≤C​d​h2\lVert\mathcal{E}_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}}\leq C\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}. Dividing by the contraction gap h/κh/\kappa gives only C​κ​d​hC\kappa\sqrt{d}\,h for the bias, one power of hh short of the theorem.

Conditional mean and centered fluctuation.

As in the overdamped case, we split

ℰh=mh​(Zh)+Rh,mh​(Zh)≔𝔼⁡[ℰh∣Zh].\mathcal{E}_{h}=m_{h}(Z_{h})+R_{h}\,,\qquad m_{h}(Z_{h})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}_{h}\mid Z_{h}]\,.

We discuss the centered fluctuation RhR_{h} below; the main issue is the conditional mean.

The conditional mean mhm_{h} is a deterministic vector field on phase space, and what matters is not its size but its effect on 𝝅\bm{\pi}. For a vector field FF on phase space, write D≔(∇x,∇p)D\coloneqq(\nabla_{x},\nabla_{p}) and define the weighted divergence δ𝝅​F\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F by ∫⟨D​φ,F⟩​𝑑𝝅=∫φ​δ𝝅​F​𝑑𝝅\int\langle D\varphi,F\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}=\int\varphi\,\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi} for all smooth test functions φ\varphi. If Z∼𝝅Z\sim\bm{\pi}, a first-order Taylor expansion gives

𝔼​φ​(Z+s​F​(Z))=𝔼​φ​(Z)+s​∫φ​δ𝝅​F​𝑑𝝅+O⁡(s2),s→0,\mathbb{E}\varphi(Z+sF(Z))=\mathbb{E}\varphi(Z)+s\int\varphi\,\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}+O(s^{2})\,,\qquad s\to 0\,,

so to first order the displacement changes the distribution only through δ𝝅​F\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F. We measure the first-order size of the displacement by the negative Sobolev norm

∥δ𝝅​F∥H˙−1​(𝝅)≔sup{∫φ​δ𝝅​F​𝑑𝝅:∥D​φ∥L2​(𝝅)⩽1},\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\coloneqq\sup\Bigl\{\int\varphi\,\delta_{\bm{\pi}}F\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}:\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant 1\Bigr\}\,,

which equals the smallest L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi}) norm of a vector field with the same weighted divergence as FF (Section B.1). In particular, it is at most ∥F∥L2​(𝝅)\lVert F\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}, but it can be much smaller. For small displacements, W2W_{2} is comparable to this norm [45].

Cancellation in the weighted divergence.

Proposition B.4 shows that ∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h3\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}, one power of hh better than the bound on ∥mh∥L2​(𝝅)\lVert m_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}. We show that δ𝝅​mh\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h} is itself the midpoint quadrature error ∫0hψt​𝑑t−h​ψh/2\int_{0}^{h}\psi_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t-h\psi_{h/2} of a curve t↦ψtt\mapsto\psi_{t} of functions on phase space, which starts at ψ0​(x,p)=⟨p,∇V​(x)⟩\psi_{0}(x,p)=\langle p,\nabla V(x)\rangle and evolves essentially by the reversed dynamics; see (B.8). The second time derivative of this curve involves third derivatives of VV, which are not available pointwise. In H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}), however, a third derivative of VV is a derivative of the bounded Hessian, and integration by parts moves this derivative onto the test function φ\varphi. Lemma B.3 makes this precise using a Hermite expansion in the momentum, and shows that the second time derivative is bounded by C​dC\sqrt{d} in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}). Thus ψt\psi_{t} is affine in tt up to an error O⁡(d​t2)O(\sqrt{d}\,t^{2}) in this norm, and the exactness of the midpoint rule for affine functions gives the bound C​d​h3C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}.

From divergence bounds to transport.

Lemma B.5 turns these estimates into a Wasserstein bound. For Y∼μY\sim\mu and a random displacement U=m⁡(Y)+RU=m(Y)+R with 𝔼⁡[R∣Y]=0\mathbb{E}[R\mid Y]=0, it bounds W2​(Law⁡(Y+U),μ)W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(Y+U),\mu) by ∥δμ​m∥H˙−1​(μ)\lVert\delta_{\mu}m\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\mu)} plus second-order terms, which are products of derivatives of UU with the size of UU or RR. It extends the Gaussian transport estimate of [10, Lemma 4.11] to the non-Gaussian phase space distribution 𝝅\bm{\pi}. We use Malliavin calculus estimates to bound these second-order terms. Together with ∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h3\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}, this proves Proposition 4.3. The construction and its regularity requirements are given in Sections B.2, B.3 and B.4.

At a high level, the bounds here and in Section 3 are related, although the techniques are not exactly comparable. Both objects, instead of directly working in L2L^{2}, use a divergence-type quantity to analyze the error, which is then related to the error in W2W_{2} via a divergence-transport lemma. The H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1} norm can be viewed as a linearization of the conditional mean’s effect on the distribution, while the Stein kernel in Section 3 can be viewed as a generalization of the former which also captures non-linear effects. However, the detailed quantification of their error contributions in Lemma B.5 and Lemma A.12 do not lead to comparable estimates in general.

5 Deterministic lower bounds

We treat deterministic Heun and underdamped exponential midpoint together. Their stationary biases give the two deterministic lower bounds in Table 1. We first present the oscillatory Heun construction and its condition number extension, then the Gaussian covariance calculation for exponential midpoint. The stationary bias proofs follow the same order in Appendix C.

5.1 Heun on oscillatory targets

The Heun lower bound uses an oscillatory target: small oscillations of wavelength h\sqrt{h} and amplitude hh produce a persistent error while keeping the Hessian bounded, and a final coordinate is added to ensure the algorithm needs to take a fixed positive time before convergence. The construction depends on the step size.

Specifically, let d⩾2d\geqslant 2, and define

Vh,d​(x,z)≔∑i=1d−1{xi22+a⋆​h​cos⁡xih}+z22,(x,z)∈ℝd−1×ℝ.{V_{h,d}(x,z)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\Bigl\{\frac{x_{i}^{2}}{2}+a_{\star}h\cos\frac{x_{i}}{\sqrt{h}}\Bigr\}+\frac{z^{2}}{2}\,,\qquad(x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}\,.} (5.1)

Here a⋆∈(0,1/4)a_{\star}\in(0,1/4) is a fixed numerical constant. It controls the oscillations and, since

(1−a⋆)​Id⪯∇2Vh,d⪯(1+a⋆)​Id,(1-a_{\star})I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V_{h,d}\preceq(1+a_{\star})I_{d}\,,

keeps the condition number bounded independently of dd and hh. Write πh\pi_{h} for the probability distribution on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with density proportional to e−Vh,d\mathrm{e}^{-V_{h,d}}. We remark that this construction was used in [16] to provide upper bounds on the conductance of MALA.

Proposition 5.1 (Heun lower bounds on an oscillatory target).

There are universal c,h0>0c,h_{0}>0 such that, for every d⩾2d\geqslant 2 and 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, the Heun sampler on (5.1) has a unique invariant distribution π^hHeun∈𝒫2\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}, and

W2​(πh​KhHeun,πh)⩾c​d​h3/2,\displaystyle W_{2}(\pi_{h}K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\pi_{h})\geqslant c\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}\,,\qquad W2​(π^hHeun,πh)⩾c​d​h3/2,\displaystyle W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\pi_{h})\geqslant c\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}\,, (5.2)
KL⁡(πh​KhHeun∥πh)⩾c​d​h2,\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(\pi_{h}K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\mathrel{\|}\pi_{h})\geqslant cdh^{2}\,,\qquad KL⁡(π^hHeun∥πh)⩾c​d​h2.\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\mathrel{\|}\pi_{h})\geqslant cdh^{2}\,.

The Heun proof in Section C.1 computes the change in expectation of the 11-Lipschitz function hcos(⋅/h)\sqrt{h}\cos(\cdot/\sqrt{h}) after one update started from the target. A Gaussian calculation shows this is of order h3/2h^{3/2}, which is then used to lower bound the Wasserstein error at stationarity. Tensorization gives the dimension dependence. Pinsker’s inequality applied to the same observable divided by h\sqrt{h} gives the KL bounds.

5.2 The condition number dependence for Heun

The preceding construction has bounded condition number. To capture the cost of a large κ\kappa, we couple the oscillatory coordinates to a coordinate whose curvature is of order κ−1\kappa^{-1}. The numerical error in the former will have an effect on the latter which is amplified by the inverse curvature. Our potential consists of numerous coupled blocks, each containing at most h−1h^{-1} oscillatory coordinates, which ensures that we can keep the Hessian bounded. To make the construction explicit, in normalized units a block with step t≍β​ht\asymp\beta h has potential

(x,y)\displaystyle(x,y) ⟼∥x∥22+y22​K+aℓ2(2+sin(y/K))∑i=1mcos(xi/ℓ),ℓ2=tτ.\displaystyle\longmapsto\frac{\lVert x\rVert^{2}}{2}+\frac{y^{2}}{2K}+a\ell^{2}\bigl(2+\sin(y/\sqrt{K})\bigr)\sum_{i=1}^{m}\cos(x_{i}/\ell)\,,\qquad\ell^{2}=\frac{t}{\tau}\,.

Here a>0a>0 is a small fixed numerical constant, τ>1\tau>1 is a large fixed numerical constant, K≍κK\asymp\kappa, and m​t⩽1mt\leqslant 1. Products of these blocks give the dimension dependence. Equation (C.9) gives the full product potential; the proof then rescales it to the prescribed α,β\alpha,\beta. A final coordinate, independent of all others with the same small curvature, supplies a lower bound on relaxation time, so that the algorithm must run for some number of iterations before it is close to convergence.

Theorem 5.2 (Condition number lower bound for Heun).

There are universal c,C,ε0>0c,C,\varepsilon_{0}>0, d0⩾4d_{0}\geqslant 4, and κ0>1\kappa_{0}>1 with the following property. Let d⩾d0d\geqslant d_{0}, κ⩾κ0\kappa\geqslant\kappa_{0}, 0<ε⩽ε00<\varepsilon\leqslant\varepsilon_{0}, and let Heun use a fixed step with 0<β​h⩽c0<\beta h\leqslant c. There is an α\alpha-strongly convex, β\beta-smooth potential VhV_{h} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with β/α=κ\beta/\alpha=\kappa, and an initial distribution νh\nu_{h} such that

𝔼X0∼νh​[Vh​(X0)−Vh​(x⋆)]⩽C​d,x⋆≔arg​min⁡Vh.\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim\nu_{h}}\bigl[V_{h}(X_{0})-V_{h}(x_{\star})\bigr]\leqslant Cd\,,\qquad x_{\star}\coloneqq\argmin V_{h}\,.

Writing πh​(d​x)∝e−Vh​(x)​d​x\pi_{h}(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V_{h}(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x, for every integer N⩾0N\geqslant 0, α​W2​(νh​(KhHeun)N,πh)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\nu_{h}(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{N},\pi_{h})\leqslant\varepsilon implies

N⩾c​κ​min⁡{d1/3ε2/3,d1/2ε1/2}​log​1ε.N\geqslant{c\kappa\min\Bigl\{\frac{d^{1/3}}{\varepsilon^{2/3}}\,,\frac{d^{1/2}}{\varepsilon^{1/2}}\Bigr\}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}\,. (5.3)

In particular, in the moderate accuracy range d−1⩽ε⩽ε0d^{-1}\leqslant\varepsilon\leqslant\varepsilon_{0},

N⩾c​κ​d1/3ε2/3​log⁡1ε.N\geqslant\frac{c\kappa d^{1/3}}{\varepsilon^{2/3}}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,. (5.4)

The estimates and the product construction are proved in Sections C.2.1 and C.2.2.

5.3 Underdamped exponential midpoint

For the underdamped Gaussian calculation, let us first consider the κ=1\kappa=1 case. Then, we choose V⁡(x)=∥x∥2/2V(x)=\lVert x\rVert^{2}/2, α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1, and γ=2\gamma=2, so π=𝖭⁡(0,Id)\pi=\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}). More generally, when κ≫1\kappa\gg 1, let d⩾2d\geqslant 2, 0<α⩽β0<\alpha\leqslant\beta, κ≔β/α⩾2\kappa\coloneqq\beta/\alpha\geqslant 2, and γ=2​β\gamma=2\sqrt{\beta}. We consider the anisotropic Gaussian target with potential

V⁡(x)≔β2​∑i=1d−1xi2+α2​xd2,V(x)\coloneqq\frac{\beta}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}x_{i}^{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\,x_{d}^{2}\,, (5.5)

to capture the dependence on κ\kappa in our bounds.

On the quadratic target, exponential midpoint is a linear update with a deterministic state matrix and additive Gaussian noise. Its invariant distribution is therefore Gaussian, and the error in its position variance gives both the isotropic lower bound and its anisotropic extension.

Proposition 5.3 (Exponential midpoint on a Gaussian target).

There are universal constants c>0c>0 and h0∈(0,1]h_{0}\in(0,1] such that, for the isotropic target V⁡(x)=∥x∥2/2V(x)=\lVert x\rVert^{2}/2, with α=β=1\alpha=\beta=1 and γ=2\gamma=2, for every d⩾1d\geqslant 1 and 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, the kernel KhExpMidK_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} has a unique invariant distribution 𝛑hExpMid\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}} with finite second moment. Its position marginal is 𝖭⁡(0,sh​Id)\mathsf{N}(0,s_{h}I_{d}), where

sh=1−h224+O⁡(h3).s_{h}=1-\frac{h^{2}}{24}+O(h^{3})\,.

The remainder is universal. In particular,

W2​((𝝅hExpMid)x,π)⩾c​d​h2.W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}})_{x},\pi\bigr)\geqslant c\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}\,. (5.6)

More generally, for the dynamics corresponding to (5.5), the kernel has a unique invariant distribution in 𝒫2​(ℝ2​d)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}) whenever 0<β​h⩽h00<\sqrt{\beta}\,h\leqslant h_{0}, and its position bias satisfies

α​W2​((𝝅hExpMid)x,π)=(β​h)248​d−1κ+1κ2​{1+O⁡(β​h)}.\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{ExpMid}})_{x},\pi\bigr)=\frac{(\sqrt{\beta}\,h)^{2}}{48}\,\sqrt{\frac{d-1}{\kappa}+\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}}\,\{1+O(\sqrt{\beta}\,h)\}\,.

All constants and remainders are uniform in d,α,βd,\alpha,\beta. Initialize

X0=α−1/2ed,P0∼𝖭(0,Id),X_{0}=\alpha^{-1/2}e_{d}\,,\qquad P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})\,,

with momentum independent of future randomness, where ede_{d} is the final coordinate vector. This start satisfies 𝔼⁡[V⁡(X0)−V⁡(x⋆)]=1/2\mathbb{E}[V(X_{0})-V(x_{\star})]=1/2. For a universal C>0C>0 and every integer N⩾0N\geqslant 0,

αW2(Law(X^N),π)⩾max{cdκ(βh)2,e−CNβh/κ}.\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(\widehat{X}_{N}),\pi\bigr)\geqslant\max\Bigl\{c\sqrt{\frac{d}{\kappa}}\,(\sqrt{\beta}\,h)^{2},\mathrm{e}^{-CN\sqrt{\beta}\,h/\kappa}\Bigr\}\,. (5.7)

Consequently, for 0<ε⩽1/20<\varepsilon\leqslant 1/2, achieving α​W2​(Law⁡(X^N),π)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\widehat{X}_{N}),\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon requires

N⩾c⁡(κ+κ3/4​d1/4ε1/2)​log⁡1ε.N\geqslant c\,\Bigl(\kappa+\frac{\kappa^{3/4}d^{1/4}}{\varepsilon^{1/2}}\Bigr)\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,. (5.8)

The coordinates of curvature β\beta impose the step size restriction through their variance error, while the coordinate of curvature α\alpha requires elapsed time of order κ​log⁡(1/ε)\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon) in normalized units. The resulting κ3/4\kappa^{3/4} dependence in (5.8) leaves a discrepancy of κ1/2\kappa^{1/2} between the accuracy-dependent terms of this lower bound and Theorem 4.1.

The proof in Section C.3 computes the invariant covariance of one position–momentum pair and applies the exact Wasserstein formula for centered Gaussian distributions.

6 Randomized lower bounds

We illustrate the technique for the randomized lower bounds at a high level. To see where the factor d1/3d^{1/3} in the iteration bounds comes from, consider RLMC on V=∥⋅∥2/2V=\lVert\cdot\rVert^{2}/2; the other randomized methods behave in the same way. Conditionally on the evaluation time Θ\Theta, one step has the form

X+=m⁡(Θ)​X+q⁡(Θ)​GdX^{+}=m(\Theta)\,X+\sqrt{q(\Theta)}\,G_{d}

with scalar coefficients m⁡(Θ)m(\Theta) and q⁡(Θ)q(\Theta) and a fresh Gd∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)G_{d}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}); see the proof of Proposition D.4. The crucial point is that a single draw of Θ\Theta is used for all dd coordinates: every coordinate is integrated with the same evaluation time. Hence, conditionally on the past draws of Θ\Theta, the iterate is exactly 𝖭⁡(0,S​Id)\mathsf{N}(0,SI_{d}) for a single random scalar S⟂GS\perp G shared by all coordinates, and at stationarity S=dm​(Θ)2​S′+q⁡(Θ)S\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}m(\Theta)^{2}S^{\prime}+q(\Theta), with S′S^{\prime} an independent copy of SS.

On average the quadrature is very accurate: 𝔼​S=1+O⁡(h3)\mathbb{E}S=1+O(h^{3}). In a single step, however, started from the target variance S=1S=1, the iterate has conditional variance m​(Θ)2+q⁡(Θ)m(\Theta)^{2}+q(\Theta), and its error m​(Θ)2+q⁡(Θ)−1=h2​(1−2​Θ)+h4​Θ2m(\Theta)^{2}+q(\Theta)-1=h^{2}\,(1-2\Theta)+h^{4}\Theta^{2} has mean only h4/3h^{4}/3 but fluctuates by order h2h^{2}. Since 1−𝔼​m​(Θ)2≈2​h1-\mathbb{E}m(\Theta)^{2}\approx 2h, the recursion for SS forgets its past after about 1/h1/h steps, so SS accumulates roughly 1/h1/h independent fluctuations of size h2h^{2}. This gives Var⁡(S)≍h4⋅h−1=h3\operatorname{Var}(S)\asymp h^{4}\cdot h^{-1}=h^{3}.

Because SS is shared, these fluctuations add up in the norm. Indeed, ∥X∥2=S​∥Gd∥2≈S​d\lVert X\rVert^{2}=S\,\lVert G_{d}\rVert^{2}\approx Sd, so ∥X∥\lVert X\rVert fluctuates by about d​h3/2\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}, whereas under 𝖭⁡(0,Id)\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) the norm has variance at most 11 by the Gaussian Poincaré inequality. (If instead each coordinate used its own independent evaluation time, the coordinate variances would fluctuate independently, and their fluctuations would largely cancel in ∥X∥\lVert X\rVert.) Since the norm is 11-Lipschitz, no coupling can hide the extra spread of ∥X∥\lVert X\rVert, and W2W_{2} is at least of order 1+d​h3−1≍min⁡{d​h3,d​h3}\sqrt{1+dh^{3}}-1\asymp\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}; this is Lemma D.3. Note that deterministic midpoint methods avoid this common scale obstruction.

The proof template is the same for all the randomized methods: derive the fixed-point equation for the conditional covariance SS, compute its variance and centered fourth moment through Lemma D.1/D.2 via Taylor expansion of the equation for small hh, and apply Lemma D.3 to translate these moments into a lower bound for the Wasserstein distance. The scalar calculation for RLMC and PLMC comes first; RULMC and PULMC require some matrix algebra instead. Appendix D supplies these calculations, followed by the unified proof of Corollary 6.3.

6.1 Overdamped randomized midpoint and Poisson midpoint

Proposition 6.1 (Randomized overdamped lower bounds on a Gaussian target).

There are universal c,h0>0c,h_{0}>0 such that, for every d⩾1d\geqslant 1 and 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, RLMC and PLMC on V⁡(x)=∥x∥2/2V(x)=\lVert x\rVert^{2}/2 have unique invariant distributions in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. Their errors satisfy

W2​(π^hRLMC,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{RLMC}},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})) ⩾c​min⁡{d​h3,d​h3},\displaystyle\geqslant c\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}\,, (6.1)
W2​(π^hPLMC,k,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{PLMC},k},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})) ⩾c​min⁡{d​h3,d​h3},k⩾2,\displaystyle\geqslant c\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}\,,\qquad k\geqslant 2\,,
W2​(π^hPLMC,1,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{PLMC},1},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})) ⩾c​d​h.\displaystyle\geqslant c\sqrt{d}\,h\,. (6.2)

The constants are uniform in kk. For k=1k=1, PLMC is the Euler–Maruyama scheme (ULA).

At any fixed sufficiently small accuracy, the first two bounds require h≲d−1/3h\lesssim d^{-1/3}, while the k=1k=1 case requires h≲d−1/2h\lesssim d^{-1/2}. The latter recovers the Gaussian calculation in [54]. For the randomized cases, the proof in Section D.3 combines moment estimates for the linear update coefficients with Lemmas D.1 and D.3 to obtain the Wasserstein lower bounds.

6.2 Underdamped randomized midpoint and Poisson midpoint

We use the same Gaussian target and underdamped normalization as in Section 5.3; its rescaling statement also applies here. The scalar covariance calculation for RLMC and PLMC is replaced by a matrix calculation for a representative position–momentum pair.

Proposition 6.2 (Randomized methods on a Gaussian target).

There are universal c,h0>0c,h_{0}>0 such that, for every d⩾1d\geqslant 1 and 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, RULMC and PULMC on V⁡(x)=∥x∥2/2V(x)=\lVert x\rVert^{2}/2 have unique invariant distributions in 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2}. Their errors satisfy

W2​((𝝅hRULMC)x,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{RULMC}})_{x},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})\bigr) ⩾c​min⁡{d​h3,d​h3},\displaystyle\geqslant c\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}\,,
W2​((𝝅hPULMC,k)x,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{PULMC},k})_{x},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})\bigr) ⩾c​min⁡{d​h3,d​h3},\displaystyle\geqslant c\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}\,, k⩾2,\displaystyle k\geqslant 2\,,
W2​((𝝅hPULMC,1)x,𝖭⁡(0,Id))\displaystyle W_{2}\bigl((\bm{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{PULMC},1})_{x},\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})\bigr) ⩾c​d​h.\displaystyle\geqslant c\sqrt{d}\,h\,.

The constants are uniform in kk. For k=1k=1, PULMC is the exponential Euler scheme (ULMC).

Sections D.4 and D.5 derive the fixed-point equation for these systems, which is then passed again through Lemma D.2 and Lemma D.3 to convert this into a Wasserstein lower bound.

6.3 Iteration lower bounds for all midpoint methods

We collect the iteration consequences of the deterministic bounds in Section 5 and the preceding randomized bounds in one statement. In each construction, a displaced position coordinate forces a positive elapsed time in order that the given coordinate converges, while the error in the remaining coordinates forces a small step size.

Corollary 6.3 (Iteration lower bounds for all midpoint methods).

There are universal c,C,ε0,h0>0c,C,\varepsilon_{0},h_{0}>0 such that, for every d⩾2d\geqslant 2, 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, each method listed below, and every Poisson grid size k⩾1k\geqslant 1, there is an initial position distribution ν0\nu_{0} satisfying

𝔼X0∼ν0​[V⁡(X0)−V⁡(x⋆)]⩽C​d,α​W22​(ν0,π)⩽C​d,x⋆≔arg​min⁡V,\mathbb{E}_{X_{0}\sim\nu_{0}}[V(X_{0})-V(x_{\star})]\leqslant Cd\,,\qquad\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\nu_{0},\pi)\leqslant Cd\,,\qquad x_{\star}\coloneqq\argmin V\,,

with the following property. Write νN\nu_{N} for the position distribution after NN steps. For every 0<ε⩽ε00<\varepsilon\leqslant\varepsilon_{0} and integer N⩾0N\geqslant 0, position accuracy α​W2​(νN,π)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\nu_{N},\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon requires:

MethodNecessary iterationsHeunN⩾cd1/3ε−2/3Exponential midpointN⩾cd1/4ε−1/2RLMC or RULMCN⩾cd1/3ε−1/3PLMC or PULMC with ​k⩾2N⩾cd1/3ε−1/3ULA or ULMC (​k=1​)N⩾c​d1/2​ε−1\begin{array}[]{l|c}\text{Method}&\text{Necessary iterations}\\ \hline\cr\text{Heun}&N\geqslant cd^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}\\ \text{Exponential midpoint}&N\geqslant cd^{1/4}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\\ \text{RLMC or RULMC}&N\geqslant cd^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3}\\ \text{PLMC or PULMC with }k\geqslant 2&N\geqslant cd^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-1/3}\\ \text{ULA or ULMC (}k=1\text{)}&N\geqslant cd^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1}\end{array}

Here, V≔Vh,dV\coloneqq V_{h,d} from (5.1) for Heun, and V≔∥⋅∥2/2V\coloneqq\lVert\cdot\rVert^{2}/2 for every other method; the condition numbers are bounded by a universal constant. The randomized methods use quadrature choices shared across coordinates, and the constants are uniform in the Poisson grid size kk.

For all underdamped methods, γ=2\gamma=2 and P0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) is independent of X0X_{0} and future randomness, and the initial positions are

ν0≔δedfor exponential midpoint,ν0≔𝖭⁡(ed,Id)for RULMC and PULMC.\nu_{0}\coloneqq\delta_{e_{d}}\quad\text{for exponential midpoint}\,,\qquad\nu_{0}\coloneqq\mathsf{N}(e_{d},I_{d})\quad\text{for RULMC and PULMC}\,.

These choices are independent of h,kh,k; the latter has W2​(ν0,π)=1W_{2}(\nu_{0},\pi)=1. The overdamped initial distributions may depend on the method, hh, and kk, but not on ε\varepsilon or NN.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.2, its Heun target and initialization satisfy the same two initialization bounds, and α​W2​(νN,π)⩽ε\sqrt{\alpha}\,W_{2}(\nu_{N},\pi)\leqslant\varepsilon requires

N⩾cκmin{d1/3ε−2/3,d1/2ε−1/2}log1ε.N\geqslant c\kappa\min\{d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3},d^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-1/2}\}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\,.

Appendix A Proof of the overdamped upper bound

We complete the deterministic Heun proof outlined in Section 3. We work throughout in the normalized units β=1\beta=1, α=κ−1\alpha=\kappa^{-1}, with the fixed threshold h0h_{0} from Section 2.1. In particular, V∈C2V\in C^{2} and κ−1​Id⪯∇2V⪯Id\kappa^{-1}I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq I_{d}. Section A.7 translates the resulting estimate back to the original units. The analytic background for this and all other appendices is collected in Appendix E.

We explain the main idea intuitively. Firstly, we will work at a shifted measure ν\nu, which removes the leading bias term without too much cost, and consider the effect of the dynamics around this measure. The remaining fluctuation term is still too large when measured in L2L^{2}. To witness additional cancellations, we instead provide estimates on the conditional Stein kernel, which in turn requires detailed analysis of Schatten norms and Witten Laplacians. This is the most technical part of the proof and involves heavy technical machinery from Malliavin calculus and sectorial functional calculus. After doing this, we apply the technique of [43, Theorem E.4] to convert this back to a transport bound, which accumulates via Lemma 3.3.

A detailed roadmap is also provided below, which follows the sequential presentation of the proof. We begin with Section A.1, which opens with some useful auxiliary estimates.

  1. 1.

    Correcting the conditional mean. Section A.2 solves the discrete Poisson equation (I−Ph)​χ=eh(I-P_{h})\chi=e_{h} and shifts the target to ν\nu. This absorbs the leading conditional bias at transport cost O⁡(d​h3/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}); the remaining conditional mean is only O⁡(d​h5/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{5/2}).

  2. 2.

    A small conditional Stein kernel. Even after centering, the remaining fluctuation is still O⁡(d​h3/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}) in L2L^{2}, which is too large. Section A.3 instead estimates its conditional Stein kernel, which captures the smaller error relevant after Gaussian smoothing.

  3. 3.

    Corrector regularity from the bounded Hessian. The Stein kernel estimate requires Schatten-44 bounds on the corrector’s derivative. Section A.4 proves the Witten Laplacian multiplier estimate that supplies these bounds without higher derivatives of VV; here, we need to invoke numerous Malliavin derivative bounds and a sectorial functional calculus argument.

  4. 4.

    Gaussian smoothing. Section A.5 converts the conditional Stein kernel bound into a transport cost of O⁡(d​h5/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{5/2}) after convolution. This is the step that improves on accumulating the size of the fluctuation itself.

  5. 5.

    Accumulation and the implementable method. Section A.6 controls the predictor replacement and applies Lemma 3.3: contraction accumulates the smoothed error with a factor of order κ/h\kappa/h, giving invariant distribution bias O⁡(κ​d​h3/2)O(\kappa\sqrt{d}\,h^{3/2}). Section A.7 adds initialization and returns to the original units.

The main ideas have established precedents. Mattingly, Stuart, and Tretyakov [38] use the continuous Poisson equation to analyze stationary discretization error, while discrete Poisson equations were used by [32] and [36] to study sampling algorithms. The direct predecessor of our construction is the discrete corrector developed by Pedrotti and Whalley [44] for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. The Malliavin–Stein approach of Nourdin and Peccati is presented in [40], and the Stein kernel representation used here is from Nourdin, Peccati, and Swan [39, Proposition 3.7]. The independent Gaussian convolution bound is due to Paulin and Whalley [43, Theorem E.4]. In Lemma A.10, we give a more direct transport proof of the preceding result with sharp numerical constant. The subsequent geometric accumulation is the standard contractive coupling argument; see [17, Chapter 4]. Here the work is to combine these tools with the corrector and its Schatten derivative estimates under C2C^{2} regularity.

A.1 Auxiliary proofs for the Heun upper bound

Throughout the appendix, XtxX_{t}^{x} denotes the Langevin diffusion (2.1) started from xx. We first record elementary bounds on its trajectory.

Lemma A.1 (Displacement estimates).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for 0<t⩽h00<t\leqslant h_{0} and x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

𝔼​∥Xtx−x∥2⩽C⁡{d​t+t2​∥∇V​(x)∥2};\mathbb{E}\lVert X_{t}^{x}-x\rVert^{2}\leqslant C\,\bigl\{dt+t^{2}\,\lVert\nabla V(x)\rVert^{2}\bigr\}\,; (A.1)

if X0∼πX_{0}\sim\pi, then

𝔼​∥Xt−X0∥2⩽C​d​t.\mathbb{E}\lVert X_{t}-X_{0}\rVert^{2}\leqslant Cdt\,. (A.2)
Proof.

The pointwise estimate is [17, Lemma 4.1.8] with deterministic initial state, β=1\beta=1, and t⩽h0⩽1/3t\leqslant h_{0}\leqslant 1/3. For a stationary initial state, apply the same lemma and use ∫∥∇V∥2​𝑑π=∫Δ​V​𝑑π⩽d\int\lVert\nabla V\rVert^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi=\int\Delta V\,\mathrm{d}\pi\leqslant d. ∎

We next prove Proposition 3.2 and Lemma 3.3, stated in Section 3.

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

so ∇V​(x)−∇V​(y)=Hinit​(x−y)\nabla V(x)-\nabla V(y)=H_{\mathrm{init}}\,(x-y) and ∇V​(Xhpred)−∇V​(Yhpred)=Hpred​(Xhpred−Yhpred)\nabla V(X_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}})-\nabla V(Y_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}})=H_{\mathrm{pred}}\,(X_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}}-Y_{h}^{\mathrm{pred}}). The predictor difference is (Id−h​Hinit)​(x−y)(I_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{init}})(x-y). Substitution into the update (2.3) therefore yields

X+−Y+={Id−h2​Hinit−h2​Hpred​(Id−h​Hinit)}​(x−y)=12​{Id+(Id−h​Hpred)​(Id−h​Hinit)}​(x−y).\begin{split}X^{+}-Y^{+}&=\bigl\{I_{d}-\tfrac{h}{2}\,H_{\mathrm{init}}-\tfrac{h}{2}\,H_{\mathrm{pred}}\,(I_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{init}})\bigr\}(x-y)\\ &=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bigl\{I_{d}+(I_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{pred}})(I_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{init}})\bigr\}(x-y)\,.\end{split} (A.3)

Both HinitH_{\mathrm{init}} and HpredH_{\mathrm{pred}} are symmetric with eigenvalues in [κ−1,1][\kappa^{-1},1]. If 0<h⩽10<h\leqslant 1, the eigenvalues of Id−h​HinitI_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{init}} and Id−h​HpredI_{d}-hH_{\mathrm{pred}} lie in [0,1−h/κ][0,1-h/\kappa]; their operator norms are therefore at most 1−h/κ1-h/\kappa. ∥X+−Y+∥⩽1+(1−h/κ)22​∥x−y∥⩽(1−h2​κ)​∥x−y∥.\lVert X^{+}-Y^{+}\rVert\leqslant\frac{1+(1-h/\kappa)^{2}}{2}\,\lVert x-y\rVert\leqslant\Bigl(1-\frac{h}{2\kappa}\Bigr)\,\lVert x-y\rVert\,.

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Let 0<h⩽10<h\leqslant 1. For j⩾1j\geqslant 1, contractivity gives

W2​(ν​(KhHeun)j+1,ν​(KhHeun)j)⩽ρj−1​W2​(ν​(KhHeun)2,ν​KhHeun).W_{2}\bigl(\nu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{j+1},\nu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{j}\bigr)\leqslant\rho^{j-1}W_{2}\bigl(\nu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{2},\nu K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}\bigr)\,.

A.2 The corrector and the discrete Poisson equation

The Heun method averages the force at the starting point and the predictor. For the analysis, replace the predictor by the exact endpoint and define

X~hx≔x−h2​{∇V​(x)+∇V​(Xhx)}+2​Bh,K~h​(x,⋅)≔Law⁡(X~hx).\widetilde{X}_{h}^{x}\coloneqq x-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(x)+\nabla V(X_{h}^{x})\}+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\,,\qquad\widetilde{K}_{h}(x,\cdot)\coloneqq\operatorname{Law}(\widetilde{X}_{h}^{x})\,. (A.4)

This auxiliary step uses the same Brownian motion as the exact diffusion. Section A.6 bounds the cost of replacing its exact endpoint by the implementable predictor.

Start both processes at X0∼πX_{0}\sim\pi. Their difference is the trapezoidal quadrature error

ℰh≔X~h−Xh=∫0h∇V​(Xt)​𝑑t−h2​{∇V​(X0)+∇V​(Xh)}.\mathcal{E}_{h}\coloneqq\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h}=\int_{0}^{h}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(X_{h})\}\,. (A.5)

We construct a corrector for its conditional mean eh​(Xh)≔𝔼⁡[ℰh∣Xh]e_{h}(X_{h})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}_{h}\mid X_{h}].

Our sign convention is numerical minus exact in (A.5), so the integral term in ehe_{h} has a positive sign. Conditionally on XhX_{h}, reversibility makes the reversed path (Xh−t)0⩽t⩽h(X_{h-t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} a Langevin diffusion started from XhX_{h}, so 𝔼[∇V(Xt)∣Xh]=(Ph−t∇V)(Xh)\mathbb{E}[\nabla V(X_{t})\mid X_{h}]=(P_{h-t}\nabla V)(X_{h}) for 0⩽t⩽h0\leqslant t\leqslant h. Taking conditional means in (A.5) term by term and substituting t↦h−tt\mapsto h-t in the integral gives

eh=∫0hPt​(∇V)​𝑑t−h2​{∇V+Ph​(∇V)},e_{h}=\int_{0}^{h}P_{t}(\nabla V)\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{h}{2}\,\bigl\{\nabla V+P_{h}(\nabla V)\bigr\}\,, (A.6)

as vector fields on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Invariance and ∫∇V​𝑑π=0\int\nabla V\,\mathrm{d}\pi=0 show that ehe_{h} integrates to zero against π\pi. Define the corrector χ\chi as the solution of the discrete Poisson equation

(I−Ph)​χ=eh,equivalentlyχ=(I−Ph)−1​eh.(I-P_{h})\chi=e_{h}\,,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\chi=(I-P_{h})^{-1}e_{h}\,. (A.7)

On the mean-zero subspace of L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi), the spectral gap gives ∥Ph∥⩽e−h/κ<1\lVert P_{h}\rVert\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-h/\kappa}<1 for every h>0h>0. Thus, the equation has a unique solution in that subspace, with the Neumann series representation

χ=∑n=0∞Phn​eh=∑n=0∞Pn​h​ehin ​L2​(π).\chi=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{h}^{n}e_{h}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{nh}e_{h}\qquad\text{in }L^{2}(\pi)\,. (A.8)

Indeed, iterating χ=eh+Ph​χ\chi=e_{h}+P_{h}\chi gives

χ−∑n=0NPn​heh=P(N+1)​hχ,∥P(N+1)​hχ∥L2​(π)⩽e−(N+1)h/κ∥χ∥L2​(π)⟶0.\chi-\sum_{n=0}^{N}P_{nh}e_{h}=P_{(N+1)h}\chi\,,\qquad\lVert P_{(N+1)h}\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-(N+1)h/\kappa}\,\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\longrightarrow 0\,.

On the mean-zero subspace, the semigroup identity

∫0hPt​𝑑t=(−L)−1​(I−Ph)\int_{0}^{h}P_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t=(-L)^{-1}(I-P_{h})

allows us to solve (A.7) directly. Substitution in (A.6), followed by Ph=eh​LP_{h}=\mathrm{e}^{hL}, gives

χ\displaystyle\chi ={(−L)−1−h2​(I−Ph)−1​(I+Ph)}​(∇V)\displaystyle=\bigl\{(-L)^{-1}-\tfrac{h}{2}\,(I-P_{h})^{-1}(I+P_{h})\bigr\}(\nabla V) (A.9)
=h​{(−h​L)−1−12​coth⁡(−h​L2)}​(∇V)=h​r​(−h​L)​(∇V).\displaystyle=h\,\Bigl\{(-hL)^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}\,\coth\Bigl(\frac{-hL}{2}\Bigr)\Bigr\}(\nabla V)=h\,r(-hL)(\nabla V)\,.

The last equality defines the scalar function

r⁡(z)≔1z−12​coth⁡z2,r⁡(0)≔0.r(z)\coloneqq\frac{1}{z}-\frac{1}{2}\,\coth\frac{z}{2}\,,\quad r(0)\coloneqq 0\,.

|r⁡(z)|⩽C​min⁡{z,1}⩽C​z,z⩾0.\lvert r(z)\rvert\leqslant C\min\{z,1\}\leqslant C\sqrt{z}\,,\qquad z\geqslant 0\,.

∥χ∥L2​(π)2\displaystyle\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2} =h2​∑j∈[d]∥r⁡(−h​L)​(∂jV)∥L2​(π)2⩽C​h3​∑j∈[d]∥(−L)1/2​(∂jV)∥L2​(π)2\displaystyle=h^{2}\sum_{j\in[d]}\lVert r(-hL)(\partial_{j}V)\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}\leqslant Ch^{3}\sum_{j\in[d]}\lVert(-L)^{1/2}(\partial_{j}V)\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2} (A.10)
=Ch3∑j∈[d]∫∥∇∂jV∥2dπ=Ch3∫∥∇2V∥HS2dπ⩽Cdh3.\displaystyle=Ch^{3}\sum_{j\in[d]}\int\lVert\nabla\partial_{j}V\rVert^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi=Ch^{3}\int\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi\leqslant Cdh^{3}\,.

W22​((I+χ)#​π,π)⩽∥χ∥L2​(π)2⩽C​d​h3.W_{2}^{2}((I+\chi)_{\#}\pi,\pi)\leqslant\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}\leqslant Cdh^{3}\,.

A.3 Malliavin–Stein kernel estimate

We now couple the auxiliary step from ν=(I+χ)#​π\nu=(I+\chi)_{\#}\pi to another sample from ν\nu. Start a stationary diffusion (Xt)0⩽t⩽h(X_{t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} at X0∼πX_{0}\sim\pi. Let X¯t\overline{X}_{t} be the diffusion started at X0+χ⁡(X0)X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}), using the same Brownian path, and set

X¯~h≔X0+χ⁡(X0)−h2​{∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))+∇V​(X¯h)}+2​Bh∼ν​K~h.\widetilde{\overline{X}}_{h}\coloneqq X_{0}+\chi(X_{0})-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))+\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})\}+\sqrt{2}\,B_{h}\sim\nu\widetilde{K}_{h}\,.

We retain ℰh=X~h−Xh\mathcal{E}_{h}=\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h} for the raw quadrature error and write ℰhcorr\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}} for the error after shifting the initial distribution and the reference endpoint by the corrector. Since Xh+χ⁡(Xh)∼νX_{h}+\chi(X_{h})\sim\nu, decompose this corrected error into its conditional mean and centered fluctuation:

ℰhcorr\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}} ≔X¯~h−{Xh+χ⁡(Xh)}=m⁡(Xh)+R,\displaystyle\coloneqq\widetilde{\overline{X}}_{h}-\{X_{h}+\chi(X_{h})\}=m(X_{h})+R\,, (A.11)
m⁡(Xh)\displaystyle m(X_{h}) ≔𝔼[ℰhcorr∣Xh],𝔼[R∣Xh]=0.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}}\mid X_{h}]\,,\qquad\mathbb{E}[R\mid X_{h}]=0\,.

Using the diffusion equation for XhX_{h} and adding and subtracting the term h2​{∇V​(X0)+∇V​(Xh)}\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(X_{h})\}, we obtain from (A.5) the pathwise identity

ℰhcorr=χ⁡(X0)+ℰh−χ⁡(Xh)−h2​{∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))−∇V​(X0)+∇V​(X¯h)−∇V​(Xh)}.\begin{split}\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}}={}&\chi(X_{0})+\mathcal{E}_{h}-\chi(X_{h})\\ &-\frac{h}{2}\,\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})-\nabla V(X_{h})\}\,.\end{split} (A.12)

The next two lemmas bound its total size and its conditional mean.

Lemma A.2 (Second moment of the corrected local error).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0},

𝔼​∥ℰhcorr∥2⩽C​d​h3.\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}}\rVert^{2}\leqslant Cdh^{3}\,.
Proof.

Stationarity and (A.10) control the two corrector terms in (A.12). The quadrature term satisfies, by 11-Lipschitzness and (A.2),

∥ℰh∥L2⩽∫0h∥Xt−X0∥L2​𝑑t+h2​∥Xh−X0∥L2⩽C​d​h3.\lVert\mathcal{E}_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}}\leqslant\int_{0}^{h}\lVert X_{t}-X_{0}\rVert_{L^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t+\frac{h}{2}\,\lVert X_{h}-X_{0}\rVert_{L^{2}}\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{3}}\,.
