∥X¯h−Xh∥⩽e−h/κ∥χ(X0)∥.\lVert\overline{X}_{h}-X_{h}\rVert\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-h/\kappa}\,\lVert\chi(X_{0})\rVert\,. (A.13)

Consequently, each force increment on the second line of (A.12) is bounded by ∥χ⁡(X0)∥\lVert\chi(X_{0})\rVert. The triangle inequality in L2L^{2} now gives ∥ℰhcorr∥L2⩽(2+h)​∥χ∥L2​(π)+C​d​h3\lVert\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}}\rVert_{L^{2}}\leqslant(2+h)\,\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}+C\sqrt{dh^{3}}, proving the claim. ∎

Lemma A.3 (Conditional mean bound).

For every h>0h>0,

∥m∥L2​(π)⩽h​∥χ∥L2​(π).\lVert m\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leqslant h\,\lVert\chi\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\,.
Proof.

Reversibility and the discrete Poisson equation give

𝔼⁡[χ⁡(X0)+ℰh−χ⁡(Xh)∣Xh]=Ph​χ​(Xh)+eh​(Xh)−χ⁡(Xh)=0.\mathbb{E}[\chi(X_{0})+\mathcal{E}_{h}-\chi(X_{h})\mid X_{h}]=P_{h}\chi(X_{h})+e_{h}(X_{h})-\chi(X_{h})=0\,.

Thus (A.12) implies

m⁡(Xh)=−h2​𝔼​[∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))−∇V​(X0)+∇V​(X¯h)−∇V​(Xh)∣Xh].m(X_{h})=-\frac{h}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})+\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})-\nabla V(X_{h})\mid X_{h}\bigr]\,.

Both increments are bounded by ∥χ⁡(X0)∥\lVert\chi(X_{0})\rVert, by 11-Lipschitzness and (A.13). Conditional Jensen’s inequality proves the result. ∎

The conditional mean therefore has size ∥m∥L2​(π)⩽C​d​h5\lVert m\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leqslant C\sqrt{dh^{5}}. To obtain the same transport cost for the centered fluctuation RR after Gaussian smoothing, we bound its conditional Stein kernel.

For a vector field φ\varphi, let ∇φ\nabla\varphi have columns ∇φj\nabla\varphi_{j}. In this convention, a Stein kernel of a centered random vector RR is a matrix field τR\tau_{R} satisfying

𝔼⟨R,φ(R)⟩=𝔼tr{τR(R)∇φ(R)⊤}\mathbb{E}\langle R\,,\varphi(R)\rangle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\{\tau_{R}(R)\nabla\varphi(R)^{\top}\} (A.14)

for smooth test fields with bounded derivative. We use the classical Malliavin representation of this kernel [39, Proposition 3.7], together with a Schatten norm estimate that preserves the desired dependence on dd. Background and notation are in Sections E.3, E.2 and E.1.

Lemma A.4 (Malliavin–Stein kernel estimate).

Let R∈L2​(Ω,ℝd)R\in L^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) be a centered, Malliavin-differentiable random vector over an isonormal Gaussian probability space with Cameron–Martin space ℋ\mathcal{H}, and suppose that DG​R∈L4​(Ω,𝔖4)D_{G}R\in L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). Then the law of RR has a Stein kernel τR\tau_{R} satisfying

𝔼​∥τR∥HS2⩽∥DG​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)4,\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\leqslant\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}^{4}\,,

where DG​R:ℋ→ℝdD_{G}R:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the Malliavin derivative of RR.

Proof.

The representation in [39, Proposition 3.7], transposed to match (A.14), gives

τR​(R)=𝔼⁡[(DG​R)​(−DG​ℒOU−1​R)∗∣R].\tau_{R}(R)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(D_{G}R)(-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}R)^{*}\mid R\bigr]\,.

Here, ℒOU\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}} is the Gaussian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator and (𝒬t)t≥0(\mathcal{Q}_{t})_{t\geq 0} its Mehler semigroup. The pseudoinverse and gradient commutation formulas give

−DG​ℒOU−1​R=∫0∞e−t​𝒬t​DG​R​𝑑t.-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}R=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\mathcal{Q}_{t}D_{G}R\,\mathrm{d}t\,. (A.15)

Jensen’s inequality in the Mehler representation makes 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} a contraction on L4​(Ω,𝔖4)L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). Minkowski’s inequality in (A.15) therefore gives

∥−DG​ℒOU−1​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽∥DG​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4).\lVert-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\,.

Conditional Jensen, the Schatten inequality ∥A​B∗∥𝔖2⩽∥A∥𝔖4​∥B∥𝔖4\lVert AB^{*}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}\leqslant\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\,\lVert B\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}, and Cauchy–Schwarz imply

𝔼​∥τR∥HS2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2} ⩽𝔼⁡[∥DG​R∥𝔖42​∥−DG​ℒOU−1​R∥𝔖42]⩽∥DG​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)4.∎\displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}^{2}\,\lVert-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}R\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}^{2}\bigr]\leqslant\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}^{4}\,.\qed

We now return to the fluctuation RR defined in (A.11). By Lemma A.4, the desired conditional Stein kernel bound reduces to controlling DG​RD_{G}R in L4​(Ω,𝔖4)L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). For each fixed endpoint Xh=yX_{h}=y, reversibility identifies the law of the reversed path with that of a Langevin diffusion started from yy. We realize this diffusion on canonical Wiener space and write DGD_{G} for the Malliavin derivative with respect to its driving Brownian path. In this realization, DG​m​(Xh)=0D_{G}m(X_{h})=0. Differentiating the representation (A.12) of ℰhcorr\mathcal{E}_{h}^{\mathrm{corr}} introduces ∇χ​(X0)\nabla\chi(X_{0}), so we first record the required regularity estimate for the corrector, proved later in Section A.4.

Lemma A.5 (Corrector derivative).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for every h>0h>0, the corrector in (A.7) satisfies

∥∇χ∥L4​(π,𝔖4)⩽C​d1/4​h.\lVert\nabla\chi\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h\,.
Proposition A.6 (Conditional 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4} derivative).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, the fluctuation RR in (A.11) satisfies

∥DG​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽C​d1/4​h3/2.\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\,. (A.16)

The norm averages over both the endpoint Xh∼πX_{h}\sim\pi and the Brownian realization with that endpoint fixed. Consequently, it has conditional Stein kernels τXh\tau_{X_{h}} such that

𝔼​∥τXh∥HS2⩽C​d​h6.\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{X_{h}}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\leqslant Cdh^{6}\,. (A.17)
Proof.

Condition on Xh=yX_{h}=y. By reversibility, the conditional law of (Xh−t)0⩽t⩽h(X_{h-t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} is the law of a Langevin diffusion started from yy, which we realize on canonical Wiener space. Write ℋ≔L2​([0,h],ℝd)\mathcal{H}\coloneqq L^{2}([0,h];\mathbb{R}^{d}), let GG be the associated isonormal Gaussian process over ℋ\mathcal{H}, and define

𝒥t≔DG​Xh−t:ℋ→ℝd,0⩽t⩽h.\mathcal{J}_{t}\coloneqq D_{G}X_{h-t}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\,,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant h\,.

Thus, 𝒥t\mathcal{J}_{t} is the Malliavin derivative of the reversed path at time tt. To identify it, fix f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H} and shift the canonical Brownian path in the Cameron–Martin direction t↦∫0tfs​𝑑st\mapsto\int_{0}^{t}f_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s. Differentiating the resulting Langevin SDE with respect to this shift shows that

dd​t​(𝒥t​f)=−∇2V​(Xh−t)​𝒥t​f+2​ft,𝒥0​f=0.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,(\mathcal{J}_{t}f)=-\nabla^{2}V(X_{h-t})\mathcal{J}_{t}f+\sqrt{2}\,f_{t}\,,\qquad\mathcal{J}_{0}f=0\,.

For 0⩽s⩽t⩽h0\leqslant s\leqslant t\leqslant h, let Jt,sJ_{t,s} be the homogeneous evolution operator, characterized by

dd​t​Jt,s=−∇2V​(Xh−t)​Jt,s,Js,s=I.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,J_{t,s}=-\nabla^{2}V(X_{h-t})J_{t,s}\,,\qquad J_{s,s}=I\,.

For fixed ss and v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, convexity of VV gives

dd​t​∥Jt,s​v∥2=−2​⟨Jt,s​v,∇2V​(Xh−t)​Jt,s​v⟩⩽0.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\lVert J_{t,s}v\rVert^{2}=-2\,\langle J_{t,s}v,\nabla^{2}V(X_{h-t})J_{t,s}v\rangle\leqslant 0\,.

Since Js,s=IJ_{s,s}=I, it follows that ∥Jt,s​v∥⩽∥v∥\lVert J_{t,s}v\rVert\leqslant\lVert v\rVert, and hence ∥Jt,s∥𝔖∞⩽1\lVert J_{t,s}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}}\leqslant 1. For every f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H}, variation of constants now yields

𝒥t​f=2​∫0tJt,s​fs​𝑑s.\mathcal{J}_{t}f=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}J_{t,s}f_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\,.

Cauchy–Schwarz and the bound on Jt,sJ_{t,s} give ∥𝒥t∥𝔖∞⩽2​t\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}}\leqslant\sqrt{2t}. The integral kernel representation gives

∥𝒥t∥𝔖22=2​∫0t∥Jt,s∥𝔖22​𝑑s⩽2​𝑑t.\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}^{2}=2\int_{0}^{t}\lVert J_{t,s}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\leqslant 2dt\,.

In summary,

∥𝒥t∥𝔖∞⩽2​t,∥𝒥t∥𝔖2⩽2​d​t.\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}}\leqslant\sqrt{2t}\,,\qquad\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}\leqslant\sqrt{2dt}\,. (A.18)

Hölder’s inequality for the singular values therefore gives

∥𝒥t∥𝔖4⩽∥𝒥t∥𝔖∞1/2​∥𝒥t∥𝔖21/2⩽2​t​d1/4.\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\leqslant\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}}^{1/2}\,\lVert\mathcal{J}_{t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}^{1/2}\leqslant\sqrt{2t}\,d^{1/4}\,. (A.19)

Because Xh=yX_{h}=y is held fixed when differentiating with respect to the driving Brownian path, DG​{m⁡(Xh)}=DG​{χ⁡(Xh)}=0D_{G}\{m(X_{h})\}=D_{G}\{\chi(X_{h})\}=0 as they depend only on this endpoint. Differentiating (A.12) gives

DG​R=DG​{χ⁡(X0)}+DG​ℰh−h2​DG​{∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))−∇V​(X0)}−h2​DG​{∇V​(X¯h)−∇V​(Xh)}.\begin{split}D_{G}R={}&D_{G}\{\chi(X_{0})\}+D_{G}\mathcal{E}_{h}\\ &\qquad{}-\frac{h}{2}\,D_{G}\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})\}-\frac{h}{2}\,D_{G}\{\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})-\nabla V(X_{h})\}\,.\end{split}

We estimate these four terms in turn. The Malliavin chain rule first gives

DG{χ(X0)}=∇χ(X0)⊤DGX0=∇χ(X0)⊤𝒥h.D_{G}\{\chi(X_{0})\}=\nabla\chi(X_{0})^{\top}D_{G}X_{0}=\nabla\chi(X_{0})^{\top}\mathcal{J}_{h}\,.

Using (A.18), then averaging over the reverse noise and the stationary endpoint, gives

∥DG​{χ⁡(X0)}∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽2​h​∥∇χ∥L4​(π,𝔖4)⩽C​d1/4​h3/2,\lVert D_{G}\{\chi(X_{0})\}\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant\sqrt{2h}\,\lVert\nabla\chi\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\,, (A.20)

where the last inequality is Lemma A.5.

We next bound DG​ℰhD_{G}\mathcal{E}_{h}. Applying the Malliavin chain rule to the formula for ℰh=X~h−Xh\mathcal{E}_{h}=\widetilde{X}_{h}-X_{h} in (A.5) gives

DG​ℰh=∫0h∇2V​(Xt)​𝒥h−t​dt−h2​∇2V​(X0)​𝒥h.\begin{split}D_{G}\mathcal{E}_{h}={}&\int_{0}^{h}\nabla^{2}V(X_{t})\mathcal{J}_{h-t}\,\mathrm{d}t-\frac{h}{2}\,\nabla^{2}V(X_{0})\mathcal{J}_{h}\,.\end{split}

This uses 𝒥0=DG​Xh=0\mathcal{J}_{0}=D_{G}X_{h}=0 because the endpoint Xh=yX_{h}=y is held fixed. Using ∥∇2V∥op⩽1\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 1, Minkowski’s inequality, and (A.19), we now obtain

∥DG​ℰh∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽∫0h∥𝒥h−t∥𝔖4​dt+h2​∥𝒥h∥𝔖4⩽2​d1/4​{∫0hh−t​dt+h2​h}⩽C​d1/4​h3/2.\begin{split}\lVert D_{G}\mathcal{E}_{h}\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}&\leqslant\int_{0}^{h}\lVert\mathcal{J}_{h-t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\,\mathrm{d}t+\frac{h}{2}\,\lVert\mathcal{J}_{h}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\leqslant\sqrt{2}\,d^{1/4}\,\Bigl\{\int_{0}^{h}\sqrt{h-t}\,\mathrm{d}t+\frac{h}{2}\,\sqrt{h}\Bigr\}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\,.\end{split}

For the term DG​{∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))−∇V​(X0)}D_{G}\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})\}, the chain rule gives

DG{∇V(X0+χ(X0))−∇V(X0)}={∇2V(X0+χ(X0))(I+∇χ(X0)⊤)−∇2V(X0)}𝒥h.\begin{split}&D_{G}\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})\}=\bigl\{\nabla^{2}V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))(I+\nabla\chi(X_{0})^{\top})-\nabla^{2}V(X_{0})\bigr\}\mathcal{J}_{h}\,.\end{split}

Using ∥∇2V∥op⩽1\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 1, Lemma A.5, (A.18), and (A.19), we obtain

h2​∥DG​{∇V​(X0+χ⁡(X0))−∇V​(X0)}∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽C​d1/4​h3/2.\begin{split}&\frac{h}{2}\,\lVert D_{G}\{\nabla V(X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}))-\nabla V(X_{0})\}\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\,.\end{split}

It remains to bound DG​{∇V​(X¯h)−∇V​(Xh)}D_{G}\{\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})-\nabla V(X_{h})\}. Return to the forward time coordinate, let X¯t\overline{X}_{t} be the diffusion started from X0+χ⁡(X0)X_{0}+\chi(X_{0}) with the same Brownian path, and put ηt≔X¯t−Xt\eta_{t}\coloneqq\overline{X}_{t}-X_{t}. Then DG​Xt=𝒥h−tD_{G}X_{t}=\mathcal{J}_{h-t} and adding and subtracting ∇2V​(X¯t)​𝒥h−t\nabla^{2}V(\overline{X}_{t})\mathcal{J}_{h-t} gives

dd​t​DG​ηt=−∇2V(X¯t)DGηt−{∇2V(X¯t)−∇2V(Xt)}𝒥h−t,DGη0=∇χ(X0)⊤𝒥h.\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,D_{G}\eta_{t}={}&-\nabla^{2}V(\overline{X}_{t})D_{G}\eta_{t}-\{\nabla^{2}V(\overline{X}_{t})-\nabla^{2}V(X_{t})\}\mathcal{J}_{h-t}\,,\qquad D_{G}\eta_{0}=\nabla\chi(X_{0})^{\top}\mathcal{J}_{h}\,.\end{split}

The fundamental solution of the homogeneous equation is a contraction. Since ∥∇2V​(X¯t)−∇2V​(Xt)∥op⩽2\lVert\nabla^{2}V(\overline{X}_{t})-\nabla^{2}V(X_{t})\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 2, variation of constants, Lemma A.5, (A.18), and (A.19) bound the initial variation by C​d1/4​h3/2Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2} and the forcing at time tt by C​d1/4​h−tCd^{1/4}\sqrt{h-t}. Integrating the latter gives

∥DG​ηh∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽C​h​∥∇χ∥L4​(π,𝔖4)+2​∫0h∥𝒥h−t∥𝔖4​dt⩽C​d1/4​h3/2.\begin{split}\lVert D_{G}\eta_{h}\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}&\leqslant C\sqrt{h}\,\lVert\nabla\chi\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}+2\int_{0}^{h}\lVert\mathcal{J}_{h-t}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\,\mathrm{d}t\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\,.\end{split}

Because XhX_{h} is fixed under the conditioning, DG​X¯h=DG​ηhD_{G}\overline{X}_{h}=D_{G}\eta_{h}. Thus,

h2​∥DG​{∇V​(X¯h)−∇V​(Xh)}∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)⩽C​d1/4​h5/2.\begin{split}&\frac{h}{2}\,\lVert D_{G}\{\nabla V(\overline{X}_{h})-\nabla V(X_{h})\}\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant Cd^{1/4}h^{5/2}\,.\end{split} (A.21)

Combining (A.20)–(A.21) and using h⩽h0⩽1h\leqslant h_{0}\leqslant 1 proves (A.16).

For π\pi-almost every endpoint yy, Lemma A.4 gives a Stein kernel τy\tau_{y} satisfying

𝔼⁡[∥τy∥HS2∣Xh=y]⩽𝔼⁡[∥DG​R∥𝔖44∣Xh=y].\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert\tau_{y}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\mid X_{h}=y\bigr]\leqslant\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}^{4}\mid X_{h}=y\bigr]\,.

Since Xh∼πX_{h}\sim\pi, integrating this inequality over the endpoint and using the tower property gives

𝔼​∥τXh∥HS2⩽𝔼​∥DG​R∥𝔖44=∥DG​R∥L4​(Ω,𝔖4)4⩽(C​d1/4​h3/2)4=C4​d​h6,\begin{split}\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{X_{h}}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}&\leqslant\mathbb{E}\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}^{4}=\lVert D_{G}R\rVert_{L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}^{4}\leqslant\bigl(Cd^{1/4}h^{3/2}\bigr)^{4}=C^{4}dh^{6}\,,\end{split}

where the inequality is (A.16). Renaming the universal constant proves (A.17). ∎

A.4 A Schatten-44 multiplier estimate for the Witten Laplacian

The remaining input to Proposition A.6 is ∥∇χ∥L4​(π,𝔖4)≲d1/4​h\lVert\nabla\chi\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\lesssim d^{1/4}h. The Witten semigroup describes the evolution of spatial gradients under Langevin dynamics; Sections E.4 and E.5 recall the background. The argument has three steps. Lemma A.7 gives real time contraction on L∞​(π,𝔖∞)L^{\infty}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}) and complex time contraction on L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}). Lemma A.8 interpolates these estimates to L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) and bounds the resolvent there. Lemma A.9 then applies the general multiplier estimate of Lemma E.1 to bound the multiplier in ∇χ=h​r​(−h​L(1))​∇2V\nabla\chi=h\,r(-hL^{(1)})\,\nabla^{2}V. The exponent 44 is needed because the Stein kernel is a product of two operators in 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4}, and therefore belongs to 𝔖2\mathfrak{S}_{2}.

We use the 11-form generator and its semigroup

L(1)≔L−∇2V,L=Δ−∇V⋅∇,Pt(1)≔et​L(1),L^{(1)}\coloneqq L-\nabla^{2}V\,,\qquad L=\Delta-\nabla V\cdot\nabla\,,\qquad P_{t}^{(1)}\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{tL^{(1)}}\,,

acting columnwise on matrix fields. The Feynman–Kac representation [31, Proposition 3.2, equation (3.2)] is

(Pt(1)​M)​(x)=𝔼⁡[(Jtx)⊤​M​(Xtx)],Jtx≔Dx​Xtx.(P_{t}^{(1)}M)(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(J_{t}^{x})^{\top}M(X_{t}^{x})\bigr]\,,\qquad J_{t}^{x}\coloneqq D_{x}X_{t}^{x}\,.

Here, JtxJ_{t}^{x} is the Jacobian with respect to the starting point. It satisfies ∂tJtx=−∇2V​(Xtx)​Jtx\partial_{t}J_{t}^{x}=-\nabla^{2}V(X_{t}^{x})J_{t}^{x}, hence ∥Jtx∥op⩽e−t/κ\lVert J_{t}^{x}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-t/\kappa}. Section E.4 motivates the generator and transpose via the scalar chain rule and explains how the cited representation applies. We now record the resulting norm estimates.

Lemma A.7 (Contraction estimates for the Witten semigroup).

For every t⩾0t\geqslant 0 and 2⩽p⩽∞2\leqslant p\leqslant\infty,

∥Pt(1)M∥Lp​(π,𝔖p)⩽e−t/κ∥M∥Lp​(π,𝔖p).\lVert P_{t}^{(1)}M\rVert_{L^{p}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{p})}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-t/\kappa}\,\lVert M\rVert_{L^{p}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{p})}\,. (A.22)

On L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}), −L(1)-L^{(1)} is positive self-adjoint and

⟨M,−L(1)​M⟩L2​(π,𝔖2)=∫∥∇M∥HS2​dπ+∫∑j∈[d]⟨Mj,∇2V​Mj⟩​dπ.\begin{split}\langle M,-L^{(1)}M\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})}={}&\int\lVert\nabla M\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}\pi+\int\sum_{j\in[d]}\langle M_{j},\nabla^{2}V\,M_{j}\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\pi\,.\end{split} (A.23)

Consequently,

∥ez​L(1)​M∥L2​(π,𝔖2)⩽∥M∥L2​(π,𝔖2)whenever ​Re⁡z⩾0.\lVert\mathrm{e}^{zL^{(1)}}M\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})}\leqslant\lVert M\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})}\qquad\text{whenever }\operatorname{Re}z\geqslant 0\,. (A.24)
Proof.

The Feynman–Kac formula and the ideal property of Schatten norms give

∥Pt(1)M(x)∥𝔖p⩽e−t/κ𝔼∥M(Xtx)∥𝔖p.\lVert P_{t}^{(1)}M(x)\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{p}}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-t/\kappa}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert M(X_{t}^{x})\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{p}}\,.

Jensen’s inequality and stationarity give (A.22) for finite pp; the essential supremum gives the case p=∞p=\infty. Integration by parts proves (A.23) on smooth compactly supported fields. Closing this symmetric form defines the non-negative self-adjoint operator −L(1)-L^{(1)}, and the spectral theorem proves (A.24). ∎

The preceding lemma supplies the contraction estimates. We now interpolate its p=∞p=\infty and p=2p=2 bounds to obtain the complex time estimate needed for the multiplier. The interpolation and sectorial calculus facts used here are recalled in Section E.5.

Lemma A.8 (Dimension-free analyticity on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})).

The semigroup ez​L(1)\mathrm{e}^{zL^{(1)}} extends to a contractive analytic semigroup on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) in the sector |arg⁡z|<π/4\lvert\arg z\rvert<\uppi/4. In particular, −L(1)-L^{(1)} is sectorial on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}): its spectrum is contained in the closed sector {|argz|⩽π/4}\{\lvert\arg z\rvert\leqslant\uppi/4\}, and for each fixed ϑ∈(π/4,π/2)\vartheta\in(\uppi/4,\uppi/2) there is a constant CϑC_{\vartheta} such that

∥(z+L(1))−1∥L4​(π,𝔖4)→L4​(π,𝔖4)⩽Cϑ|z|whenever ​|arg⁡z|⩾ϑ.\lVert(z+L^{(1)})^{-1}\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})\to L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant\frac{C_{\vartheta}}{\lvert z\rvert}\qquad\text{whenever }\lvert\arg z\rvert\geqslant\vartheta\,. (A.25)
Proof.

The interpolation identity for Bochner–Schatten spaces (Section E.5) gives

[L∞​(π,𝔖∞),L2​(π,𝔖2)]1/2=L4​(π,𝔖4),[L^{\infty}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}),L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})]_{1/2}=L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})\,, (A.26)

isometrically [5].

Fix |θ|<π/4\lvert\theta\rvert<\uppi/4 and, for t>0t>0, consider on the strip 0⩽Re⁡ζ⩽10\leqslant\operatorname{Re}\zeta\leqslant 1 the analytic family

ℱ⁡(ζ)≔exp⁡(t​e2​𝒊​θ​ζ​L(1)).\mathcal{F}(\zeta)\coloneqq\exp(t\mathrm{e}^{2\bm{i}\theta\zeta}L^{(1)})\,.

If ζ=𝒊​y\zeta=\bm{i}y, then t​e2​𝒊​θ​ζ=t​e−2​θ​y>0t\mathrm{e}^{2\bm{i}\theta\zeta}=t\mathrm{e}^{-2\theta y}>0, so Lemma A.7 shows that ℱ⁡(𝒊​y)\mathcal{F}(\bm{i}y) is a contraction on L∞​(π,𝔖∞)L^{\infty}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}). If ζ=1+𝒊​y\zeta=1+\bm{i}y, then t​e−2​θ​y​e2​𝒊​θt\mathrm{e}^{-2\theta y}\mathrm{e}^{2\bm{i}\theta} has positive real part, so (A.24) shows that ℱ⁡(1+𝒊​y)\mathcal{F}(1+\bm{i}y) is a contraction on L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}). Stein’s interpolation theorem [51] at ζ=1/2\zeta=1/2 and (A.26) yield

∥exp⁡(t​e𝒊​θ​L(1))∥L4​(π,𝔖4)→L4​(π,𝔖4)⩽1.\lVert\exp(t\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\theta}L^{(1)})\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})\to L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant 1\,.

The argument is first applied on the dense compatible core L∞​(π,𝔖∞)∩L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{\infty}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{\infty})\cap L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}) and then extended to L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). Strong continuity on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) follows from the same density argument. This proves the first assertion.

The resolvent of −L(1)-L^{(1)} is the Laplace transform of the semigroup, and analyticity lets the integration ray be rotated by any angle below π/4\uppi/4, as in (E.4). Choosing the rotation as in Section E.5 gives (A.25) with Cϑ=1/sin⁡((ϑ−π/4)/2)C_{\vartheta}=1/\sin((\vartheta-\uppi/4)/2). ∎

Sectoriality puts the contour calculus of Section E.5 at our disposal, and with it the multiplier bound, uniform in the step size; the proof reduces to checking the hypotheses of Lemma E.1.

Lemma A.9 (Uniform 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4} Witten–Laplacian multiplier).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that for every h>0h>0,

∥r⁡(−h​L(1))∥L4​(π,𝔖4)→L4​(π,𝔖4)⩽C.\lVert r(-hL^{(1)})\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})\to L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})}\leqslant C\,. (A.27)
Proof.

We apply Lemma E.1 on 𝒳=L4​(π,𝔖4)\mathcal{X}=L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) with 𝒯=−L(1)\mathcal{T}=-L^{(1)} and f=rf=r, which also defines r⁡(−h​L(1))r(-hL^{(1)}) on this space. By Lemma A.8, −L(1)-L^{(1)} is sectorial of angle π/4\uppi/4, with constants depending only on the angle. Fix ϑ≔3​π/8\vartheta\coloneqq 3\uppi/8. It remains to verify the hypotheses on rr in the sector Σϑ≔{z∈ℂ∖{0}:|arg⁡z|<ϑ}\Sigma_{\vartheta}\coloneqq\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:\lvert\arg z\rvert<\vartheta\}, recalled in Section E.5, with r⁡(0)=0r(0)=0, r(∞)=−1/2r(\infty)=-1/2, and s=1s=1.

Holomorphy. The poles of coth⁡(z/2)\coth(z/2) are at 2​π​𝒊​k2\uppi\bm{i}k, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}. The pole at zero cancels with z−1z^{-1}, since 12​coth⁡(z/2)=z−1+z/12+O⁡(z3)\tfrac{1}{2}\coth(z/2)=z^{-1}+z/12+O(z^{3}); the other poles lie on the imaginary axis, outside Σϑ\Sigma_{\vartheta}. Thus rr is holomorphic in Σϑ\Sigma_{\vartheta} and in the disc {|z|<2π}\{\lvert z\rvert<2\uppi\}.

Behavior at zero. Since rr is holomorphic in {|z|<2π}\{\lvert z\rvert<2\uppi\} with r⁡(0)=0r(0)=0, there is a universal constant CC such that |r⁡(z)|⩽C​|z|\lvert r(z)\rvert\leqslant C\,\lvert z\rvert for |z|⩽1\lvert z\rvert\leqslant 1.

Behavior at infinity. The identity coth⁡(z/2)=1+2/(ez−1)\coth(z/2)=1+2/(\mathrm{e}^{z}-1) gives

r⁡(z)+12=1z−1ez−1.r(z)+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{z}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{z}-1}\,.

For z∈Σϑz\in\Sigma_{\vartheta}, we have Re⁡z⩾|z|​cos⁡ϑ\operatorname{Re}z\geqslant\lvert z\rvert\cos\vartheta, so |ez−1|⩾eRe⁡z−1⩾|z|​cos⁡ϑ\lvert\mathrm{e}^{z}-1\rvert\geqslant\mathrm{e}^{\operatorname{Re}z}-1\geqslant\lvert z\rvert\cos\vartheta. Hence |r⁡(z)+1/2|⩽(1+1/cos⁡ϑ)/|z|\lvert r(z)+1/2\rvert\leqslant(1+1/\cos\vartheta)/\lvert z\rvert.

Lemma E.1 now bounds ∥r⁡(−h​L(1))∥L4​(π,𝔖4)→L4​(π,𝔖4)\lVert r(-hL^{(1)})\rVert_{L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})\to L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})} uniformly in h>0h>0 by a universal constant, which proves (A.27). ∎

We can now differentiate the corrector and prove the deferred estimate.

Proof of Lemma A.5.

Gradient intertwining gives ∇Pt=Pt(1)∇\nabla P_{t}=P_{t}^{(1)}\nabla. Differentiate the finite partial sums in (A.8) and use (A.22) to pass to the limit in L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). Since ∇χ=h​r​(−h​L(1))​∇2V\nabla\chi=h\,r(-hL^{(1)})\,\nabla^{2}V, we can apply Lemma A.9 and the pointwise bound ∥∇2V∥𝔖4⩽d1/4\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\leqslant d^{1/4}. ∎

A.5 W2W_{2} estimates after Gaussian convolution

We next convert the conditional Stein kernel bound into a transport estimate. An independent Gaussian convolution bound of this form follows from [43, Theorem E.4 and Remark E.6(ii)]. The following direct proof sharpens its numerical constant. Its hypotheses require only a centered perturbation with a square-integrable Stein kernel; no density or Poincaré inequality for the perturbation is needed.

Lemma A.10 (Gaussian convolution inequality).

Let R∈L2​(Ω,ℝd)R\in L^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) be centered, suppose that its law admits a square-integrable Stein kernel τR\tau_{R}, and let ξ∼𝖭⁡(0,σ2​Id)\xi\sim\mathsf{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}) be independent of RR. Then,

W22​(Law⁡(R+ξ),Law⁡(ξ))⩽14​σ2​𝔼​∥τR∥HS2.W_{2}^{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(R+\xi),\operatorname{Law}(\xi)\bigr)\leqslant{\frac{1}{4\sigma^{2}}}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,.
Proof.

Set 𝖷θ≔ξ+θ​R\mathsf{X}_{\theta}\coloneqq\xi+\theta R, for 0⩽θ⩽10\leqslant\theta\leqslant 1. For φ∈Cc∞​(ℝd)\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the Stein identity (A.14), followed by Gaussian integration by parts, gives

dd​θ​𝔼​φ​(𝖷θ)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\,\mathbb{E}\varphi(\mathsf{X}_{\theta}) =𝔼⁡⟨R,∇φ​(𝖷θ)⟩=θ​𝔼​tr⁡{τR​∇2φ​(𝖷θ)}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\langle R,\nabla\varphi(\mathsf{X}_{\theta})\rangle=\theta\,\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\{\tau_{R}\nabla^{2}\varphi(\mathsf{X}_{\theta})\}
=θσ2​𝔼​⟨τR​ξ,∇φ​(𝖷θ)⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{\theta}{\sigma^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\langle\tau_{R}\,\xi,\nabla\varphi(\mathsf{X}_{\theta})\rangle\,.

Here the first integration by parts holds with ξ\xi fixed, and the second with RR fixed. Thus vθ​(𝖷θ)≔θσ2​𝔼​[τR​ξ∣𝖷θ]v_{\theta}(\mathsf{X}_{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{\theta}{\sigma^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}[\tau_{R}\,\xi\mid\mathsf{X}_{\theta}] is a velocity for the continuity equation of Law⁡(𝖷θ)\operatorname{Law}(\mathsf{X}_{\theta}). Conditional Jensen’s inequality and independence imply

∥vθ∥L2​(Law⁡(𝖷θ))2⩽θ2σ4​𝔼​∥τR​ξ∥2=θ2σ2​𝔼​∥τR∥HS2.\lVert v_{\theta}\rVert_{L^{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\mathsf{X}_{\theta}))}^{2}\leqslant\frac{\theta^{2}}{\sigma^{4}}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\,\xi\rVert^{2}=\frac{\theta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,.

The metric speed bound [4, Theorem 8.3.1] therefore yields

W2​(Law⁡(R+ξ),Law⁡(ξ))⩽∫01∥vθ∥L2​(Law⁡(𝖷θ))​𝑑θ⩽12​σ​(𝔼​∥τR∥HS2)1/2.∎W_{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(R+\xi),\operatorname{Law}(\xi)\bigr)\leqslant\int_{0}^{1}\lVert v_{\theta}\rVert_{L^{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\mathsf{X}_{\theta}))}\,\mathrm{d}\theta\leqslant\frac{1}{2\sigma}\,\bigl(\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}\,.\qed
Remark A.11 (Comparison with Paulin–Whalley).

Theorem E.4 and Remark E.6(ii) of [43] give the same squared Wasserstein bound with coefficient (log⁡2)/σ2(\log 2)/\sigma^{2}, by combining a relative entropy estimate with Gaussian Talagrand. The direct transport proof gives 1/(4​σ2)1/(4\sigma^{2}) under the same square-integrable Stein kernel assumption; their theorem additionally controls relative entropy. The numerical constant 1/41/4 is sharp: in dimension one, for independent R∼𝖭⁡(0,ε)R\sim\mathsf{N}(0,\varepsilon) and ξ∼𝖭⁡(0,σ2)\xi\sim\mathsf{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), one may take τR=ε\tau_{R}=\varepsilon, and

W22​(Law⁡(R+ξ),Law⁡(ξ))=(σ2+ε−σ)2∼ε24​σ2,ε↓0.W_{2}^{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(R+\xi),\operatorname{Law}(\xi)\bigr)=\bigl(\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\varepsilon}-\sigma\bigr)^{2}\sim\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\,,\qquad\varepsilon\downarrow 0\,.

The next lemma carries this Gaussian convolution estimate through one full auxiliary step. Its additional term pays for the change in the two force evaluations caused by perturbing the initial point. For the model update x↦x+2​h​Gx\mapsto x+\sqrt{2h}\,G, the comparison is simply between z+R+2​h​Gz+R+\sqrt{2h}\,G and z+2​h​Gz+\sqrt{2h}\,G, so the preceding lemma gives the Stein kernel cost divided by hh. Restoring the drift adds an O⁡(h​∥R∥2)O(h\,\lVert R\rVert_{2}) cost.

Lemma A.12 (W2W_{2} estimate for one auxiliary step).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 with the following property. Let 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0} and z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let R∈L2​(Ω,ℝd)R\in L^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{d}) be centered and independent of the Brownian motion driving the auxiliary step (A.4), with a law admitting a square-integrable Stein kernel τR\tau_{R}. W22​(Law⁡(X~hz+R),Law⁡(X~hz))⩽C⁡{𝔼​∥τR∥HS2h+h2​𝔼​∥R∥2}.W_{2}^{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(\widetilde{X}_{h}^{z+R}),\operatorname{Law}(\widetilde{X}_{h}^{z})\bigr)\leqslant C\,\Bigl\{\frac{\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}}{h}+h^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert R\rVert^{2}\Bigr\}\,. (A.28)

The same estimate holds conditionally on a preceding σ\sigma-field when zz is measurable with respect to it and the Brownian motion of the auxiliary step is fresh and independent of that field and RR.

Proof.

Let the auxiliary step from z+Rz+R be driven by a Brownian motion BB independent of RR, and the step from zz by a second Brownian motion B~\widetilde{B}; the joint law of (R,B,B~)(R,B,\widetilde{B}) is constructed as follows. 𝔼​∥δ∥2⩽18​h​𝔼​∥τR∥HS2,δ≔R+2​Bh−2​B~h.\mathbb{E}\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}\leqslant{\frac{1}{8h}}\,\mathbb{E}\lVert\tau_{R}\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\,,\qquad\delta\coloneqq R+\sqrt{2}B_{h}-\sqrt{2}\widetilde{B}_{h}\,. (A.29)

R+2​Bt−2​B~t=(1−th)​R+th​δ,R+\sqrt{2}B_{t}-\sqrt{2}\widetilde{B}_{t}=\Bigl(1-\frac{t}{h}\Bigr)\,R+\frac{t}{h}\,\delta\,,

whose norm never exceeds ∥R∥+∥δ∥\lVert R\rVert+\lVert\delta\rVert. By 11-Lipschitzness of ∇V\nabla V and Grönwall’s inequality, the diffusions Xtz+RX_{t}^{z+R} and XtzX_{t}^{z}, driven by BB and by B~\widetilde{B} respectively, therefore satisfy, for 0⩽t⩽h⩽h00\leqslant t\leqslant h\leqslant h_{0},

∥Xtz+R−Xtz∥⩽C⁡(∥R∥+∥δ∥).\lVert X_{t}^{z+R}-X_{t}^{z}\rVert\leqslant C\,\bigl(\lVert R\rVert+\lVert\delta\rVert\bigr)\,.

and the two preceding bounds, with h⩽1h\leqslant 1, give

A.7 Completion of the overdamped upper bound

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

The normalization in Section 2.1 turns (A.30) into (3.1). Existence and uniqueness follow from Proposition 3.2 and its rescaling.

Contractivity and invariance give, for a universal c0>0c_{0}>0,

W2​(μ​(KhHeun)N,π^hHeun)⩽e−c0​N​α​h​W2​(μ,π^hHeun).W_{2}(\mu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{N},\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-c_{0}N\alpha h}W_{2}(\mu,\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})\,.

Consequently,

W2​(μ​(KhHeun)N,π)⩽e−c0​N​α​h​{W2​(μ,π)+W2​(π,π^hHeun)}+W2​(π^hHeun,π).\begin{split}W_{2}(\mu(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})^{N},\pi)&\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-c_{0}N\alpha h}\,\bigl\{W_{2}(\mu,\pi)+W_{2}(\pi,\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}})\bigr\}+W_{2}(\widehat{\pi}_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}},\pi)\,.\end{split}

Squaring this inequality and applying (3.1) proves (3.2), after changing the universal constants.

Choose a sufficiently small universal c1>0c_{1}>0 and set

β​h=c1​h0​min⁡{1,(ε2κ​d)1/3},N=⌈C​κ​(β​h)−1​log⁡(e+α​W22​(μ,π)ε2)⌉.\beta h=c_{1}h_{0}\min\Bigl\{1,\Bigl(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa d}\Bigr)^{1/3}\Bigr\}\,,\qquad N=\Bigl\lceil C\kappa\,(\beta h)^{-1}\log\Bigl(\mathrm{e}+\frac{\alpha W_{2}^{2}(\mu,\pi)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\Bigr)\Bigr\rceil\,.

The two terms in (3.2) are then each at most ε2/2\varepsilon^{2}/2, proving the query bound for arbitrary initialization. If μ=δx⋆\mu=\delta_{x_{\star}}, strong convexity and integration by parts give

α​𝔼​∥X−x⋆∥2⩽𝔼⁡⟨∇V​(X),X−x⋆⟩=d,X∼π.\alpha\,\mathbb{E}\lVert X-x_{\star}\rVert^{2}\leqslant\mathbb{E}\langle\nabla V(X),X-x_{\star}\rangle=d\,,\qquad X\sim\pi\,.

For 0<ε⩽d/20<\varepsilon\leqslant\sqrt{d}/2, we have d/ε2⩾4d/\varepsilon^{2}\geqslant 4, and hence log⁡(e+d/ε2)⩽2​log⁡(d/ε2)\log(\mathrm{e}+d/\varepsilon^{2})\leqslant 2\log(d/\varepsilon^{2}). Since κ(βh)−1≲κ+κ4/3d1/3ε−2/3\kappa\,(\beta h)^{-1}\lesssim\kappa+\kappa^{4/3}d^{1/3}\varepsilon^{-2/3}, this gives (3.3).

Each iteration uses two gradient queries, which is absorbed in the universal constant. ∎

Appendix B Proof of the underdamped upper bound

We prove the ingredients and assemble the argument outlined in Section 4. Throughout this appendix, except Section B.6, the Langevin dynamics are normalized as in Section 2.1: V∈C2V\in C^{2}, κ−1​Id⪯∇2V⪯Id\kappa^{-1}I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq I_{d}, and γ=2\gamma=2. Unless another measure is specified, L2L^{2} norms are under the stationary phase space distribution, with auxiliary Gaussian noise included for quantities depending on the path. We use HS\mathrm{HS} and op\mathrm{op} for Hilbert–Schmidt and operator norms, respectively.

The goal is a one step Wasserstein error of C​d​h3C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3} from stationarity, which contraction turns into the second-order invariant distribution bound. The essential plan is to separate the error into a conditional mean and a centered remainder portion. The former would dominate the error when analyzed in L2L^{2}. However, if one works instead in the negative Sobolev norm, then one witnesses additional cancellations via careful Malliavin estimates, which can then be translated into Wasserstein guarantees via a new heat interpolation lemma; this is combined with standard estimates for the remainder in order to conclude.

More concretely, we proceed in four steps, which roughly follow the sequential flow of this appendix.

  1. 1.

    Conditional mean and centered fluctuation. For a stationary exact endpoint Zh∼𝝅Z_{h}\sim\bm{\pi}, Section B.2 decomposes the exact midpoint local error as ℰh≕mh​(Zh)+Rh\mathcal{E}_{h}\eqqcolon m_{h}(Z_{h})+R_{h}, with mh​(Zh)≔𝔼⁡[ℰh∣Zh]m_{h}(Z_{h})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}_{h}\mid Z_{h}] and 𝔼⁡[Rh∣Zh]=0\mathbb{E}[R_{h}\mid Z_{h}]=0.

  2. 2.

    Cancellation in the conditional mean. The weighted divergence of mhm_{h} determines its first-order effect on the distribution. The key point is that the negative Sobolev norm measures the smallest L2L^{2} size of a vector field possessing this divergence, detecting cancellations invisible in the size of mhm_{h}. Although ∥mh∥L2​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h2\lVert m_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}, Section B.3 proves ∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h3\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3} using its action on a Hermite decomposition. We mention that Section B.1 contains some initial details about the negative Sobolev norm.

  3. 3.

    From mean and fluctuation to transport. Section B.4 translates negative Sobolev bounds on the conditional mean, along with other L2L^{2} error and derivative bounds, into errors measured in the transport cost. These give bounds of O⁡(d​h3)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}) and O⁡(d​h7/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,h^{7/2}), respectively.

  4. 4.

    Predictor replacement and contraction. Section B.5 takes care of one additional minor detail of replacing the exact midpoint gradient by the gradient evaluated at the predictor. It then proves the one-step estimate and numerical contraction. Section B.6 combines them and returns to the original units, completing Theorem 4.1.

The separation of a local error into its conditional mean and a centered fluctuation is the organizing principle of local error analysis; see [17, Section 5.1.1 and Lemma 5.1.2]. For small perturbations, W2W_{2} is comparable to a weighted H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1} norm [45]; the minimum flux characterization of this norm is recalled in Section E.6, and Lemma B.5 proves the finite displacement bound used here. The same lemma extends the Gaussian transport estimate of [10, Lemma 4.11] to the stationary phase space distribution.

B.1 Normalization and the negative Sobolev norm on phase space

The invariant distribution is

𝝅⁡(d​x,d​p)≔π⁡(d​x)​𝖭​(0,Id)​(d​p),π⁡(d​x)∝e−V⁡(x)​d​x.\bm{\pi}(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}p)\coloneqq\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\,\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})(\mathrm{d}p)\,,\qquad\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x\,.

The exact underdamped generator and its adjoint in L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi}) are

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} ≔p⋅∇x−∇V⋅∇p+2(Δp−p⋅∇p),\displaystyle\coloneqq p\cdot\nabla_{x}-\nabla V\cdot\nabla_{p}+2\,(\Delta_{p}-p\cdot\nabla_{p})\,, (B.1)
ℒ†\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\dagger} ≔−p⋅∇x+∇V⋅∇p+2(Δp−p⋅∇p).\displaystyle\coloneqq-p\cdot\nabla_{x}+\nabla V\cdot\nabla_{p}+2\,(\Delta_{p}-p\cdot\nabla_{p})\,.

The Hamiltonian part is skew-adjoint, whereas the momentum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck part is self-adjoint. Thus ℒ†\mathcal{L}^{\dagger} generates the stationary reverse dynamics. We write (et​ℒ)t≥0(\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}})_{t\geq 0} for the forward semigroup and (et​ℒ†)t≥0(\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}})_{t\geq 0} for its L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi})-adjoint. For a vector field FF,

∥F∥L2​(𝝅)2≔∫∥F⁡(x,p)∥2​𝝅​(𝑑x,𝑑p);\lVert F\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\coloneqq\int\lVert F(x,p)\rVert^{2}\,\bm{\pi}(\mathrm{d}x,\mathrm{d}p)\,;

if FF depends only on xx, this equals ∥F∥L2​(π)2\lVert F\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}.

Let D≔(∇x,∇p)D\coloneqq(\nabla_{x},\nabla_{p}), and let δ𝝅≔D∗\delta_{\bm{\pi}}\coloneqq D^{*} be the adjoint in L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi}), characterized by

∫⟨D​φ,A⟩​𝑑𝝅=∫φ​δ𝝅​A​𝑑𝝅.\int\langle D\varphi,A\rangle\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}=\int\varphi\,\delta_{\bm{\pi}}A\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}\,.

For an ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued field FF on phase space, let δx\delta_{x} and δp\delta_{p} be the weighted divergences in the position and momentum variables, respectively:

δx​F\displaystyle\delta_{x}F ≔−∇x⋅F+⟨∇V,F⟩,\displaystyle\coloneqq-\nabla_{x}\cdot F+\langle\nabla V,F\rangle\,, δp​F\displaystyle\delta_{p}F ≔−∇p⋅F+⟨p,F⟩,\displaystyle\coloneqq-\nabla_{p}\cdot F+\langle p,F\rangle\,,
δ𝝅​(Fx,Fp)\displaystyle\delta_{\bm{\pi}}(F^{x},F^{p}) =δx​Fx+δp​Fp.\displaystyle=\delta_{x}F^{x}+\delta_{p}F^{p}\,.

The non-negative weighted Laplacian on phase space is

𝒜≔δ𝝅D=𝒜x+𝒜p,𝒜x≔−Δx+∇V⋅∇x,𝒜p≔−Δp+p⋅∇p.\mathcal{A}\coloneqq\delta_{\bm{\pi}}D=\mathcal{A}_{x}+\mathcal{A}_{p}\,,\qquad\mathcal{A}_{x}\coloneqq-\Delta_{x}+\nabla V\cdot\nabla_{x}\,,\qquad\mathcal{A}_{p}\coloneqq-\Delta_{p}+p\cdot\nabla_{p}\,. (B.2)

The spatial adjoint δπ≔∇x∗\delta_{\pi}\coloneqq\nabla_{x}^{*} in L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi) acts on a vector field FF by δπF=−∇x⋅F+⟨∇V,F⟩\delta_{\pi}F=-\nabla_{x}\cdot F+\langle\nabla V,F\rangle, and 𝒜x=δπ​∇x\mathcal{A}_{x}=\delta_{\pi}\nabla_{x}. Thus δx​F=δπ​F\delta_{x}F=\delta_{\pi}F when FF depends only on position; we retain δπ\delta_{\pi} for such fields. The operator 𝒜\mathcal{A} differs from the generator ℒ\mathcal{L}. In particular, 𝒜p\mathcal{A}_{p} is the negative of the momentum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator and acts as multiplication by nn on the nn-th Wiener chaos in pp; see Section E.2 for the normalized Hermite basis and this eigenvalue identity.

Let H˙1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{1}(\bm{\pi}) be the homogeneous Sobolev space given by completion of smooth functions modulo constants for the norm ∥D​φ∥2\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{2}. Its continuous dual is H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}), with norm

∥r∥H˙−1​(𝝅)≔sup∥D​φ∥2⩽1⟨r,φ⟩.\lVert r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\coloneqq\sup_{\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{2}\leqslant 1}\langle r,\varphi\rangle\,.

The Riesz representation theorem gives

∥r∥H˙−1​(𝝅)=∥𝒜−1/2r∥2=∥D𝒜−1r∥2=infδ𝝅​A=r∥A∥2.\lVert r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}=\lVert\mathcal{A}^{-1/2}r\rVert_{2}=\lVert D\mathcal{A}^{-1}r\rVert_{2}=\inf_{\delta_{\bm{\pi}}A=r}\,\lVert A\rVert_{2}\,. (B.3)

The minimizing field D​𝒜−1​rD\mathcal{A}^{-1}r is the orthogonal projection of any field AA satisfying δ𝝅​A=r\delta_{\bm{\pi}}A=r onto the closure of gradients; see [17, Theorem 1.3.20] and Section E.6.

Lemma B.1 (Short-time stability in H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1}).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for every r∈H˙−1​(𝛑)r\in\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}) and 0⩽t⩽10\leqslant t\leqslant 1,

∥et​ℒ†​r∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​∥r∥H˙−1​(𝝅).\lVert\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\,\lVert r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\,.

Moreover, (et​ℒ†)t≥0(\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}})_{t\geq 0} extends to a strongly continuous semigroup on H˙−1​(𝛑)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}).

Proof.

First let r≔δ𝝅​Ar\coloneqq\delta_{\bm{\pi}}A with AA smooth. Write (Φt​(z))t≥0(\Phi_{t}(z))_{t\geq 0} for the exact forward underdamped Langevin flow and Jt​(z)≔Dz​Φt​(z)J_{t}(z)\coloneqq D_{z}\Phi_{t}(z), with the Brownian path argument suppressed. Then,

D​et​ℒ​φ​(z)=𝔼⁡[Jt​(z)⊤​D​φ​(Φt​(z))].D\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}}\varphi(z)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[J_{t}(z)^{\top}D\varphi(\Phi_{t}(z))\bigr]\,.

The drift Jacobian has universally bounded operator norm because 0⪯∇2V⪯Id0\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq I_{d}, so ∥Jt∥op⩽eC​t\lVert J_{t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{Ct}. Jensen’s inequality and the bound on JtJ_{t} give

∥D​et​ℒ​φ∥L2​(𝝅)2≤e2​C​t​∥D​φ∥L2​(𝝅)2.\lVert D\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}}\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\leq\mathrm{e}^{2Ct}\,\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\,.

Duality immediately gives

∥et​ℒ†​r∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽eC​t​∥r∥H˙−1​(𝝅).\lVert\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{Ct}\,\lVert r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\,.

Divergences of smooth compactly supported vector fields are dense by (B.3). On these divergences, L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi})-strong continuity and Poincaré’s inequality imply strong continuity in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}). The displayed bound extends it to the completion. ∎

B.2 Conditional mean of the exact midpoint local error

As in Sections A.2 and A.3, we condition the quadrature error on the endpoint of a stationary exact step and separate its conditional mean from its centered fluctuation. The Gaussian derivative estimates in Lemma B.2 adapt the argument of Proposition A.6 to the underdamped dynamics: time reversal uses a momentum flip, and noise reaches the position through the momentum. The conditional mean will be controlled by the negative Sobolev estimate in Section B.3.

Let (Xt,Pt)0⩽t⩽h(X_{t},P_{t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} be a stationary underdamped Langevin process and put Zh≔(Xh,Ph)Z_{h}\coloneqq(X_{h},P_{h}). Applying midpoint quadrature to the integrals of ah−t∇V(Xt)a_{h-t}\nabla V(X_{t}) and e−2​(h−t)∇V(Xt)\mathrm{e}^{-2(h-t)}\nabla V(X_{t}) in the exact position and momentum formulas gives the midpoint local error ℰh\mathcal{E}_{h}, taken as numerical minus exact:

ℰhx\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{h}^{x} ≔∫0hah−t∇V(Xt)dt−hah/2∇V(Xh/2),\displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{0}^{h}a_{h-t}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-ha_{h/2}\nabla V(X_{h/2})\,, (B.4)
ℰhp\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{h}^{p} ≔∫0he−2​(h−t)∇V(Xt)dt−he−h∇V(Xh/2),\displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-2(h-t)}\nabla V(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t-h\mathrm{e}^{-h}\nabla V(X_{h/2})\,,
ℰh\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{h} ≔(ℰhx,ℰhp).\displaystyle\coloneqq(\mathcal{E}_{h}^{x},\mathcal{E}_{h}^{p})\,.

Decompose the local error into its conditional mean and centered fluctuation:

mh​(Zh)≔𝔼⁡[ℰh∣Zh],Rh≔ℰh−mh​(Zh).m_{h}(Z_{h})\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}_{h}\mid Z_{h}]\,,\qquad R_{h}\coloneqq\mathcal{E}_{h}-m_{h}(Z_{h})\,.

The numerical endpoint using the exact midpoint is Zh+mh​(Zh)+RhZ_{h}+m_{h}(Z_{h})+R_{h}. To describe the randomness in RhR_{h}, fix the endpoint Zh=z=(x,p)Z_{h}=z=(x,p). By stationarity, the conditional law of (Xh−t,Ph−t)0⩽t⩽h(X_{h-t},P_{h-t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h} is the diffusion generated by ℒ†\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}, started at zz. The formulas in (B.1) show that changing the sign of momentum transforms these reverse dynamics into the forward underdamped dynamics. Thus (Xh−t,−Ph−t)0⩽t⩽h(X_{h-t},-P_{h-t})_{0\leqslant t\leqslant h}, conditionally on Zh=zZ_{h}=z, has the law of the forward diffusion started at (x,−p)(x,-p).

We can therefore construct this conditional path on canonical Wiener space by solving the forward SDE from (x,−p)(x,-p), driven by a fresh standard Brownian motion B~\widetilde{B}, and then undoing the momentum flip. Sampling Zh∼𝝅Z_{h}\sim\bm{\pi} independently of B~\widetilde{B} gives the required joint law of the endpoint and the reversed path. Represent this Brownian noise by the isonormal Gaussian process

ℋ≔L2​([0,h],ℝd),G⁡(f)≔∫0h⟨fs,d​B~s⟩,f∈ℋ.\mathcal{H}\coloneqq L^{2}([0,h];\mathbb{R}^{d})\,,\qquad G(f)\coloneqq\int_{0}^{h}\langle f_{s},\mathrm{d}\widetilde{B}_{s}\rangle\,,\qquad f\in\mathcal{H}\,.

Write Ω\Omega for the probability space carrying the independent pair (Zh,G)(Z_{h},G); see Section E.2 for the Gaussian differentiation conventions.

Substituting the reconstructed positions into (B.4) makes ℰh\mathcal{E}_{h} a function of (Zh,G)(Z_{h},G). Averaging over GG with Zh=zZ_{h}=z fixed gives mh​(z)m_{h}(z), so subtracting this average yields

Rh=Rh(Zh,G),𝔼G[Rh(z,G)]=0for 𝝅-almost every z,R_{h}=R_{h}(Z_{h},G)\,,\qquad\mathbb{E}_{G}[R_{h}(z,G)]=0\quad\text{for $\bm{\pi}$-almost every }z\,,

where 𝔼G\mathbb{E}_{G} denotes expectation over the Gaussian noise alone.

We collect the local estimates. Here DzD_{z} differentiates this realization with respect to the terminal state while holding GG fixed, and DGD_{G} is the Malliavin derivative with respect to GG while holding the terminal state fixed. In particular, DG​Rh=DG​ℰhD_{G}R_{h}=D_{G}\mathcal{E}_{h}, since mh​(Zh)m_{h}(Z_{h}) depends only on the terminal state. The operator and Hilbert–Schmidt norms below are those used in the unified displacement bound (B.11).

Lemma B.2 (Local differential estimates).

With Euclidean norms on phase space, there is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for every 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0},

∥mh∥2\displaystyle\lVert m_{h}\rVert_{2} ⩽C​d​h2,\displaystyle\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}\,, ∥Dz​mh∥L∞​(𝝅,op)\displaystyle\lVert D_{z}m_{h}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\bm{\pi};\mathrm{op})} ⩽C​h,\displaystyle\leqslant Ch\,, (B.5)
∥Dz​Rh∥L2​(Ω,HS)\displaystyle\lVert D_{z}R_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega;\mathrm{HS})} ⩽C​d​h,\displaystyle\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h\,, ∥DG​Rh∥L∞​(Ω,op)\displaystyle\lVert D_{G}R_{h}\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathrm{op})} ⩽C​h5/2,\displaystyle\leqslant Ch^{5/2}\,,

We next prove the terminal state derivative bounds for mhm_{h} and RhR_{h}, keeping GG fixed. Differentiating the SDE for (Xh−t,−Ph−t)(X_{h-t},-P_{h-t}) with respect to z=(x,p)z=(x,p) gives

The initial matrix comes from the starting point (x,−p)(x,-p) of the reversed path after the momentum flip. Since ∥∇2V∥op⩽1\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 1, the coefficient matrix in this variational equation has operator norm at most a universal constant. Grönwall’s inequality therefore gives, uniformly in zz and GG,

∥Dz​Xh−t∥op+∥Dz​Ph−t∥op⩽C​eC​t⩽C,0⩽t⩽h⩽h0⩽1.\lVert D_{z}X_{h-t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}+\lVert D_{z}P_{h-t}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant C\mathrm{e}^{Ct}\leqslant C\,,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant h\leqslant h_{0}\leqslant 1\,.

The chain rule then bounds Dz​[∇V​(Xh−t)]=∇2V​(Xh−t)​Dz​Xh−tD_{z}[\nabla V(X_{h-t})]=\nabla^{2}V(X_{h-t})D_{z}X_{h-t} in operator norm by CC. Applying this bound to each integral and midpoint term in (B.4), with tt denoting reverse time, yields

∥Dz​ℰhp∥op\displaystyle\lVert D_{z}\mathcal{E}_{h}^{p}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} ⩽C⁡(∫0he−2​t​dt+h​e−h)⩽C​h.\displaystyle\leqslant C\,\Bigl(\int_{0}^{h}\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\,\mathrm{d}t+h\mathrm{e}^{-h}\Bigr)\leqslant Ch\,.

Here we used at⩽ta_{t}\leqslant t and e−2​t⩽1\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\leqslant 1. Combining the two components gives ∥Dz​ℰh∥op⩽C​h\lVert D_{z}\mathcal{E}_{h}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant Ch. The uniform derivative bound and independence of GG from the terminal state justify differentiation under 𝔼G\mathbb{E}_{G}:

Dz​mh​(z)=𝔼G​[Dz​ℰh​(z,G)],Dz​Rh​(z,G)=Dz​ℰh​(z,G)−Dz​mh​(z).D_{z}m_{h}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{G}[D_{z}\mathcal{E}_{h}(z,G)]\,,\qquad D_{z}R_{h}(z,G)=D_{z}\mathcal{E}_{h}(z,G)-D_{z}m_{h}(z)\,.

ξ˙t=ηt,η˙t=−2​ηt−∇2V​(Xh−t)​ξt+2​ft,ξ0=η0=0.\dot{\xi}_{t}=\eta_{t}\,,\qquad\dot{\eta}_{t}=-2\eta_{t}-\nabla^{2}V(X_{h-t})\,\xi_{t}+2f_{t}\,,\qquad\xi_{0}=\eta_{0}=0\,.

B.3 H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1} estimate for the weighted divergence

We prove the weighted divergence bound for the conditional mean, ∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h3\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}. The extra power of hh comes from cancellation of the constant and linear terms under midpoint quadrature. We bound the quadrature remainder in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}) using only the bounded Hessian assumption.

The proof uses an auxiliary estimate on (ℒ†)2​ζ(\mathcal{L}^{\dagger})^{2}\zeta, where ζ⁡(x,p)≔⟨p,∇V​(x)⟩\zeta(x,p)\coloneqq\langle p,\nabla V(x)\rangle. This estimate controls the second-order semigroup term; we establish it first.

Lemma B.3 (Second action of the adjoint generator).

There is a universal C>0C>0 such that

∥(ℒ†)2​ζ∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d.\lVert(\mathcal{L}^{\dagger})^{2}\zeta\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,.
Proof.

We first bound the generator on functions with bounded momentum Hermite degree, then apply duality. Let Π⩽r\Pi_{\leqslant r} be the orthogonal projection onto momentum Hermite degrees at most r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}. Here the momentum Hermite basis HℓH_{\ell} is the normalized basis defined in Section E.2; the range of Π⩽r\Pi_{\leqslant r} is the span of Mℓ​(x)​Hℓ​(p)M_{\ell}(x)H_{\ell}(p) with |ℓ|⩽r\lvert\ell\rvert\leqslant r. With the component weighted divergences defined in Section B.1,

ℒ=δp​∇x−δx​∇p−2​𝒜p.\mathcal{L}=\delta_{p}\nabla_{x}-\delta_{x}\nabla_{p}-2\mathcal{A}_{p}\,.

For a smooth function ψ\psi of momentum degree at most rr, the weighted divergence estimate (E.5), in the Gaussian and spatial variables respectively, gives

∥δp​∇xψ∥L2​(𝝅)2\displaystyle\lVert\delta_{p}\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2} ⩽(r+1)​∥∇xψ∥L2​(𝝅)2,\displaystyle\leqslant(r+1)\,\lVert\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\,,
∥δx​∇pψ∥L2​(𝝅)2\displaystyle\lVert\delta_{x}\nabla_{p}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2} ⩽r​∥∇xψ∥L2​(𝝅)2+∥∇pψ∥L2​(𝝅)2,\displaystyle\leqslant r\,\lVert\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}+\lVert\nabla_{p}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\,,
∥𝒜p​ψ∥L2​(𝝅)2\displaystyle\lVert\mathcal{A}_{p}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2} ⩽r​∥∇pψ∥L2​(𝝅)2.\displaystyle\leqslant r\,\lVert\nabla_{p}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\,.

Indeed, the first two estimates use ∥∇p∇x​ψ∥L2​(𝝅)2⩽r​∥∇xψ∥L2​(𝝅)2\lVert\nabla_{p}\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}\leqslant r\,\lVert\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2}, and the last follows from 𝒜p​Hℓ=|ℓ|​Hℓ\mathcal{A}_{p}H_{\ell}=\lvert\ell\rvert H_{\ell}. Taking square roots, the triangle inequality bounds ∥ℒ​ψ∥L2​(𝝅)\lVert\mathcal{L}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})} by (r+1+r)​∥∇xψ∥L2​(𝝅)+(1+2​r)​∥∇pψ∥L2​(𝝅)(\sqrt{r+1}+\sqrt{r})\,\lVert\nabla_{x}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}+(1+2\sqrt{r})\,\lVert\nabla_{p}\psi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}. Since Π⩽r\Pi_{\leqslant r} contracts the full gradient seminorm,

∥ℒ​Π⩽r​φ∥L2​(𝝅)⩽C​r+1​∥D​φ∥L2​(𝝅),\lVert\mathcal{L}\Pi_{\leqslant r}\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{r+1}\,\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\,,

where CC is a universal constant. For f∈L2​(𝝅)f\in L^{2}(\bm{\pi}) of momentum degree at most rr, the generator changes the momentum degree by at most one. Consequently,

|⟨ℒ†f,φ⟩|\displaystyle\bigl\lvert\langle\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}f,\varphi\rangle\bigr\rvert =|⟨f,ℒ​Π⩽r+1​φ⟩L2​(𝝅)|⩽C​r+2​∥f∥L2​(𝝅)​∥D​φ∥L2​(𝝅).\displaystyle=\bigl\lvert\langle f,\mathcal{L}\Pi_{\leqslant r+1}\varphi\rangle_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\bigr\rvert\leqslant C\sqrt{r+2}\,\lVert f\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\,\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\,.

Thus, ∥ℒ†​f∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​r+2​∥f∥L2​(𝝅)\lVert\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}f\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{r+2}\,\lVert f\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}, with the left side interpreted distributionally. Apply this estimate with r=2r=2 and f≔ℒ†​ζf\coloneqq\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta. Direct calculation gives

ℒ†​ζ=−{⟨p,∇2V​p⟩−tr⁡(∇2V)}+δπ​(∇V)−2​ζ.\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta=-\bigl\{\langle p,\nabla^{2}V\,p\rangle-\operatorname{tr}(\nabla^{2}V)\bigr\}+\delta_{\pi}(\nabla V)-2\zeta\,. (B.7)

The three terms are Hermite polynomials in momentum of exact degrees 22, 00, and 11, so they are orthogonal. Gaussian moments, ∥∇V∥L2​(π)2⩽d\lVert\nabla V\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}\leqslant d, and (E.5) give

∥⟨p,∇2V​p⟩−tr⁡(∇2V)∥L2​(𝝅)2\displaystyle\lVert\langle p,\nabla^{2}V\,p\rangle-\operatorname{tr}(\nabla^{2}V)\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2} =2​∥∇2V∥L2​(π,HS)2⩽2​d,\displaystyle=2\,\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathrm{HS})}^{2}\leqslant 2d\,,
∥δπ​(∇V)∥L2​(π)2\displaystyle\lVert\delta_{\pi}(\nabla V)\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2} =∥∇2V∥L2​(π,HS)2+𝔼π⟨∇V,∇2V∇V⟩⩽2d,\displaystyle=\lVert\nabla^{2}V\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathrm{HS})}^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\langle\nabla V,\nabla^{2}V\,\nabla V\rangle\leqslant 2d\,,
∥ζ∥L2​(𝝅)2\displaystyle\lVert\zeta\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}^{2} =∥∇V∥L2​(π)2⩽d.\displaystyle=\lVert\nabla V\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}\leqslant d\,.

It follows that ∥f∥L2​(𝝅)⩽C​d\lVert f\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}, which proves the lemma by the dual estimate. Approximation of the spatial coefficients of ff in L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi), keeping their momentum degrees fixed, extends that estimate to the present C2C^{2} potential. ∎

By (B.5), the conditional mean satisfies ∥mh∥L2​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h2\lVert m_{h}\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{2}. The following proposition gains an additional power of hh when bounding its weighted divergence in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}).

Proposition B.4 (H˙−1\dot{H}^{-1} estimate for the weighted divergence).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for every 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0},

∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​h3.\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}\,.
Proof.

We express δ𝝅​mh\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h} as a midpoint quadrature error and separate the adjoint semigroup contribution from a remainder. From (B.6),

δ𝝅​mh=∫0hψt​𝑑t−h​ψh/2,ψt≔at​δx​gt+e−2​t​δp​gt.\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}=\int_{0}^{h}\psi_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t-h\psi_{h/2}\,,\qquad\psi_{t}\coloneqq a_{t}\delta_{x}g_{t}+\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\delta_{p}g_{t}\,. (B.8)

The commutator identities

δx​ℒ†​F−ℒ†​δx​F\displaystyle\delta_{x}\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}F-\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\delta_{x}F =δp​(∇2V​F),δp​ℒ†​F−ℒ†​δp​F=−δx​F+2​δp​F\displaystyle=\delta_{p}(\nabla^{2}V\,F)\,,\qquad\delta_{p}\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}F-\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\delta_{p}F=-\delta_{x}F+2\delta_{p}F

involve only ∇2V\nabla^{2}V. Combining them with a˙t=e−2​t\dot{a}_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{-2t}, dd​t​e−2​t=−2​e−2​t\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{e}^{-2t}=-2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}, and g˙t=ℒ†​gt\dot{g}_{t}=\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}g_{t} gives

ψ˙t−ℒ†​ψt=at​δp​(∇2V​gt),ψ0=ζ.\dot{\psi}_{t}-\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\psi_{t}=a_{t}\delta_{p}(\nabla^{2}V\,g_{t})\,,\qquad\psi_{0}=\zeta\,.

Hence, in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}),

ψt=et​ℒ†​ζ+ℛt,ℛt≔∫0te(t−s)​ℒ†​{as​δp​(∇2V​gs)}​𝑑s.\psi_{t}=\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}\zeta+\mathcal{R}_{t}\,,\qquad\mathcal{R}_{t}\coloneqq\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{e}^{(t-s)\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}\bigl\{a_{s}\delta_{p}(\nabla^{2}V\,g_{s})\bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}s\,.

Since δ𝝅​(0,∇2V​gs)=δp​(∇2V​gs)\delta_{\bm{\pi}}(0,\nabla^{2}V\,g_{s})=\delta_{p}(\nabla^{2}V\,g_{s}), (B.3) and the L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi}) contractivity of the adjoint semigroup give

∥δp​(∇2V​gs)∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽∥∇2V​gs∥L2​(𝝅)⩽∥gs∥L2​(𝝅)⩽∥∇V∥L2​(π)⩽d.\lVert\delta_{p}(\nabla^{2}V\,g_{s})\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant\lVert\nabla^{2}V\,g_{s}\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant\lVert g_{s}\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant\lVert\nabla V\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}\leqslant\sqrt{d}\,.

By Lemma B.1 and as⩽sa_{s}\leqslant s,

∥ℛt∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​t2.\lVert\mathcal{R}_{t}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,t^{2}\,.

Integrating the bound on ∥ℛt∥H˙−1​(𝝅)\lVert\mathcal{R}_{t}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})} over [0,h][0,h] and evaluating it at h/2h/2 gives

∥∫0hℛtdt−hℛh/2∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽Cdh3.\Bigl\lVert\int_{0}^{h}\mathcal{R}_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t-h\mathcal{R}_{h/2}\Bigr\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}\,.

It remains to bound the contribution of et​ℒ†​ζ\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}\zeta to δ𝝅​mh\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}. We use the second-order integral expansion in H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}):

et​ℒ†​ζ=ζ+t​ℒ†​ζ+∫0t(t−s)​es​ℒ†​(ℒ†)2​ζ​𝑑s.\mathrm{e}^{t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}\zeta=\zeta+t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta+\int_{0}^{t}(t-s)\mathrm{e}^{s\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}}(\mathcal{L}^{\dagger})^{2}\zeta\,\mathrm{d}s\,. (B.9)

To justify (B.9), first note that (B.7) can be written as

ℒ†​ζ=−{⟨p,∇2V​p⟩−tr⁡(∇2V)}+δπ​(∇V)−2​ζ.\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta=-\{\langle p,\nabla^{2}V\,p\rangle-\operatorname{tr}(\nabla^{2}V)\}+\delta_{\pi}(\nabla V)-2\zeta\,.

Gaussian moments and (E.5) give

∥δπ(∇V)∥L2​(π)2=𝔼πtr((∇2V)2)+𝔼π⟨∇V,∇2V∇V⟩⩽2d,∥ℒ†ζ∥L2​(𝝅)⩽Cd.\lVert\delta_{\pi}(\nabla V)\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\operatorname{tr}((\nabla^{2}V)^{2})+\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\langle\nabla V,\nabla^{2}V\nabla V\rangle\leqslant 2d\,,\qquad\lVert\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta\rVert_{L^{2}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,.

Lemma B.3 gives (ℒ†)2​ζ∈H˙−1​(𝝅)(\mathcal{L}^{\dagger})^{2}\zeta\in\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}). Testing against a smooth function in the generator core and integrating the weak generator identity twice proves the expansion. The flow derivative bound in the proof of Lemma B.1 controls the gradient of the forward semigroup in these pairings; approximation in the generator core extends the identity to H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}).

The bound on ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}, (B.9), and Lemmas B.1 and B.3 give the affine approximation

∥ψt−ζ−t​ℒ†​ζ∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​t2,0⩽t⩽h.\lVert\psi_{t}-\zeta-t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,t^{2}\,,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant h\,. (B.10)

The midpoint rule is exact on the affine function t↦ζ+t​ℒ†​ζt\mapsto\zeta+t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta, so subtracting this function from both the integrand and the midpoint evaluation in (B.8) leaves the error unchanged:

δ𝝅​mh=\displaystyle\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}={} ∫0h(ψt−ζ−t​ℒ†​ζ)​dt−h⁡(ψh/2−ζ−h2​ℒ†​ζ).\displaystyle\int_{0}^{h}\bigl(\psi_{t}-\zeta-t\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t-h\bigl(\psi_{h/2}-\zeta-\tfrac{h}{2}\mathcal{L}^{\dagger}\zeta\bigr)\,.

Applying (B.10) to these two remainders and using the triangle inequality gives

∥δ𝝅​mh∥H˙−1​(𝝅)⩽C​d​(∫0ht2​𝑑t+h​(h/2)2)⩽C​d​h3.∎\lVert\delta_{\bm{\pi}}m_{h}\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi})}\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,\Bigl(\int_{0}^{h}t^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t+h\,(h/2)^{2}\Bigr)\leqslant C\sqrt{d}\,h^{3}\,.\qed

B.4 Transport bounds for the conditional mean and fluctuation

We convert the conditional mean cancellation and centered fluctuation bounds into transport bounds. We first remove a divergence-free field, which keeps only the part of the mean that moves the distribution; the remaining terms are products of the local error and its derivatives. The following lemma extends the Gaussian transport estimate of [10, Lemma 4.11] to a non-Gaussian base distribution.

For a base distribution μ\mu on ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q}, write DD for the gradient and δμ\delta_{\mu} for its L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) adjoint. Define H˙−1​(μ)\dot{H}^{-1}(\mu) by duality against the gradient seminorm ∥D​φ∥L2​(μ)\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{L^{2}(\mu)}, as in Section B.1 for H˙−1​(𝝅)\dot{H}^{-1}(\bm{\pi}).

Lemma B.5 (Transport bound for a random displacement).

Let μ∈𝒫2​(ℝq)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{q}) have density proportional to e−𝒱μ\mathrm{e}^{-\mathcal{V}_{\mu}}, where 𝒱μ∈C2​(ℝq)\mathcal{V}_{\mu}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{q}) and ∇2𝒱μ⪯Λ​Iq\nabla^{2}\mathcal{V}_{\mu}\preceq\Lambda I_{q} for some Λ>0\Lambda>0. On a probability space Ω\Omega, let Y∼μY\sim\mu and let GG be an independent isonormal Gaussian process with separable Cameron–Martin space ℋ\mathcal{H}. Let U⁡(Y,G)∈L2​(Ω,ℝq)U(Y,G)\in L^{2}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^{q}) be weakly differentiable in YY and Malliavin-differentiable in GG, with DY​U,DG​U∈L∞​(Ω,op)D_{Y}U,D_{G}U\in L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathrm{op}). Each derivative holds the other variable fixed, and norms over Ω\Omega include both variables. Define m⁡(Y)≔𝔼⁡[U∣Y]m(Y)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[U\mid Y] and R≔U−m⁡(Y)R\coloneqq U-m(Y). Then,

W2​(Law⁡(Y+U),μ)\displaystyle W_{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(Y+U),\mu\bigr) ⩽∥δμ​m∥H˙−1​(μ)+12​∥DY​U∥L∞​(Ω,op)​∥U∥L2​(Ω)\displaystyle\leqslant\lVert\delta_{\mu}m\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\mu)}+\frac{1}{2}\,\lVert D_{Y}U\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathrm{op})}\,\lVert U\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)} (B.11)
+12​∥DG​U∥L∞​(Ω,op)​(∥DY​R∥L2​(Ω,HS)2+Λ​∥R∥L2​(Ω)2)1/2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\,\lVert D_{G}U\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathrm{op})}\,\bigl(\lVert D_{Y}R\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega;\mathrm{HS})}^{2}+\Lambda\,\lVert R\rVert_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}\,.

Thus, the product field (U−w,F)(U-w,F) has zero weighted divergence:

The range h⩽cκ−1/4h\leqslant c\kappa^{-1/4} cannot be improved in general: when the averaged Hessians at the initial and predictor positions do not commute, the exponential midpoint kernel can expand W2,MW_{2,M} by a term of order h5h^{5}. Appendix C Proofs of the deterministic lower bounds

This appendix proves the deterministic quadrature lower bounds in Section 5, which are separated into the three theorems in that section (overdamped with κ=O⁡(1)\kappa=O(1), κ≫1\kappa\gg 1 respectively, and the underdamped case).

  1. 1.

    κ=O⁡(1)\kappa=O(1) lower bound. Recall that in this construction, we have a quadratic potential perturbed by an oscillation of amplitude hh and wavelength h\sqrt{h}. This yields a high-frequency error, which is captured by Lemma C.1. This lemma computes the expectation change of hcos(⋅/h)\sqrt{h}\cos(\cdot/\sqrt{h}) after one Heun update started from the target. Invariance and contractivity turn this change into the stationary h3/2h^{3/2} lower bound in Section C.1.3.

  2. 2.

    Coupling to a weakly confined coordinate. Generalizing the above to the κ≫1\kappa\gg 1 case, we consider, in addition to the oscillatory coordinates, an additional coordinate with small curvature, coupled to the others. Lemma C.4 shows how the oscillation in the other coordinates shifts the mean of this final, weakly confined coordinate, which creates the leading discretization error. We leverage this phenomenon to prove Theorem 5.2 in Section C.2.2.

  3. 3.

    A Gaussian obstruction for exponential midpoint. Section C.3 performs some elementary calculations in the underdamped case to obtain the invariant covariance. Its position variance can be solved explicitly, and differs from the target’s by order h2h^{2}; the Gaussian Wasserstein formula then proves Proposition 5.3. This is generalized, via a simple anisotropic quadratic, to the case where κ≫1\kappa\gg 1.

For the application of these bounds to get iteration lower bounds in Corollary 6.3, the proof is deferred to Section D.7, which combines these bias estimates to obtain iteration lower bounds for some initialization.

C.1 Heun at bounded condition number

The oscillation wavelength h\sqrt{h} matches the Brownian displacement in one step, while its amplitude hh keeps the Hessian bounded. We compute the change of a Lipschitz observable in one update from the target; this avoids expanding the numerical invariant distribution. For a probability distribution μ\mu, write μ⁡(f)≔∫f​𝑑μ\mu(f)\coloneqq\int f\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

C.1.1 The expectation change in one update

The following lemma supplies the scalar stationary obstruction.

Lemma C.1 (Oscillatory expectation change for Heun).

Fix a numerical 0<a⋆<1/40<a_{\star}<1/4, and let

V⁡(x)≔x22+a⋆​h​cos⁡(x/h),π∝e−V,f⁡(x)≔h​cos⁡(x/h).V(x)\coloneqq\frac{x^{2}}{2}+a_{\star}h\cos(x/\sqrt{h})\,,\qquad\pi\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V}\,,\qquad f(x)\coloneqq\sqrt{h}\cos(x/\sqrt{h})\,.

W2​(μ,π)⩾12|π⁡(KhHeun​f−f)|⩾c​h3/2.W_{2}(\mu,\pi)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\,\bigl\lvert\pi(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}f-f)\bigr\rvert\geqslant ch^{3/2}\,.

Proof.

For fixed g=2​h​Gg=\sqrt{2h}\,G, put Eg​(x)≔x−h​V′​(x)+gE_{g}(x)\coloneqq x-hV^{\prime}(x)+g. The Heun update is {x+Eg​(Eg​(x))}/2\{x+E_{g}(E_{g}(x))\}/2. |π⁡(KhHeun​f−f)|=|(π−μ)​(KhHeun​f−f)|⩽2​W2​(μ,π).\lvert\pi(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}f-f)\rvert=\lvert(\pi-\mu)(K_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}f-f)\rvert\leqslant 2W_{2}(\mu,\pi)\,.

θ≔Z/h,U≔(AhHeun​Z+σhHeun​G)/h,W≔((1−h)​Z+2​h​G)/h.\theta\coloneqq Z/\sqrt{h}\,,\qquad U\coloneqq(A_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}Z+\sigma_{h}^{\mathrm{Heun}}G)/\sqrt{h}\,,\qquad W\coloneqq((1-h)\,Z+\sqrt{2h}\,G)/\sqrt{h}\,.

𝔼e−a⋆​h​cos⁡θ=1−a⋆he−1/(2h)+O(h2)=1+O(h2).\mathbb{E}\mathrm{e}^{-a_{\star}h\cos\theta}=1-a_{\star}h\mathrm{e}^{-1/(2h)}+O(h^{2})=1+O(h^{2})\,.

On a purely Gaussian target, the same affine recursion has only an h2h^{2} bias. This explains why the oscillatory perturbation is needed for the larger h3/2h^{3/2} Heun lower bound.

Proposition C.2 (Gaussian lower bound for Heun).

For every d⩾1d\geqslant 1 and 0<h⩽h00<h\leqslant h_{0}, Heun on V=∥⋅∥2/2V=\lVert\cdot\rVert^{2}/2 has a unique invariant distribution with finite second moment, and

C.2 The condition number dependence for Heun

We use blocks with mm coordinates x∈ℝmx\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and one coordinate y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, where m​h⩽1mh\leqslant 1. We take ℓ2≔h/τ\ell^{2}\coloneqq h/\tau, with a fixed numerical τ\tau chosen large enough, and use θ≔x/ℓ\theta\coloneqq x/\ell, η≔y/K\eta\coloneqq y/\sqrt{K}.

C.2.1 A modulated block and its stationary mean

We first record the stationary expansion used for the moment estimates.

Lemma C.3 (Stationary affine recursion with a bounded perturbation).

Let (Un,Gn,ξn)n∈ℤ(U_{n},G_{n},\xi_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{Z}} be jointly stationary, with Un,ξn∈ℝpU_{n},\xi_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, 𝔼​∥U0∥2<∞\mathbb{E}\lVert U_{0}\rVert^{2}<\infty, and independent Gn∼𝖭⁡(0,Ip)G_{n}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{p}). Suppose

Un+1=Λ​Un+Σ​Gn+ξn,Λ≔diag⁡(λ1,…,λp),Σ≔diag⁡(σ1,…,σp),U_{n+1}=\Lambda U_{n}+\Sigma G_{n}+\xi_{n}\,,\qquad\Lambda\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{p})\,,\quad\Sigma\coloneqq\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{p})\,,

where 0⩽λi<10\leqslant\lambda_{i}<1 and |ξn,i|⩽bi\lvert\xi_{n,i}\rvert\leqslant b_{i} almost surely for 1⩽i⩽p1\leqslant i\leqslant p. Then, for every 1⩽i⩽p1\leqslant i\leqslant p,

∥U0,i∥L2⩽|σi|1−λi2+bi1−λi.\lVert U_{0,i}\rVert_{L^{2}}\leqslant\frac{\lvert\sigma_{i}\rvert}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{i}^{2}}}+\frac{b_{i}}{1-\lambda_{i}}\,.
Proof.

For every integer N⩾1N\geqslant 1, iteration gives

U0=ΛN​U−N+∑j=0N−1Λj​Σ​G−1−j+∑j=0N−1Λj​ξ−1−j.U_{0}=\Lambda^{N}U_{-N}+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda^{j}\Sigma G_{-1-j}+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\Lambda^{j}\xi_{-1-j}\,.

For 1⩽i⩽p1\leqslant i\leqslant p, stationarity and independence give ∥λiN​U−N,i∥L2=λiN​∥U0,i∥L2→0\lVert\lambda_{i}^{N}U_{-N,i}\rVert_{L^{2}}=\lambda_{i}^{N}\,\lVert U_{0,i}\rVert_{L^{2}}\to 0. Also, ∑j=0∞λij​|ξ−1−j,i|⩽bi/(1−λi)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{i}^{j}\,\lvert\xi_{-1-j,i}\rvert\leqslant b_{i}/(1-\lambda_{i}) almost surely. The asserted bounds follow from the triangle inequality, by letting N→∞N\to\infty. ∎

Appendix D Proofs of the randomized lower bounds

This appendix proves Propositions 6.1 and 6.2 on the standard Gaussian target, then gives the common proof of the iteration lower bounds in Corollary 6.3. The stationary position vector has a scale-Gaussian decomposition S​Gd\sqrt{S}\,G_{d}, where SS is a random variable independent of the standard Gaussian GdG_{d}. Its conditional covariance solves a fixed-point equation derived from the update. Expanding this equation gives the variance and centered fourth moment of SS, which Lemma D.3 converts into a Wasserstein lower bound. We then obtain iteration lower bounds from initial distributions with controlled energy and Wasserstein gaps. The roadmap is as follows.

  1. 1.

    A common covariance calculation. Lemmas D.1 and D.2 give a scale-Gaussian decomposition of a stationary random vector and compute moments of its conditional covariance, assuming it satisfies a fixed point equation at stationarity.

  2. 2.

    From covariance moments to transport. Lemma D.3 converts the moments in the previous lemmas into the position lower bound c​min⁡{d​h3,d​h3}c\min\{dh^{3},\sqrt{dh^{3}}\}, using only the variance and centered fourth moment, via some Gaussian analysis.

  3. 3.

    The coefficients for each quadrature rule. Section D.3 computes scalar coefficients for RLMC and PLMC. The matrix calculations for RULMC and PULMC are in Sections D.4 and D.5. These are then combined with the previous results to give W2W_{2} bounds at stationarity.

  4. 4.

    From bias to iteration lower bounds. The common proof in Section D.7 combines the stationarity lower bounds with a particular choice of initialization, converting the error bounds into iteration lower bounds for all the methods.

All constants are independent of dd and, for the Poisson methods, of kk.

D.1 Scale-Gaussian decompositions from random linear recursions

A scale-Gaussian decomposition represents a random vector as an independent Gaussian multiplied by a random scalar or matrix. Conditional on this scale, the vector is Gaussian; its unconditional distribution need not be Gaussian. We first state the scalar case used for RLMC and PLMC.

Henceforth throughout this appendix, SS denotes a random conditional state covariance matrix, ss a scalar conditional position variance, and bars denote their expectations. Each algorithm has its own SS or ss.

Lemma D.1 (Scalar scale-Gaussian decomposition).

Let X+≔m​X+q​GdX^{+}\coloneqq mX+\sqrt{q}\,G_{d}, where q⩾0q\geqslant 0, the pair (m,q)(m,q) is fresh, and Gd∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)G_{d}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) is independent of (X,m,q)(X,m,q). If 𝔼​m8<1\mathbb{E}m^{8}<1 and 𝔼​q4<∞\mathbb{E}q^{4}<\infty, the unique invariant distribution in 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is Law⁡(s​Gd)\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt{s}\,G_{d}), with s⩾0s\geqslant 0 independent of GdG_{d}, and

s=dm2​s′+q,s′⟂(m,q),s′=ds.s\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}m^{2}s^{\prime}+q\,,\qquad s^{\prime}\perp(m,q)\,,\qquad s^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}s\,.

The moments satisfy

s¯≔𝔼​s=𝔼​q1−𝔼​m2,Var(s)=Var⁡(m2​s¯+q)1−𝔼​m4,𝔼|s−s¯|4⩽C​𝔼​|m2​s¯+q−s¯|4(1−𝔼​m8)2.\begin{split}\overline{s}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}s&=\frac{\mathbb{E}q}{1-\mathbb{E}m^{2}}\,,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(s)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(m^{2}\,\overline{s}+q)}{1-\mathbb{E}m^{4}}\,,\qquad\mathbb{E}\lvert s-\overline{s}\rvert^{4}\leqslant\frac{C\,\mathbb{E}\lvert m^{2}\,\overline{s}+q-\overline{s}\rvert^{4}}{(1-\sqrt{\mathbb{E}m^{8}})^{2}}\,.\end{split} (D.1)

This is the p=1p=1 case of the following matrix statement, with M=mM=m and Q=qQ=q.

D.2 Wasserstein distance for Gaussian scale perturbations

The next estimate compares a Gaussian scale mixture with the standard Gaussian target, without any assumption on the mean scale.

Lemma D.3 (Wasserstein lower bound for Gaussian scale perturbations).

Let XX have a scale-Gaussian decomposition X=ds​GdX\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sqrt{s}\,G_{d}, where s⩾0s\geqslant 0 is independent of Gd∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)G_{d}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}), with vs≔Var⁡(s)<∞v_{\sqrt{s}}\coloneqq\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{s})<\infty. Then,

W2​(Law⁡(X),𝖭⁡(0,Id))⩾c​min⁡{d​vs,d​vs}.W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(X),\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}))\geqslant c\min\{dv_{\sqrt{s}},\sqrt{dv_{\sqrt{s}}}\}\,.

In particular, if

vs≔Var⁡(s)∈(0,1],𝔼​|s−𝔼​s|4⩽C4​vs2,v_{s}\coloneqq\operatorname{Var}(s)\in(0,1]\,,\qquad\mathbb{E}\lvert s-\mathbb{E}s\rvert^{4}\leqslant C_{4}v_{s}^{2}\,,

then, with cC4>0c_{C_{4}}>0 depending only on C4C_{4},

W2​(Law⁡(X),𝖭⁡(0,Id))⩾cC4​min⁡{d​vs,d​vs}.W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(X),\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}))\geqslant c_{C_{4}}\min\{dv_{s},\sqrt{dv_{s}}\}\,. (D.5)
Proof.

Put ρd≔𝔼⁡∥Gd∥\rho_{d}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\lVert G_{d}\rVert, vd≔Var⁡(∥Gd∥)v_{d}\coloneqq\operatorname{Var}(\lVert G_{d}\rVert), b≔𝔼​sb\coloneqq\mathbb{E}\sqrt{s}, and δ≔W2​(Law⁡(s​Gd),𝖭⁡(0,Id))\delta\coloneqq W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt{s}\,G_{d}),\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d})). Gaussian Poincaré gives vd⩽1v_{d}\leqslant 1 [17, Theorem 2.2.9]; hence, ρd2=d−vd⩾d−1\rho_{d}^{2}=d-v_{d}\geqslant d-1 for d⩾2d\geqslant 2, while ρ12=2/π\rho_{1}^{2}=2/\uppi. The norm is 11-Lipschitz, so the differences of radial means and standard deviations give

ρd​|b−1|⩽δ,d​vs+b2​vd⩽vd+δ.\rho_{d}\,\lvert b-1\rvert\leqslant\delta\,,\qquad\sqrt{dv_{\sqrt{s}}+b^{2}v_{d}}\leqslant\sqrt{v_{d}}+\delta\,.

Since b2⩾2​b−1⩾1−2​δ/ρdb^{2}\geqslant 2b-1\geqslant 1-2\delta/\rho_{d},

d​vs⩽δ2+2​(vd+vd/ρd)​δ⩽δ2+C​δ,dv_{\sqrt{s}}\leqslant\delta^{2}+2\,(\sqrt{v_{d}}+v_{d}/\rho_{d})\,\delta\leqslant\delta^{2}+C\delta\,,

which proves the first assertion.

For the second, let s¯≔𝔼​s\overline{s}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}s and let s′s^{\prime} be an independent copy. Hölder and Cauchy–Schwarz give

(𝔼​|s−s′|)2⩾(𝔼​|s−s′|2)3𝔼​|s−s′|4=8​vs32​𝔼​|s−s¯|4+6​vs2⩾4​vsC4+3,(𝔼​|s−s′|)2⩽𝔼​(s−s′)2​𝔼​(s+s′)2⩽8​s¯​Var⁡(s).\begin{split}(\mathbb{E}\lvert s-s^{\prime}\rvert)^{2}&\geqslant\frac{(\mathbb{E}\lvert s-s^{\prime}\rvert^{2})^{3}}{\mathbb{E}\lvert s-s^{\prime}\rvert^{4}}=\frac{8v_{s}^{3}}{2\,\mathbb{E}\lvert s-\overline{s}\rvert^{4}+6v_{s}^{2}}\geqslant\frac{4v_{s}}{C_{4}+3}\,,\\ (\mathbb{E}\lvert s-s^{\prime}\rvert)^{2}&\leqslant\mathbb{E}(\sqrt{s}-\sqrt{s^{\prime}})^{2}\,\mathbb{E}(\sqrt{s}+\sqrt{s^{\prime}})^{2}\leqslant 8\,\overline{s}\,\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{s})\,.\end{split}

If s¯⩽2\overline{s}\leqslant 2, then Var⁡(s)⩾vs/(4​(C4+3))\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{s})\geqslant v_{s}/(4\,(C_{4}+3)), and the first assertion applies. If s¯>2\overline{s}>2, reverse Minkowski’s inequality gives

W2​(Law⁡(s​Gd),𝖭⁡(0,Id))⩾d​(s¯−1)⩾(2−1)​d⩾(2−1)​min⁡{d​vs,d​vs},W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\sqrt{s}G_{d}),\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}))\geqslant\sqrt{d}\,(\sqrt{\overline{s}}-1)\geqslant(\sqrt{2}-1)\sqrt{d}\geqslant(\sqrt{2}-1)\min\{dv_{s},\sqrt{dv_{s}}\}\,,

since vs⩽1v_{s}\leqslant 1. ∎

For PLMC, the calculation reduces to the variance of a weighted Bernoulli sum; all required moments are uniform in k⩾2k\geqslant 2.

D.3.3 Stationary bias

The scale estimates give the randomized stationary bounds immediately. Their common conversion to iteration lower bounds is in Section D.7.

Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Apply Propositions D.4 and D.5 in dimension dd. They give existence, uniqueness, finite second moments, and (6.1)–(6.2), with constants uniform in kk. A fixed sufficiently small stationary accuracy forces h≲d−1/3h\lesssim d^{-1/3} for RLMC and PLMC with k⩾2k\geqslant 2, and h≲d−1/2h\lesssim d^{-1/2} for PLMC with k=1k=1. ∎

Γ~j≔h3​σ2​∫0j​het​F​v​v⊤​et​F⊤​𝑑t\widetilde{\Gamma}_{j}\coloneqq h^{3}\sigma^{2}\int_{0}^{jh}\mathrm{e}^{tF}vv^{\top}\mathrm{e}^{tF^{\top}}\,\mathrm{d}t

satisfy the same recursion with a residual O⁡(h5)O(h^{5}): stability of FF gives Γ~j=O⁡(h3)\widetilde{\Gamma}_{j}=O(h^{3}) uniformly, so the O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) difference between 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the exact covariance flow contributes only O⁡(h5)O(h^{5}). For the fourth moment, the finite expansion

∥Rn∥L42⩽C​∑j=0n−1e−c⁡(n−1−j)​h​∥𝔡j∥L42⩽C​h3.\lVert R_{n}\rVert_{L^{4}}^{2}\leqslant C\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathrm{e}^{-c(n-1-j)h}\,\lVert\mathfrak{d}_{j}\rVert_{L^{4}}^{2}\leqslant Ch^{3}\,.

For PULMC with k=1k=1, the deterministic covariance defect computed in Lemma D.7 is Ψj​(I2)−I2=h2​e2​e2⊤+O⁡(h3)\Psi_{j}(I_{2})-I_{2}=h^{2}e_{2}e_{2}^{\top}+O(h^{3}), and Mj=I2+h​A+O⁡(h2)M_{j}=I_{2}+hA+O(h^{2}). The same comparison of recursions, now for Sn−I2S_{n}-I_{2}, gives

uniformly in nn. Since e1⊤​et​A​e2=t​e−te_{1}^{\top}\mathrm{e}^{tA}e_{2}=t\mathrm{e}^{-t}, its position entry is the asserted formula. ∎

D.7 From bias to iteration lower bounds

The idea of the following proof is that the displaced final coordinate forces the elapsed time N​hNh to exceed a universal constant τ\tau before the accuracy can be reached. The remaining coordinates start at, or close to, numerical stationarity; their bias, quantified in the preceding results, then forces hh to be small. The underdamped case requires more work, since P0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) is independent of X0X_{0} and the initial distribution is therefore not numerically stationary, but the principle is the same.

Proof of Corollary 6.3.

We first prove the bounds at bounded condition number. For each overdamped method, let μh\mu_{h} be the numerical invariant distribution of its first d−1d-1 coordinates. Use the position starts

Law⁡(X0)={μh⊗δ1,Heun, RLMC, and PLMC,δed,exponential midpoint,𝖭⁡(ed,Id),RULMC and PULMC.\operatorname{Law}(X_{0})=\begin{cases}\mu_{h}\otimes\delta_{1}\,,&\text{Heun, RLMC, and PLMC}\,,\\ \delta_{e_{d}}\,,&\text{exponential midpoint}\,,\\ \mathsf{N}(e_{d},I_{d})\,,&\text{RULMC and PULMC}\,.\end{cases}

For every underdamped method take P0∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P_{0}\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) independently of X0X_{0}, and make every initialization independent of future innovations. All the targets are centered, and α≍1\alpha\asymp 1, so normalized and unnormalized accuracy differ only by universal constants.

A common lower bound on elapsed time. For any algorithm, let M¯h\overline{M}_{h} denote the expected one-step coefficient of the final coordinate: in the overdamped case, the mean of the scalar coefficient multiplying the current dd-th position; in the underdamped case, the mean of the 2×22\times 2 state matrix acting on the ddth position–momentum pair. For Heun and RLMC it is 1−h+h2/21-h+h^{2}/2; for PLMC it is 1−h+(k−1)​h2/(2​k)1-h+(k-1)h^{2}/(2k). |𝔼​XN,d−1|⩽∥M¯hN−I∥⩽(1+C​h)N−1⩽eC​N​h−1.\lvert\mathbb{E}X_{N,d}-1\rvert\leqslant\lVert\overline{M}_{h}^{N}-I\rVert\leqslant(1+Ch)^{N}-1\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{CNh}-1\,.
