Appendix E Analytic background and notation

This appendix records the conventions needed for the upper bounds. For Wasserstein geometry, functional inequalities, and kinetic contraction, we follow [17, Sections 1.3, 2.2, and 5.3]. For Gaussian differentiation and heat interpolation, the closest reference is [10, Appendix C]. We recall the formulas used here, including motivation for the Witten semigroup representation; for the other standard proofs, we refer to these references and the monographs cited below.

The tools enter the upper bounds in three groups.

  1. 1.

    Derivative norms and Gaussian smoothing. Sections E.1, E.2 and E.3 recall Schatten norms, Gaussian differentiation, and Stein kernels. Together they turn bounds on derivatives of centered fluctuations into transport bounds in Appendices A and B.

  2. 2.

    Regularity of the overdamped corrector. Sections E.4 and E.5 explain the Witten semigroup and the interpolation and functional calculus used in Section A.4. The key identity passes a derivative through the scalar semigroup to the semigroup on vector fields.

  3. 3.

    The transport cost of the underdamped conditional mean. Section E.6 relates weighted divergence and negative Sobolev norms to Wasserstein transport. This explains why Section B.3 estimates the divergence of the conditional mean rather than only its size.

E.1 Schatten norms

For Schatten norms and their ideal and Hölder inequalities, see [49] for a general reference.

For a compact operator AA with singular values (σj)j⩾1(\sigma_{j})_{j\geqslant 1}, set

∥A∥𝔖p≔(∑j⩾1σjp)1/p,∥A∥𝔖∞≔∥A∥op.\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{p}}\coloneqq\Bigl(\sum_{j\geqslant 1}\sigma_{j}^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p}\,,\qquad\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}}\coloneqq\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\,.

Thus, 𝔖2\mathfrak{S}_{2} is the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. We use the ideal property and the Schatten Hölder inequality:

∥A​B∥𝔖p⩽∥A∥op​∥B∥𝔖p,∥A​B∗∥𝔖2⩽∥A∥𝔖4​∥B∥𝔖4.\lVert AB\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{p}}\leqslant\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\,\lVert B\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{p}}\,,\qquad\lVert AB^{*}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}\leqslant\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\,\lVert B\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\,.

The ideal inequality also holds with the two norms interchanged. In particular,

∥A∥𝔖4⩽∥A∥op1/2​∥A∥𝔖21/2.\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{4}}\leqslant\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}\,\lVert A\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}^{1/2}\,.

For an operator ℋ→ℝd\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, an operator norm bound of order one and a Hilbert–Schmidt bound of order d\sqrt{d} therefore give an 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4} bound of order d1/4d^{1/4}. Squaring the latter in the Stein kernel estimate gives the required d\sqrt{d} dependence.

E.2 Gaussian differentiation

For Gaussian differentiation and Wiener chaos, see [41, Chapter 1] for a general reference.

Let GG be an isonormal Gaussian process over a separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}: the random variables G⁡(f)G(f), f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H}, are jointly centered Gaussian, with covariance 𝔼⁡[G⁡(f)​G​(f′)]=⟨f,f′⟩ℋ\mathbb{E}[G(f)G(f^{\prime})]=\langle f,f^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. For Brownian noise on [0,h][0,h], we use

ℋ≔L2​([0,h],ℝd),G⁡(f)≔∫0h⟨fs,d​Bs⟩.\mathcal{H}\coloneqq L^{2}([0,h];\mathbb{R}^{d})\,,\qquad G(f)\coloneqq\int_{0}^{h}\langle f_{s},\mathrm{d}B_{s}\rangle\,.

A direction f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H} acts by the path shift B↦B+ε​∫0⋅fs​𝑑sB\mapsto B+\varepsilon\int_{0}^{\cdot}f_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s. The Malliavin derivative DG​FD_{G}F is the derivative along these shifts, initially defined for smooth cylindrical functionals and then closed in the Gaussian Sobolev spaces 𝔻1,p\mathbb{D}^{1,p}; see [41, 40]. For a vector-valued functional RR, it is an operator DG​R:ℋ→ℝdD_{G}R:\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}. Under our Hessian assumptions, differentiating the SDE gives the usual first variation equation. In the overdamped case,

DG​Xt​f=2​∫0tJt,s​fs​𝑑s,∂tJt,s=−∇2V​(Xt)​Jt,s,Js,s=Id.D_{G}X_{t}f=\sqrt{2}\int_{0}^{t}J_{t,s}f_{s}\,\mathrm{d}s\,,\qquad\partial_{t}J_{t,s}=-\nabla^{2}V(X_{t})J_{t,s}\,,\quad J_{s,s}=I_{d}\,.

Convexity gives ∥Jt,s∥op⩽1\lVert J_{t,s}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant 1. Only first variations, and hence only the Hessian of VV, enter our Malliavin estimates.

Write ℒOU\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}} for the Gaussian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator and (𝒬t)t≥0(\mathcal{Q}_{t})_{t\geq 0} for its semigroup. The Mehler formula and derivative commutation are

𝒬t​F​(G)=𝔼′​F​(e−t​G+1−e−2​t​G′),DG​𝒬t​F=e−t​𝒬t​DG​F.\mathcal{Q}_{t}F(G)=\mathbb{E}^{\prime}F\bigl(\mathrm{e}^{-t}G+\sqrt{1-\mathrm{e}^{-2t}}\,G^{\prime}\bigr)\,,\qquad D_{G}\mathcal{Q}_{t}F=\mathrm{e}^{-t}\mathcal{Q}_{t}D_{G}F\,.

Here, G′G^{\prime} is an independent copy of GG. Conditional Jensen makes 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} a contraction also for vector and operator values, including in L4​(Ω,𝔖4)L^{4}(\Omega;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). On the nn-th Wiener chaos, −ℒOU-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}} acts as multiplication by nn. Its inverse is taken on centered functionals. The formula used in the Malliavin–Stein argument is

−DG​ℒOU−1​F=∫0∞e−t​𝒬t​DG​F​𝑑t.-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}F=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-t}\mathcal{Q}_{t}D_{G}F\,\mathrm{d}t\,. (E.1)

It follows by integrating the semigroup and commuting the derivative; the same identity holds for cylindrical approximations on Wiener space and passes to the limit by closability.

Normalized Hermite polynomials.

For P∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)P\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) and a multi-index ℓ∈ℕ0d\ell\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}, write |ℓ|≔∑i∈[d]ℓi\lvert\ell\rvert\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[d]}\ell_{i} and ℓ!≔∏i∈[d]ℓi!\ell!\coloneqq\prod_{i\in[d]}\ell_{i}!. The orthonormal Hermite basis is

Hℓ(p)≔∏i∈[d]Heℓi​(pi)ℓi!,𝔼[Hℓ(P)Hk(P)]=𝟏{ℓ=k},H_{\ell}(p)\coloneqq\prod_{i\in[d]}\frac{\mathrm{He}_{\ell_{i}}(p_{i})}{\sqrt{\ell_{i}!}}\,,\qquad\mathbb{E}[H_{\ell}(P)H_{k}(P)]=\mathbf{1}_{\{\ell=k\}}\,,

where the probabilists’ Hermite polynomials are defined by exp⁡(t​q−t2/2)=∑n∈ℕ0Hen​(q)​tn/n!\exp(tq-t^{2}/2)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}}\mathrm{He}_{n}(q)\,t^{n}/n!. In particular, He0=1\mathrm{He}_{0}=1, He1​(q)=q\mathrm{He}_{1}(q)=q, He2​(q)=q2−1\mathrm{He}_{2}(q)=q^{2}-1, and He3​(q)=q3−3​q\mathrm{He}_{3}(q)=q^{3}-3q. The nn-th momentum Wiener chaos means the span of the polynomials HℓH_{\ell} with |ℓ|=n\lvert\ell\rvert=n; different degrees are orthogonal.

These polynomials diagonalize the weighted Laplacian on phase space. Let π⁡(d​x)∝e−V⁡(x)​d​x\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x, let 𝝅≔π⊗𝖭⁡(0,Id)\bm{\pi}\coloneqq\pi\otimes\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}) on phase space ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} with coordinates (x,p)(x,p), and set

𝒜x≔−Δx+∇V⋅∇x,𝒜p≔−Δp+p⋅∇p,𝒜≔𝒜x+𝒜p.\mathcal{A}_{x}\coloneqq-\Delta_{x}+\nabla V\cdot\nabla_{x}\,,\qquad\mathcal{A}_{p}\coloneqq-\Delta_{p}+p\cdot\nabla_{p}\,,\qquad\mathcal{A}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}_{x}+\mathcal{A}_{p}\,.

Integration by parts gives ∫φ​𝒜​ψ​𝑑𝝅=∫(⟨∇xφ,∇xψ⟩+⟨∇pφ,∇pψ⟩)​𝑑𝝅\int\varphi\,\mathcal{A}\psi\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}=\int(\langle\nabla_{x}\varphi,\nabla_{x}\psi\rangle+\langle\nabla_{p}\varphi,\nabla_{p}\psi\rangle)\,\mathrm{d}\bm{\pi}, so 𝒜\mathcal{A} is non-negative and self-adjoint in L2​(𝝅)L^{2}(\bm{\pi}); these are the operators of (B.2). The operator 𝒜p\mathcal{A}_{p} is the negative of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator in the momentum variable pp, and 𝒜x\mathcal{A}_{x} is the weighted Laplacian of π\pi. The Hermite differential equation gives

𝒜p​Hℓ=|ℓ|​Hℓ.\mathcal{A}_{p}H_{\ell}=\lvert\ell\rvert H_{\ell}\,.

Consequently, if Mℓ:ℝd→ℝM_{\ell}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is a function of position alone, then

𝒜⁡(Mℓ​(x)​Hℓ​(p))=((𝒜x+|ℓ|)​Mℓ)​(x)​Hℓ​(p).\mathcal{A}\bigl(M_{\ell}(x)H_{\ell}(p)\bigr)=\bigl((\mathcal{A}_{x}+\lvert\ell\rvert)M_{\ell}\bigr)(x)\,H_{\ell}(p)\,.

Thus, 𝒜\mathcal{A} acts on the coefficient of HℓH_{\ell} through the shifted spatial operator 𝒜x+|ℓ|\mathcal{A}_{x}+\lvert\ell\rvert. The momentum degree projections therefore contract the full gradient seminorm, as used in Lemma B.3; see also [41].

E.3 Stein kernels and Gaussian convolution

For Malliavin–Stein theory and Gaussian convolution bounds, see [40, 43] for general references.

A Stein kernel of a centered vector R∈ℝdR\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a matrix-valued function τR\tau_{R} satisfying

𝔼⟨R,φ(R)⟩=𝔼tr{τR(R)∇φ(R)⊤}\mathbb{E}\langle R,\varphi(R)\rangle=\mathbb{E}\operatorname{tr}\bigl\{\tau_{R}(R)\nabla\varphi(R)^{\top}\bigr\}

for smooth test fields, with ∇φ=[∇φ1,…,∇φd]\nabla\varphi=[\nabla\varphi_{1},\ldots,\nabla\varphi_{d}] as in (A.14). This extends Gaussian integration by parts: if R∼𝖭⁡(0,Σ)R\sim\mathsf{N}(0,\Sigma), one can take τR=Σ\tau_{R}=\Sigma. For a centered Malliavin-differentiable functional, the standard construction is

τR​(R)=𝔼⁡[(DG​R)​(−DG​ℒOU−1​R)∗∣R];\tau_{R}(R)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(D_{G}R)(-D_{G}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OU}}^{-1}R)^{*}\mid R\bigr]\,;

see [40]. The Schatten inequalities and (E.1) give the quantitative bound used in Lemma A.4.

The relevance to discretization is a gain under Gaussian convolution. For independent R∼𝖭⁡(0,τ)R\sim\mathsf{N}(0,\tau) and G∼𝖭⁡(0,Id)G\sim\mathsf{N}(0,I_{d}), with σ>0\sigma>0,

W2​(Law⁡(R+σ​G),Law⁡(σ​G))=∥(σ2​Id+τ)1/2−σ​Id∥𝔖2⩽∥τ∥𝔖22​σ.W_{2}\bigl(\operatorname{Law}(R+\sigma G),\operatorname{Law}(\sigma G)\bigr)=\lVert(\sigma^{2}I_{d}+\tau)^{1/2}-\sigma I_{d}\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}\leqslant\frac{\lVert\tau\rVert_{\mathfrak{S}_{2}}}{2\sigma}\,.

The cost depends on the covariance, so it is quadratic in the size of RR. Lemma A.10, from [43], replaces the covariance by a Stein kernel. The direct interpolation proof in Lemma A.10 retains the sharp coefficient 1/(2​σ)1/(2\sigma) from the Gaussian example. For a perturbation that depends on the Gaussian variable, [10, Lemma 4.11] bounds the transport cost through products of its size and derivatives. Lemma B.5 extends this principle to a non-Gaussian base measure by removing a divergence-free field from the interpolation current.

E.4 The Witten Laplacian

For the Witten Laplacian and its relation to diffusion operators, see [29] for a general reference.

We explain the representation used in Section A.4. Throughout this subsection, assume α​I⪯∇2V⪯β​I\alpha I\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\beta I, as in the overdamped setting; the normalized bound in Appendix A takes α=κ−1\alpha=\kappa^{-1}.

Recall that Pt​f​(x)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(Xtx)]P_{t}f(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t}^{x})] and L​f=Δ​f−⟨∇V,∇f⟩Lf=\Delta f-\langle\nabla V,\nabla f\rangle, where XtxX_{t}^{x} is the Langevin diffusion started at xx. The Jacobian Jtx≔Dx​XtxJ_{t}^{x}\coloneqq D_{x}X_{t}^{x}, with entries (Jtx)i​j=∂xj(Xtx)i(J_{t}^{x})_{ij}=\partial_{x_{j}}(X_{t}^{x})_{i} for i,j∈[d]i,j\in[d], satisfies

∂tJtx=−∇2V​(Xtx)​Jtx,J0x=I.\partial_{t}J_{t}^{x}=-\nabla^{2}V(X_{t}^{x})J_{t}^{x}\,,\qquad J_{0}^{x}=I\,.

Differentiating under the expectation gives the chain rule identity

∇(Ptf)(x)=𝔼[(Jtx)⊤∇f(Xtx)].\nabla(P_{t}f)(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(J_{t}^{x})^{\top}\nabla f(X_{t}^{x})\bigr]\,.

This motivates averaging vector fields with the transposed Jacobian. Differentiating the drift in LL identifies the corresponding generator:

∇Lf=(L−∇2V)∇f,\nabla Lf=(L-\nabla^{2}V)\nabla f\,,

where LL acts componentwise and ∇2V\nabla^{2}V by matrix multiplication. We therefore define

L(1)≔L−∇2V,Pt(1)≔et​L(1).L^{(1)}\coloneqq L-\nabla^{2}V\,,\qquad P_{t}^{(1)}\coloneqq\mathrm{e}^{tL^{(1)}}\,.

Equivalently, u⁡(t,x)≔(Pt(1)​M)​(x)u(t,x)\coloneqq(P_{t}^{(1)}M)(x) solves

∂tu=L​u−∇2V​u,u⁡(0,x)=M⁡(x).\partial_{t}u=Lu-\nabla^{2}V\,u\,,\qquad u(0,x)=M(x)\,.

For M=∇fM=\nabla f, this is exactly the equation obtained by spatially differentiating ∂tPt​f=L​Pt​f\partial_{t}P_{t}f=LP_{t}f. Thus ∇Ptf=Pt(1)∇f\nabla P_{t}f=P_{t}^{(1)}\nabla f. A 11-form in Euclidean coordinates is a column vector, and −L(1)-L^{(1)} is the Witten Laplacian on 11-forms. For matrix fields MM, these operators act on each column separately.

The chain rule motivates the representation for gradient fields. For arbitrary bounded 11-forms, the Feynman–Kac representation is given in [31, Proposition 3.2, equation (3.2)]; applying it to each column gives, for bounded matrix fields MM,

(Pt(1)​M)​(x)=𝔼⁡[(Jtx)⊤​M​(Xtx)].(P_{t}^{(1)}M)(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(J_{t}^{x})^{\top}M(X_{t}^{x})\bigr]\,. (E.2)

In Euclidean space, the deformed parallel transport in that reference is JtxJ_{t}^{x}, since its defining equation reduces to the Jacobian equation above.

The Jacobian equation also gives the contraction used in Lemma A.7. For v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the lower Hessian bound gives

dd​t​∥Jtx​v∥2=−2​⟨Jtx​v,∇2V​(Xtx)​Jtx​v⟩⩽−2​α​∥Jtx​v∥2,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\lVert J_{t}^{x}v\rVert^{2}=-2\,\langle J_{t}^{x}v,\nabla^{2}V(X_{t}^{x})J_{t}^{x}v\rangle\leqslant-2\alpha\,\lVert J_{t}^{x}v\rVert^{2}\,,

so ∥Jtx∥op⩽e−α​t\lVert J_{t}^{x}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leqslant\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}. Thus, (E.2) combines averaging along the Langevin diffusion with a contracting matrix factor. Lemma A.7 makes this observation quantitative in the normalized setting of Appendix A and extends the representation to M∈Lp​(π,𝔖p)M\in L^{p}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{p}), for π\pi-almost every starting point.

E.5 Interpolation and the sectorial calculus

For complex interpolation and sectorial functional calculus, see [5, 27] for general references.

The spectral theorem bounds multipliers on L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}). To obtain the L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) bound needed for the Stein kernel, we use complex interpolation:

[L∞​(π,𝔖∞),L2​(π,𝔖2)]1/2=L4​(π,𝔖4)[L^{\infty}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{\infty}),L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})]_{1/2}=L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4})

with equal norms. The complex interpolation method [5] and Stein’s theorem for analytic operator families [51] transfer the endpoint semigroup estimates to complex times on this intermediate space.

Why a functional calculus is needed.

The proof of Lemma A.5 writes the corrector gradient as a function of the Witten Laplacian, ∇χ=h​r​(−h​L(1))​∇2V\nabla\chi=h\,r(-hL^{(1)})\,\nabla^{2}V, and requires a bound on r⁡(−h​L(1))r(-hL^{(1)}) on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) that is uniform in hh. On L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}), the operator −L(1)-L^{(1)} is non-negative and self-adjoint (Lemma A.7), and the spectral theorem gives directly

∥r⁡(−h​L(1))∥L2​(π,𝔖2)→L2​(π,𝔖2)⩽supλ⩾0|r⁡(λ)|.\lVert r(-hL^{(1)})\rVert_{L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})\to L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2})}\leqslant\sup_{\lambda\geqslant 0}\,\lvert r(\lambda)\rvert\,.

The space L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) is not a Hilbert space, so there is no spectral theorem there. The sectorial calculus replaces the spectral theorem by the Cauchy integral formula; its only input is a bound on the resolvent.

The Cauchy integral formula.

For 0<η<π0<\eta<\uppi, let Ση≔{z≠0:|arg⁡z|<η}\Sigma_{\eta}\coloneqq\{z\neq 0:\lvert\arg z\rvert<\eta\} be the open sector of half-angle η\eta around the positive real axis. Orient its boundary ∂Ση\partial\Sigma_{\eta} from ∞​e𝒊​η\infty\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\eta} to 00 and then to ∞​e−𝒊​η\infty\mathrm{e}^{-\bm{i}\eta}, so that Ση\Sigma_{\eta} lies to the left of the boundary. Let gg be holomorphic on a larger sector Σϑ\Sigma_{\vartheta}, ϑ>η\vartheta>\eta, with |g⁡(z)|⩽C​min⁡{|z|s,|z|−s}\lvert g(z)\rvert\leqslant C\min\{\lvert z\rvert^{s},\lvert z\rvert^{-s}\} for some s>0s>0. Cauchy’s formula gives, for every λ∈Ση\lambda\in\Sigma_{\eta},

g⁡(λ)=12​π​𝒊​∫∂Σηg⁡(z)z−λ​𝑑z.g(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\uppi\bm{i}}\int_{\partial\Sigma_{\eta}}\frac{g(z)}{z-\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}z\,.

Substituting a closed operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} on a Banach space 𝒳\mathcal{X} for λ\lambda turns 1/(z−λ)1/(z-\lambda) into the resolvent (z−𝒯)−1(z-\mathcal{T})^{-1} and suggests the definition

g⁡(𝒯)≔12​π​𝒊​∫∂Σηg⁡(z)​(z−𝒯)−1​𝑑z.g(\mathcal{T})\coloneqq\frac{1}{2\uppi\bm{i}}\int_{\partial\Sigma_{\eta}}g(z)\,(z-\mathcal{T})^{-1}\,\mathrm{d}z\,. (E.3)

This makes sense provided that the resolvent exists on ∂Ση\partial\Sigma_{\eta} and the integral converges; by Cauchy’s theorem, it does not depend on the choice of η\eta. For a non-negative self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space, (E.3) agrees with the spectral theorem, by applying the scalar formula inside the spectral integral.

Sectorial operators.

Convergence of (E.3) is guaranteed by the following resolvent condition. A closed operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} on a Banach space 𝒳\mathcal{X} is sectorial of angle ω∈[0,π)\omega\in[0,\uppi) if its spectrum lies in the closed sector Σω¯\overline{\Sigma_{\omega}}, and, for every ϑ∈(ω,π)\vartheta\in(\omega,\uppi),

Mϑ(𝒯)≔sup{|z|∥(z−𝒯)−1∥𝒳→𝒳:z≠0,|argz|⩾ϑ}<∞.M_{\vartheta}(\mathcal{T})\coloneqq\sup\bigl\{\lvert z\rvert\,\lVert(z-\mathcal{T})^{-1}\rVert_{\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}}:z\neq 0\,,\ \lvert\arg z\rvert\geqslant\vartheta\bigr\}<\infty\,.

The size 1/|z|1/\lvert z\rvert is that of the scalar resolvent 1/(z−λ)1/(z-\lambda) when zz and λ⩾0\lambda\geqslant 0 are separated by a fixed angle. Since (z−h​𝒯)−1=h−1​(z/h−𝒯)−1(z-h\mathcal{T})^{-1}=h^{-1}\,(z/h-\mathcal{T})^{-1}, the constants are invariant under scaling: Mϑ​(h​𝒯)=Mϑ​(𝒯)M_{\vartheta}(h\mathcal{T})=M_{\vartheta}(\mathcal{T}) for every h>0h>0. For example, on L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}), the resolvent norm of the self-adjoint operator −L(1)-L^{(1)} is the reciprocal of the distance from zz to its spectrum in [0,∞)[0,\infty), which is at least |z|​sin⁡ϑ\lvert z\rvert\sin\vartheta when |arg⁡z|⩾ϑ\lvert\arg z\rvert\geqslant\vartheta; so −L(1)-L^{(1)} is sectorial of angle 00 there. The angle π/4\uppi/4 obtained on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) in Lemma A.8 is worse, but any angle below π/2\uppi/2 suffices here: the multiplier rr has poles on the imaginary axis, so the contour must stay in the right half-plane.

From analytic semigroups to sectoriality.

We describe a standard equivalence used in the proof of Lemma A.8; see [27] for the general statement. The resolvent is the Laplace transform of the semigroup. If Re⁡w>0\operatorname{Re}w>0, contractivity of et​L(1)\mathrm{e}^{tL^{(1)}} on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) gives

(w−L(1))−1=∫0∞e−w​t​et​L(1)​𝑑t,∥(w−L(1))−1∥⩽1Re⁡w,(w-L^{(1)})^{-1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-wt}\,\mathrm{e}^{tL^{(1)}}\,\mathrm{d}t\,,\qquad\lVert(w-L^{(1)})^{-1}\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{\operatorname{Re}w}\,,

with operator norms on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}). With z=−wz=-w, this covers only Re⁡z<0\operatorname{Re}z<0, and the bound 1/Re⁡w1/\operatorname{Re}w degenerates near the imaginary axis. Analyticity lets us rotate the integration ray. By Lemma A.8, ζ↦eζ​L(1)\zeta\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{\zeta L^{(1)}} is holomorphic and contractive in |arg⁡ζ|<π/4\lvert\arg\zeta\rvert<\uppi/4. By Cauchy’s theorem, for |ϕ|<π/4\lvert\phi\rvert<\uppi/4 and Re⁡(w​e𝒊​ϕ)>0\operatorname{Re}(w\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\phi})>0,

(w−L(1))−1\displaystyle(w-L^{(1)})^{-1} =e𝒊​ϕ​∫0∞exp⁡(−w​e𝒊​ϕ​s)​exp⁡(s​e𝒊​ϕ​L(1))​ds,\displaystyle=\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\phi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-w\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\phi}s)\,\exp(s\mathrm{e}^{\bm{i}\phi}L^{(1)})\,\mathrm{d}s\,, (E.4)
∥(w−L(1))−1∥\displaystyle\lVert(w-L^{(1)})^{-1}\rVert ⩽1|w|​cos⁡(arg⁡w+ϕ).\displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{\lvert w\rvert\cos(\arg w+\phi)}\,.

Now fix ϑ∈(π/4,π/2)\vartheta\in(\uppi/4,\uppi/2) and let |arg⁡z|⩾ϑ\lvert\arg z\rvert\geqslant\vartheta, so that |arg⁡w|⩽π−ϑ\lvert\arg w\rvert\leqslant\uppi-\vartheta. Choose ϕ\phi with sign opposite to arg⁡w\arg w and |ϕ|=min⁡{|arg⁡w|,(3​π/4−ϑ)/2}\lvert\phi\rvert=\min\{\lvert\arg w\rvert,(3\uppi/4-\vartheta)/2\}. Then |arg⁡w+ϕ|⩽π/2−(ϑ−π/4)/2\lvert\arg w+\phi\rvert\leqslant\uppi/2-(\vartheta-\uppi/4)/2, and (E.4) gives

∥(z+L(1))−1∥⩽1sin⁡((ϑ−π/4)/2)​|z|.\lVert(z+L^{(1)})^{-1}\rVert\leqslant\frac{1}{\sin((\vartheta-\uppi/4)/2)\,\lvert z\rvert}\,.

In particular, every zz outside Σπ/4¯\overline{\Sigma_{\uppi/4}} lies in the resolvent set, so the spectrum of −L(1)-L^{(1)} lies in Σπ/4¯\overline{\Sigma_{\uppi/4}}, and the resolvent bound (A.25) holds with a constant depending only on ϑ\vartheta. In general, the negative of the generator of a bounded analytic semigroup on the sector |arg⁡ζ|<δ\lvert\arg\zeta\rvert<\delta is sectorial of angle π/2−δ\uppi/2-\delta, and the converse is also true.

The multiplier estimate.

The following estimate is standard. It is the elementary part of the holomorphic functional calculus for sectorial operators constructed in [27, Section 2.3], applied to functions that decay polynomially at zero and at infinity after subtracting a constant and a multiple of (1+z)−1(1+z)^{-1} (the extended Dunford–Riesz class). For completeness, we include the short proof, which also makes the uniformity under scaling explicit.

Lemma E.1 (Uniform multiplier bound for sectorial operators).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a closed operator on a Banach space 𝒳\mathcal{X} that is sectorial of angle ω∈[0,π)\omega\in[0,\uppi), and let ϑ∈(ω,π)\vartheta\in(\omega,\uppi). Let f:Σϑ→ℂf\colon\Sigma_{\vartheta}\to\mathbb{C} be holomorphic, and suppose that there are f⁡(0),f⁡(∞)∈ℂf(0),f(\infty)\in\mathbb{C} and constants Cf,s>0C_{f},s>0 such that, for z∈Σϑz\in\Sigma_{\vartheta},

|f⁡(z)−f⁡(0)|⩽Cf​|z|sif ​|z|⩽1,|f⁡(z)−f⁡(∞)|⩽Cf​|z|−sif ​|z|⩾1.\lvert f(z)-f(0)\rvert\leqslant C_{f}\,\lvert z\rvert^{s}\quad\text{if }\lvert z\rvert\leqslant 1\,,\qquad\lvert f(z)-f(\infty)\rvert\leqslant C_{f}\,\lvert z\rvert^{-s}\quad\text{if }\lvert z\rvert\geqslant 1\,.

For h>0h>0, define

f⁡(h​𝒯)≔f⁡(∞)​I+(f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞))​(I+h​𝒯)−1+g⁡(h​𝒯),g⁡(z)≔f⁡(z)−f⁡(∞)−f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞)1+z,f(h\mathcal{T})\coloneqq f(\infty)\,I+(f(0)-f(\infty))\,(I+h\mathcal{T})^{-1}+g(h\mathcal{T})\,,\quad g(z)\coloneqq f(z)-f(\infty)-\frac{f(0)-f(\infty)}{1+z}\,,

where g⁡(h​𝒯)g(h\mathcal{T}) is given by (E.3) with η≔(ω+ϑ)/2\eta\coloneqq(\omega+\vartheta)/2. Then,

suph>0∥f⁡(h​𝒯)∥𝒳→𝒳⩽|f⁡(∞)|+|f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞)|​Mη​(𝒯)+2​Cg​Mη​(𝒯)π​min⁡{s,1},Cg≔Cf+|f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞)|cos⁡(ϑ/2).\sup_{h>0}\,\lVert f(h\mathcal{T})\rVert_{\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}}\leqslant\lvert f(\infty)\rvert+\lvert f(0)-f(\infty)\rvert\,M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T})+\frac{2C_{g}M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T})}{\uppi\min\{s,1\}}\,,\quad C_{g}\coloneqq C_{f}+\frac{\lvert f(0)-f(\infty)\rvert}{\cos(\vartheta/2)}\,.
Proof.

First, gg decays at zero and at infinity. For z∈Σϑz\in\Sigma_{\vartheta},

|1+z|2=(1+|z|)2−4​|z|​sin2⁡arg⁡z2⩾cos2⁡ϑ2​(1+|z|)2,\lvert 1+z\rvert^{2}=(1+\lvert z\rvert)^{2}-4\,\lvert z\rvert\sin^{2}\frac{\arg z}{2}\geqslant\cos^{2}\frac{\vartheta}{2}\,(1+\lvert z\rvert)^{2}\,,

since 4​|z|⩽(1+|z|)24\,\lvert z\rvert\leqslant(1+\lvert z\rvert)^{2}. If |z|⩽1\lvert z\rvert\leqslant 1, write g⁡(z)=f⁡(z)−f⁡(0)+(f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞))​z/(1+z)g(z)=f(z)-f(0)+(f(0)-f(\infty))\,z/(1+z); if |z|⩾1\lvert z\rvert\geqslant 1, write g⁡(z)=f⁡(z)−f⁡(∞)−(f⁡(0)−f⁡(∞))/(1+z)g(z)=f(z)-f(\infty)-(f(0)-f(\infty))/(1+z). With the lower bound on |1+z|\lvert 1+z\rvert, both cases give

|g⁡(z)|⩽Cg​min⁡{|z|s′,|z|−s′},s′≔min⁡{s,1},z∈Σϑ.\lvert g(z)\rvert\leqslant C_{g}\min\{\lvert z\rvert^{s^{\prime}},\lvert z\rvert^{-s^{\prime}}\}\,,\qquad s^{\prime}\coloneqq\min\{s,1\}\,,\qquad z\in\Sigma_{\vartheta}\,.

Next, on the rays z=t​e±𝒊​ηz=t\mathrm{e}^{\pm\bm{i}\eta}, t>0t>0, of ∂Ση\partial\Sigma_{\eta}, scale invariance gives ∥(z−h​𝒯)−1∥⩽Mη​(h​𝒯)/t=Mη​(𝒯)/t\lVert(z-h\mathcal{T})^{-1}\rVert\leqslant M_{\eta}(h\mathcal{T})/t=M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T})/t. The integral in (E.3) therefore converges absolutely, and

∥g⁡(h​𝒯)∥⩽22​π​∫0∞Cg​min⁡{ts′,t−s′}​Mη​(𝒯)t​𝑑t=2​Cg​Mη​(𝒯)π​s′.\lVert g(h\mathcal{T})\rVert\leqslant\frac{2}{2\uppi}\int_{0}^{\infty}C_{g}\min\{t^{s^{\prime}},t^{-s^{\prime}}\}\,\frac{M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T})}{t}\,\mathrm{d}t=\frac{2C_{g}M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T})}{\uppi s^{\prime}}\,.

The decay of gg at zero compensates for the growth of the resolvent near the origin, and its decay at infinity makes the integral over the unbounded contour converge. Finally, (I+h​𝒯)−1=−(−1−h​𝒯)−1(I+h\mathcal{T})^{-1}=-(-1-h\mathcal{T})^{-1} is a resolvent at z=−1z=-1, where |arg⁡z|=π⩾η\lvert\arg z\rvert=\uppi\geqslant\eta, so its norm is at most Mη​(h​𝒯)=Mη​(𝒯)M_{\eta}(h\mathcal{T})=M_{\eta}(\mathcal{T}). The triangle inequality completes the proof. ∎

For 𝒯=−L(1)\mathcal{T}=-L^{(1)}, the resolvents on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) and L2​(π,𝔖2)L^{2}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{2}) are Laplace transforms of the same semigroup, so they agree on the intersection of the two spaces; hence so do the operators f⁡(−h​L(1))f(-hL^{(1)}) defined on either space. Lemma A.9 applies Lemma E.1 with 𝒯=−L(1)\mathcal{T}=-L^{(1)} on L4​(π,𝔖4)L^{4}(\pi;\mathfrak{S}_{4}) and f=rf=r.

E.6 Weighted divergence, negative Sobolev norms, and transport

For weighted differential operators and Wasserstein tangent norms, see [29] and [17, Section 1.3] for general references.

For π⁡(d​x)∝e−V⁡(x)​d​x\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}\,\mathrm{d}x, integration by parts gives ∂i∗=−∂i+∂iV\partial_{i}^{*}=-\partial_{i}+\partial_{i}V in L2​(π)L^{2}(\pi). If Ψ=(Ψ1,…,Ψd)\Psi=(\Psi_{1},\ldots,\Psi_{d}), with each Ψi\Psi_{i} valued in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space EE, the weighted divergence is

δπΨ≔∑j∈[d]∂j∗Ψj=∑j∈[d](−∂jΨj+(∂jV)Ψj).\delta_{\pi}\Psi\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[d]}\partial_{j}^{*}\Psi_{j}=\sum_{j\in[d]}\bigl(-\partial_{j}\Psi_{j}+(\partial_{j}V)\Psi_{j}\bigr)\,.

The Bochner–Witten identity used in Lemmas B.3 and B.5 is the following weighted integration by parts formula for smooth compactly supported fields:

∥δπ​Ψ∥22=∫∑i,j∈[d]⟨∂iΨj,∂jΨi⟩E​dπ+∫∑i,j∈[d](∂i∂jV)​⟨Ψi,Ψj⟩E​dπ.\begin{split}\lVert\delta_{\pi}\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}={}&\int\sum_{i,j\in[d]}\langle\partial_{i}\Psi_{j},\partial_{j}\Psi_{i}\rangle_{E}\,\mathrm{d}\pi+\int\sum_{i,j\in[d]}(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}V)\,\langle\Psi_{i},\Psi_{j}\rangle_{E}\,\mathrm{d}\pi\,.\end{split} (E.5)

Indeed, differentiating the weight term gives ∂i∂j∗=∂j∗∂i+∂i∂jV\partial_{i}\partial_{j}^{*}=\partial_{j}^{*}\partial_{i}+\partial_{i}\partial_{j}V. Applying the adjoint relation twice therefore yields

∥δπ​Ψ∥22=∑i∈[d]⟨Ψi,∂iδπ​Ψ⟩L2​(π,E)=∑i,j∈[d]⟨Ψi,∂j∗∂iΨj⟩L2​(π,E)+∫∑i,j∈[d](∂i∂jV)​⟨Ψi,Ψj⟩E​𝑑π=∑i,j∈[d]⟨∂jΨi,∂iΨj⟩L2​(π,E)+∫∑i,j∈[d](∂i∂jV)​⟨Ψi,Ψj⟩E​dπ.\begin{split}\lVert\delta_{\pi}\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}&=\sum_{i\in[d]}\langle\Psi_{i},\partial_{i}\delta_{\pi}\Psi\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi;E)}\\ &=\sum_{i,j\in[d]}\langle\Psi_{i},\partial_{j}^{*}\partial_{i}\Psi_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi;E)}+\int\sum_{i,j\in[d]}(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}V)\,\langle\Psi_{i},\Psi_{j}\rangle_{E}\,\mathrm{d}\pi\\ &=\sum_{i,j\in[d]}\langle\partial_{j}\Psi_{i},\partial_{i}\Psi_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi;E)}+\int\sum_{i,j\in[d]}(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}V)\,\langle\Psi_{i},\Psi_{j}\rangle_{E}\,\mathrm{d}\pi\,.\end{split}

The second integral is abbreviated as ∫⟨Ψ,∇2V​Ψ⟩E​𝑑π\int\langle\Psi,\nabla^{2}V\,\Psi\rangle_{E}\,\mathrm{d}\pi: the Hessian acts on the spatial indices. If ∇2V⪯β​I\nabla^{2}V\preceq\beta I, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the first sum by ∥∇xΨ∥22\lVert\nabla_{x}\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}, giving ∥δπ​Ψ∥22⩽∥∇xΨ∥22+β​∥Ψ∥22\lVert\delta_{\pi}\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}\leqslant\lVert\nabla_{x}\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}+\beta\,\lVert\Psi\rVert_{2}^{2}. Thus, the divergence is controlled using the bounded Hessian, even though its definition contains the possibly unbounded gradient of VV.

Let μ\mu have a positive density, let DD be the gradient, and let δμ≔D∗\delta_{\mu}\coloneqq D^{*} be its adjoint in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu). The homogeneous space H˙1​(μ)\dot{H}^{1}(\mu) is the completion of smooth functions modulo constants under ∥D​φ∥2\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{2}. For a continuous functional rr which is zero on constants, its dual norm has the minimum flux characterization

∥r∥H˙−1​(μ)=sup∥D​φ∥2⩽1⟨r,φ⟩=infδμ​A=r∥A∥2.\lVert r\rVert_{\dot{H}^{-1}(\mu)}=\sup_{\lVert D\varphi\rVert_{2}\leqslant 1}\langle r,\varphi\rangle=\inf_{\delta_{\mu}A=r}\,\lVert A\rVert_{2}\,.

The minimizing field belongs to the closure of gradients. This is the same orthogonal projection that identifies Wasserstein tangent vectors in [17, Theorem 1.3.20]: adding a divergence-free field leaves the continuity equation unchanged, whereas removing that field reduces the transport cost without changing the endpoints.
